knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A smooth equality system is full-row regular when its Jacobian rank equals the number of equations. It is constant-rank redundant when a lower rank persists locally, and rank-changing singular when the rank is not locally constant. These regimes determine the dimension of the linearized tangent space and whether constraint-generated normal coordinates can be unique.

knowledge_statements.title: Full-Row-Rank Equalities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regular-level-set consequence of linearly independent equality gradients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(c:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be continuously differentiable, let \(c(\bar x)=0\), and suppose \(J(\bar x)\) has row rank \(m\). Then there exists a neighborhood of \(\bar x\) in which the feasible level set \(F=c^{-1}(0)\) is an embedded \(C^1\) manifold of dimension \(n-m\). After a permutation of variables \(x=(u,v)\) with \(v\in\mathbb{R}^m\), there are neighborhoods and a \(C^1\) map \(v=\phi(u)\) that parameterizes all nearby feasible points uniquely. In particular, tangent dimension and normal dimension are locally \(n-m\) and \(m\), respectively.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Independent equality gradients yield a smooth feasible manifold and a local elimination of m variables as functions of the remaining variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Locally, \(F\) is a \(C^1\) manifold of dimension \(n-m\) admitting the graph representation \(v=\phi(u)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local Persistence and Quantitative Margin of Full Row Rank
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Openness and singular-value margin underlying stable local reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(c:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) be continuously differentiable near \(\bar x\), with \(m\le n\), and suppose \(J(\bar x)=Dc(\bar x)\) has row rank \(m\). Then \(\sigma_{\min}(J(\bar x))>0\). By continuity, there are a neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and \(\gamma>0\) such that \[\sigma_{\min}(J(x))\ge\gamma\quad(x\in U).\] Consequently, \(J(x)J(x)^{\mathsf T}\) is invertible throughout \(U\), the Jacobian retains row rank \(m\), and \[P_T(x)=I-J(x)^{\mathsf T}(J(x)J(x)^{\mathsf T})^{-1}J(x)\] is continuous on \(U\). This uniform guarantee can fail only as the smallest singular value approaches zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Full row rank persists locally with a positive smallest-singular-value margin, yielding a continuous tangent projector; singular-value collapse is the stability boundary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Locally \(\sigma_{\min}(J(x))\ge\gamma>0\), \(J(x)J(x)^{\mathsf T}\) is invertible, and \(P_T(x)\) is continuous.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
An equality system has full row rank at the specified point when \[\operatorname{rank}J=m.\] Equivalently, its row vectors are linearly independent, \(J\) is surjective onto \(\mathbb R^m\), \(JJ^T\) is symmetric positive definite, and \(J^T\) is injective. In this regime \[\dim\ker J=n-m,
\qquad \mathbb R^n=\ker J\oplus\operatorname{range}J^T,
\qquad J^{\dagger}=J^T(JJ^T)^{-1}.\] Hence normal coordinates \(J^Tunction{\lambda}\) are unique and every linearized residual equation \(Jp=r\) is solvable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matrix or constraint Jacobian has full row rank when its rank equals its number of rows. This is equivalent to independent constraint gradients, surjectivity, positive definiteness of \(JJ^T\), and injectivity of \(J^T\). The null space then has dimension \(n-m\), the full-row-rank pseudoinverse is \(J^T(JJ^T)^{-1}\), and normal multiplier coordinates are unique.

\[\forall r\in\mathbb R^m\ \exists p\in\mathbb R^n:\ Jp=r.\]

\[m=1:\quad \operatorname{rank}J=1\iff J\ne0.\]

\[P_T=I-J^T(JJ^T)^{-1}J\text{ is the Euclidean tangent projector}.\]

children.title: Redundant Equality Constraints
children.top_down_role: Dependent equalities that preserve the underlying feasible geometry.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A sufficient condition for removing displayed equalities without changing the local zero set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(c=(c_I,c_R)\) near \(\bar x\). If a neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and a mapping \(\Phi\) satisfy \(c_R(x)=\Phi(c_I(x))\) for every \(x\in U\) and \(\Phi(0)=0\), then \(c_I(x)=0\) implies \(c_R(x)=0\) on \(U\). Hence
\[\{x\in U:c(x)=0\}=\{x\in U:c_I(x)=0\},\]
so the components indexed by \(R\) are locally redundant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equalities that are local functional consequences of retained equalities can be deleted without changing nearby feasibility.

notation.meaning: Map expressing removed equalities as consequences of retained ones.

knowledge_statements.title: Functional-Consequence Criterion for Redundancy

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Jacobian Dependence Does Not Imply Constraint Redundancy
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates first-order gradient dependence from removable equality equations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(c_1(x,y)=x^2\) and \(c_2(x,y)=y^2\) at \(\bar x=(0,0)\). The full zero set is \(\{(0,0)\}\), while \(Dc(0,0)=0\). Removing \(c_1\) produces \(\{y=0\}\), and removing \(c_2\) produces \(\{x=0\}\). Thus neither equality is locally redundant although the displayed gradients are maximally dependent.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two squared coordinate constraints have zero gradients at the origin, yet neither can be removed without enlarging the nearby feasible set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{rank}Dc(0,0)=0\), but neither \(c_1\) nor \(c_2\) is locally removable.
knowledge_statements.title: Jacobian Dependence Does Not Imply Constraint Redundancy

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Primal Invariance under Deletion of Redundant Equalities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Set-determined local consequences of replacing equalities by a locally equivalent proper subsystem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F=\{x:c(x)=0\}\) and \(F_I=\{x:c_i(x)=0\ (i\in I)\}\). If \(F\cap U=F_I\cap U\) for a neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\), then every objective has the same local minimizers and local maximizers over the two representations near \(\bar x\). Any tangent or normal cone defined solely from the local feasible set is likewise identical for \(F\) and \(F_I\), although representation-dependent multiplier coordinates need not agree.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Deleting locally redundant equalities preserves local primal optima and all set-determined tangent and normal geometry, but need not preserve multiplier coordinates.
assumptions_latex: \(F\cap U=F_I\cap U\) for a neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{locopt}(f,F,\bar x)=\operatorname{locopt}(f,F_I,\bar x)\), and corresponding set-defined tangent and normal cones coincide.

notation.meaning: Feasible set of the retained equality subsystem.
Neighborhood on which the two feasible representations agree.

knowledge_statements.title: Primal Invariance under Deletion of Redundant Equalities

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Constant-Rank Extraction of a Nonredundant Subsystem
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local removal of excess displayed equalities when the constraint mapping has constant rank.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(c:U\subset\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) be \(C^1\), let \(c(\bar x)=0\), and suppose \(\operatorname{rank}Dc(x)=r<m\) throughout a neighborhood of \(\bar x\). Choose \(I\subset\{1,\ldots,m\}\) with \(|I|=r\) and \(\operatorname{rank}Dc_I(\bar x)=r\). After shrinking to a neighborhood \(V\), there is a \(C^1\) mapping \(\Phi\) such that \(c=\Phi\circ c_I\) on \(V\) and \(\Phi(0)=0\). Consequently, \[c^{-1}(0)\cap V=c_I^{-1}(0)\cap V.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constant-rank equality system admits a locally equivalent subsystem containing as many original equalities as its rank.

notation.meaning: Submapping formed from selected independent component equalities.
Local constant rank of the equality mapping.

knowledge_statements.title: Constant-Rank Extraction of a Nonredundant Subsystem

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Redundancy is a property of the displayed equations, not of the feasible set alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The same feasible set can have redundant and irredundant equality representations. Near \(0\in\mathbb R\), \(c(x)=x\) is irredundant, whereas \(\widetilde c(x)=(x,2x)\) defines the same zero set but either component can be deleted without changing it.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding a duplicate or scalar-multiple equality can make a representation redundant without changing its feasible set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: c^{-1}(0)=\widetilde c^{-1}(0)=\{0\},\qquad \widetilde c\text{ is redundant while }c\text{ is irredundant}.

notation.meaning: Two equality representations of the same feasible set.

knowledge_statements.title: Representation Dependence of Equality Redundancy
Redundant Equality Constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local redundancy defined by removable equalities that do not alter feasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(c=(c_1,\ldots,c_m):\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\), let \(\bar x\) satisfy \(c(\bar x)=0\), and let \(F=c^{-1}(0)\). The equality representation is locally redundant at \(\bar x\) if there exist a neighborhood \(U\) of \(\bar x\) and a proper index set \(I\subsetneq\{1,\ldots,m\}\) such that
\[
F\cap U=\{x\in U:c_i(x)=0\ \text{for every}\ i\in I\}.
\]
Thus at least one equality can be removed locally without changing the feasible set. Duplicate constraints, or smooth functional consequences of retained constraints, are redundant in this sense.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equality constraints are locally redundant when a proper subset defines exactly the same nearby feasible set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A proper subset of the component equalities defines \(F\cap U\) unchanged.

notation.meaning: Index set of retained equality constraints.
Neighborhood on which redundancy is assessed.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact algebraic certificate that removed affine equalities are consequences of a retained feasible subsystem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let the retained affine equalities be \(A_Ix=b_I\), assume \(\{x:A_Ix=b_I\}\ne\varnothing\), and let the proposed removed equalities be \(A_Rx=b_R\). Then
\[
\{x:A_Ix=b_I\}=\{x:A_Ix=b_I,\ A_Rx=b_R\}
\]
if and only if there exists a matrix \(T\) such that
\[
A_R=TA_I,\qquad b_R=Tb_I.
\]
Thus \(T\) certifies that every removed affine equality is a consequence of the retained subsystem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a consistent affine system, removed equalities are redundant exactly when their coefficient rows and right-hand sides are matching linear combinations of retained rows.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dimension and Unboundedness of a Nonunique Equality-Multiplier Set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Size of a consistent equality-multiplier family under equality-gradient dependence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(J\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) has rank \(r\) and \(g+J^\mathsf{T}\lambda=0\) is consistent. Then the multiplier set is an affine subspace of dimension \(\dim\ker J^\mathsf{T}=m-r\). It is a singleton when \(r=m\), and it is nonunique and unbounded when \(r<m\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A consistent equality-multiplier family has dimension m minus the Jacobian row rank and is unbounded whenever it is nonunique.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\dim\Lambda=m-r\); \(\Lambda\) is a singleton iff \(r=m\), and is nonunique and unbounded iff \(r<m\).
knowledge_statements.title: Dimension and Unboundedness of a Nonunique Equality-Multiplier Set
Nonunique Multiplier Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine description of all equality multipliers satisfying stationarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For differentiable \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) and \(c:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\), fix a feasible point \(\bar x\) and write \(g=\nabla f(\bar x)\) and \(J=J(\bar x)\). If the stationarity equation
\[
g+J^\mathsf{T}\lambda=0
\]
has one solution \(\lambda_0\), then its complete multiplier set is
\[
\Lambda(\bar x)=\lambda_0+\ker J^\mathsf{T}.
\]
Hence the multiplier is unique exactly when \(J\) has full row rank. If \(J\) is row-rank deficient and stationarity is consistent, every nonzero element of \(\ker J^\mathsf{T}\) generates a distinct multiplier with the same Lagrangian gradient.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: All stationary equality multipliers form an affine translate of the transposed Jacobian’s null space; rank deficiency therefore causes nonuniqueness when solutions exist.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) and \(c\) are differentiable at the feasible point \(\bar x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\Lambda(\bar x)=\lambda_0+\ker J(\bar x)^\mathsf{T}\), and uniqueness holds if and only if \(\operatorname{rank}J(\bar x)=m\).

children.top_down_role: Criteria for choosing a representative from a nonunique multiplier family.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Metric-dependent canonical selection from a consistent equality-multiplier family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(J\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), \(g\in\mathbb{R}^n\), and \(W\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m}\) be symmetric positive definite, and assume \(J^\mathsf{T}\lambda=-g\) is consistent. Then
\[\lambda_W=\operatorname*{argmin}_{J^\mathsf{T}\lambda=-g}\tfrac12\lambda^\mathsf{T}W\lambda\]
exists uniquely. It is characterized by \(J^\mathsf{T}\lambda_W=-g\) and \(\lambda_W^\mathsf{T}Wz=0\) for every \(z\in\ker J^\mathsf{T}\), and satisfies
\[\lambda_W=-W^{-1}J\bigl(J^\mathsf{T}W^{-1}J\bigr)^\dagger g.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive-definite multiplier metric selects a unique weighted-minimum-norm representative from every consistent multiplier family.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lambda_W\) is the unique feasible multiplier that is \(W\)-orthogonal to \(\ker J^\mathsf{T}\).
knowledge_statements.title: Weighted Minimum-Norm Multiplier Selection

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of Euclidean minimum-norm invariance under rescaling of a redundant displayed equality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For scalar \(x\), the equalities \(c(x)=(x,2x)=0\) and objective gradient \(g=1\) give stationarity \(1+\lambda_1+2\lambda_2=0\), whose Euclidean minimum-norm solution is \((-1/5,-2/5)\). Replacing the second equality by \(4x=0\) leaves the feasible set unchanged but gives minimum-norm multiplier \((-1/17,-4/17)\). Thus Euclidean minimum-norm selection is canonical only relative to the displayed constraint coordinates and scaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rescaling a redundant equality leaves primal feasibility unchanged but can change the Euclidean minimum-norm multiplier.
assumptions_latex: The ordinary Euclidean norm is used in the displayed multiplier coordinates.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((-1/5,-2/5)\neq(-1/17,-4/17)\), although both systems define \(\{0\}\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimum-Euclidean-norm selection from a nonempty affine multiplier set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
At a feasible point \(\bar x\), set \(g=\nabla f(\bar x)\) and \(J=J(\bar x)\), and assume \(J^\mathsf{T}\lambda=-g\) is consistent. Select the canonical multiplier by
\[
\lambda_\star:=\underset{\lambda}{\operatorname{argmin}}\ \tfrac12\|\lambda\|_2^2\quad\text{subject to}\quad J^\mathsf{T}\lambda=-g.
\]
The unique output is
\[
\lambda_\star=-(J^\mathsf{T})^\dagger g,
\]
where the dagger denotes the Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse. Equivalently, \(\lambda_\star\) is the unique stationary multiplier orthogonal to \(\ker J^\mathsf{T}\). If \(J\) has full row rank, this selection coincides with the sole multiplier.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose the unique stationary multiplier of smallest Euclidean norm, computed with the Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse.
assumptions_latex: The equation \(J(\bar x)^\mathsf{T}\lambda=-\nabla f(\bar x)\) is consistent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lambda_\star=-(J^\mathsf{T})^\dagger g\) is the unique minimum-norm element of the multiplier set.

notation.meaning: Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse of the transposed Jacobian.
Objective gradient at the feasible point.

children.title: Rank-Dependent Feasible-Dimension Failures
children.top_down_role: Local breakdown of constant-rank geometry and standard reduction.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Rank-Dependent Failure of Local Feasible Dimension
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(U\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be open, let \(c:U\to\mathbb R^m\) be continuously differentiable, and let \(F=\{x\in U:c(x)=0\}\). Write \(A(x)=Dc(x)\), \(r(x)=\operatorname{rank}A(x)\), and \(L(x)=\ker A(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional smooth equality systems. The definition concerns failure of constant-rank manifold geometry, not merely numerical ill-conditioning of a full-rank Jacobian.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A feasible point \(\bar x\in F\) has a rank-dependent feasible-dimension failure if the Jacobian rank is not locally constant on the feasible set: \[\forall\,V\text{ open with }\bar x\in V\subseteq U,\quad \exists x\in F\cap V\text{ such that }r(x)\ne r(\bar x).\] Equivalently, the linearized dimension \(\dim L(x)=n-r(x)\) is not locally constant along \(F\). Consequently, no single integer \(d=n-r(\bar x)\) is justified by the constant-rank theorem as the dimension of all nearby feasible strata. A stronger pointwise geometric failure occurs when the linearized space is not the actual tangent space, \[T_F(\bar x)\ne L(\bar x),\] where \(T_F(\bar x)\) is the Bouligand tangent cone. These two failures are distinguished: rank variation obstructs a uniform local reduction, while tangent-linearization mismatch may already occur at a singular point even when only that point is inspected.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a smooth equality set \(F=\{x:c(x)=0\}\), a feasible point \(\bar x\) exhibits rank-dependent feasible-dimension failure when every neighborhood of \(\bar x\) contains a feasible point at which the rank of \(Dc\) differs from its rank at \(\bar x\). Thus the dimension \(n-\operatorname{rank}Dc(x)\) of the linearized feasible space is not locally constant. The related stronger pointwise failure is that the Bouligand tangent cone differs from \(\ker Dc(\bar x)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\bar x\text{ is rank-dimension singular}\iff \forall V\ni\bar x\;\exists x\in F\cap V:\operatorname{rank}Dc(x)\ne\operatorname{rank}Dc(\bar x).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[\forall V\ni\bar x,\quad \{\dim\ker Dc(x):x\in F\cap V\}\text{ is not a singleton}.\]
special_cases_latex: For one equality \(c:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\), a rank drop from one to zero changes the linearized dimension from \(n-1\) to \(n\).
If \(Dc(x)\) has constant full row rank \(m\) near \(\bar x\), this failure is absent and \(F\) is locally a smooth manifold of dimension \(n-m\).
immediate_consequences_latex: A fixed-size null-space coordinate vector in \(\mathbb R^{n-r(\bar x)}\) need not parameterize all nearby feasible points.
Multiplier uniqueness and standard implicit-function reductions cannot be inferred at a rank-drop point.
boundary_notes: Rank deficiency at one point does not by itself imply rank variation; a constant rank smaller than \(m\) may still define a regular lower-codimension level set after redundant equations are removed.
The linearized dimension is not automatically the dimension of the feasible set at a singular point.

notation.meaning: Bouligand tangent cone to the feasible set at the reference point.

source_refs.locator: §12.2, example (12.32), Definition 12.4, and the tangent/linearized-set discussion on pp. 320–324

children.title: Constraint-Jacobian Rank Loss
children.top_down_role: Locations or regimes where the effective constraint rank decreases.

knowledge_statements.title: Constraint-Jacobian Rank Loss
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local rank loss for smooth equality constraints relative to approaching feasible points of a higher fixed rank.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(h:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be continuously differentiable, let \(F=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:h(x)=0\}\), and write \(J(x)=Dh(x)\). A feasible point \(x_*\in F\) exhibits constraint-Jacobian rank loss relative to an integer \(r\) if there is a sequence \((x_k)\subset F\) such that \(x_k\to x_*\), \(\operatorname{rank}J(x_k)=r\) for every \(k\), and \(\operatorname{rank}J(x_*)<r\). Consequently, \(\dim\ker J(x_*)=n-\operatorname{rank}J(x_*)>n-r\), and no neighborhood of \(x_*\) containing the approaching points can have constant Jacobian rank \(r\). Thus a constant-rank reduction based on rank \(r\) does not extend across \(x_*\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Constraint-Jacobian rank loss occurs when feasible points of rank r approach a feasible point of lower rank. The linearized null space becomes larger at the limit, so a constant-rank-r reduction cannot extend across that point.
assumptions_latex: \(x_*\in F\), and there is a sequence \((x_k)\subset F\) with \(x_k\to x_*\) and \(\operatorname{rank}Dh(x_k)=r\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\dim\ker J(x_*)=n-\operatorname{rank}J(x_*)>n-r\), and the Jacobian cannot have constant rank \(r\) across \(x_*\).

notation.meaning: Fixed Jacobian rank at the approaching feasible points.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dimension Formula on Constant-Rank Feasible Pieces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic dimension on locally constant-rank pieces and the resulting dimension difference between such pieces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(h:U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be \(C^1\), let \(F=h^{-1}(0)\), and suppose \(\operatorname{rank}Dh(x)=r\) throughout a neighborhood of \(\bar x\in F\). Then \(F\) is locally a \(C^1\) embedded submanifold of dimension \(n-r\). Thus locally constant-rank feasible pieces of ranks \(r_1\) and \(r_2\) have dimensions \(n-r_1\) and \(n-r_2\), respectively.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A locally constant-rank feasible piece has dimension n minus its Jacobian rank, so rank differences give the dimension differences between such pieces.

notation.meaning: Constant Jacobian rank on feasible piece i.

knowledge_statements.title: Dimension Formula on Constant-Rank Feasible Pieces

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomial equalities whose nearby feasible pieces have different local dimensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(h:\mathbb{R}^3\to\mathbb{R}^2\) by \[h(x,y,z)=\bigl(zx,\ z(y-z^2)\bigr).\] Then \[F=h^{-1}(0)=\{z=0\}\cup\{x=0,\ y=z^2\}.\] At every \((0,z^2,z)\) with \(z\ne0\), a sufficiently small neighborhood meets only the parabolic curve, so the local feasible dimension is one. At the origin the plane \(\{z=0\}\) is present, and the local dimension is two.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The zero set is a plane joined to a parabola; its local dimension is one along the nonzero parabola and two at the junction.
assumptions_latex: Local dimension is the maximal dimension of the local smooth feasible pieces through the point.

notation.meaning: Zero set of the displayed polynomial equality system.

knowledge_statements.title: Plane-and-Parabola Feasible-Dimension Change
Feasible-Dimension Changes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A smooth equality whose feasible set has strata of different local dimensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(h:\mathbb{R}^3\to\mathbb{R}\) by \(h(x,y,z)=(x^2+y^2)z\). Its feasible set is \(F=\{z=0\}\cup\{x=y=0\}\). At every point \((0,0,z)\) with \(z\ne0\), a sufficiently small neighborhood meets \(F\) only in the \(z\)-axis, so the local feasible dimension is one. At the origin, every neighborhood contains the plane \(\{z=0\}\), and the local dimension is two. Moreover, \(Dh(0,0,z)=0\) on the axis, showing that Jacobian nullity alone need not equal the actual local feasible dimension when constant rank fails.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The zero set of \((x^2+y^2)z\) is a plane joined to an axis; its local feasible dimension changes from one along the nonzero axis to two at the origin.
assumptions_latex: Local dimension is understood as the maximal dimension of smooth feasible strata meeting a sufficiently small neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\dim_{(0,0,z)}F=1\) for \(z\ne0\), whereas \(\dim_{(0,0,0)}F=2\), although \(Dh\) vanishes along the entire \(z\)-axis.

notation.meaning: Zero set of the displayed equality constraint.
Local dimension of the feasible set at \(p\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasible dimension on each locally constant-rank piece and the dimension change between such pieces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let h:U\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m be C^1 and let F=h^{-1}(0). If \operatorname{rank}Dh(x)=r throughout a neighborhood of \bar x\in F, then F is locally a C^1 embedded submanifold of dimension n-r. Consequently, if two locally constant-rank feasible pieces have ranks r_1 and r_2, their manifold dimensions are n-r_1 and n-r_2, so the dimension change from the first piece to the second is r_1-r_2.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constant-rank feasible piece has dimension n minus its Jacobian rank; rank differences therefore give the dimension differences between regular pieces.
assumptions_latex: Dh has constant rank r near \bar x.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \dim_{\bar x}F=n-r;\quad (n-r_2)-(n-r_1)=r_1-r_2.

children.title: Constant-Rank Regime Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Limits of neighborhoods supporting a fixed-rank geometric description.

knowledge_statements.title: Constant-Rank Regime Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary separating feasible strata on which a fixed-rank reduction is valid.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(h:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be continuously differentiable and \(F=h^{-1}(0)\). For an integer \(r\), define the feasible rank regime \(F_r=\{x\in F:\operatorname{rank}Dh(x)=r\}\). A point \(x_*\in F\) lies on a constant-rank regime boundary if every relative neighborhood of \(x_*\) in \(F\) meets both \(F_r\) and \(F\setminus F_r\) for some \(r\). No neighborhood of such a point has constant Jacobian rank; consequently, the constant-rank theorem cannot supply one smooth reduction of dimension \(n-r\) valid throughout that neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A constant-rank regime boundary is a feasible point arbitrarily close to both rank-\(r\) and different-rank feasible points; one fixed-dimensional constant-rank reduction cannot cross it.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every neighborhood \(U\) of \(x_*\), \((U\cap F_r)\ne\varnothing\) and \((U\cap(F\setminus F_r))\ne\varnothing\); hence \(Dh\) has no constant rank on \(U\cap F\).

notation.meaning: Feasible points where the constraint Jacobian has rank \(r\).

children.title: Standard-Reduction Failure
children.top_down_role: Breakdown of conventional null-space or local-elimination representations near singular geometry.

knowledge_statements.title: Standard-Reduction Failure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of implicit-function elimination at a singular equality constraint.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider minimizing a smooth function subject to \(h(x)=x^2=0\) on \(\mathbb{R}\). The feasible set is the singleton \(F=\{0\}\), but \(Dh(0)=0\). Thus no nonzero square constraint-Jacobian block exists at the feasible point, and the implicit-function theorem cannot eliminate a dependent variable there. The null-space dimension predicted directly from the Jacobian is \(1-\operatorname{rank}Dh(0)=1\), while the actual feasible set has local dimension zero. Hence the standard full-rank reduced-coordinate construction produces neither a valid local parameterization nor the correct feasible dimension.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For the constraint \(x^2=0\), the feasible set is an isolated point but the Jacobian vanishes, so full-rank implicit elimination and its dimension formula fail.
assumptions_latex: The standard reduction requires a nonsingular constraint-Jacobian block.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: At \(x=0\), \(Dh(0)=0\), \(\dim F=0\), and \(1-\operatorname{rank}Dh(0)=1\); therefore the standard implicit reduction is inapplicable.

notation.meaning: Constraint derivative at the feasible point.

source_refs.locator: 3.2.1 Equality constrained problems and the Lagrangian function p. 76

source_witnesses.locator: 3.2.1 Equality constrained problems and the Lagrangian function p. 76

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes failure of conventional m-variable elimination from failure of every lower-rank local description.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(h:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) be \(C^1\), let \(\bar x\in h^{-1}(0)\), and suppose \(\operatorname{rank}Dh(\bar x)<m\). Then every \(m\times m\) column minor of \(Dh(\bar x)\) is singular, so no standard partition can solve \(m\) dependent variables from all \(m\) displayed equalities by the implicit-function theorem. This does not exclude a lower-rank description: if \(Dh\) has constant rank \(r<m\) near \(\bar x\), the zero set may still be a local manifold of dimension \(n-r\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Row-rank deficiency destroys every standard m-variable elimination using all displayed equalities, but it does not rule out a lower-rank constant-rank description.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\det Dh_D(\bar x)=0\) for every \(|D|=m\); standard full-row-rank elimination fails, while lower-rank reduction is not excluded.

notation.meaning: Square Jacobian column block selected by D.
Possible locally constant rank below m.

children.title: Equality-Constrained KKT Curvature Theory
children.top_down_role: First- and second-order equality geometry, multiplier representations, reduced curvature, and saddle-point regularity.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Consider \(\min_{x\in\mathbb R^n}f(x)\) subject to \(c(x)=0\), where \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) and \(c:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) are twice continuously differentiable. Set \(A(x)=Dc(x)\) and \(\mathcal L(x,\lambda)=f(x)-\lambda^Tc(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional, twice-smooth equality-constrained optimization at a feasible KKT pair. Full row rank is imposed when uniqueness, reduced coordinates, or KKT-matrix regularity is asserted.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An equality-constrained KKT curvature datum at \((x_*,\lambda_*)\) consists of \[c(x_*)=0,\qquad \nabla_x\mathcal L(x_*,\lambda_*)=0,\qquad H_*:=\nabla_{xx}^2\mathcal L(x_*,\lambda_*),\] together with the tangent space \(T_*:=\ker A_*\), where \(A_*=A(x_*)\), and the restricted quadratic form \(q_*(d)=d^TH_*d\) for \(d\in T_*\). If \(Z\in\mathbb R^{n\times(n-m)}\) has full column rank and \(A_*Z=0\), the coordinate representation is the reduced Hessian \(R_*=Z^TH_*Z\). The associated saddle-point linearization is \[K_*:=\begin{bmatrix}H_*&-A_*^T\\A_*&0\end{bmatrix}.\] Thus the theory records first-order primal-dual stationarity, second-order curvature only along feasible tangent directions, and the regularity of the coupled KKT system as distinct but linked objects.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a feasible equality-constrained KKT pair, the curvature datum comprises the Lagrangian Hessian, its quadratic form restricted to the Jacobian null space, any null-space matrix representation of that form, and the saddle-point KKT matrix. It separates stationarity from curvature and tests curvature on feasible tangent directions rather than on all of \(\mathbb R^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathfrak K(x_*,\lambda_*)=\bigl(A_*,H_*,T_*,q_*|_{T_*},K_*\bigr),\qquad T_*=\ker A_*.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: For \(d=Zu\), \[q_*(d)=u^TR_*u,\qquad R_*=Z^TH_*Z.\]
special_cases_latex: For affine constraints, \(H_*=\nabla^2 f(x_*)\).
When \(m=0\), the datum reduces to the ordinary unconstrained Hessian and its quadratic form.
immediate_consequences_latex: Positive definiteness of \(R_*\) is the standard reduced second-order sufficiency condition.
Under full row rank, nonsingularity and inertia of \(K_*\) are controlled by the reduced Hessian.
boundary_notes: Positive definiteness of the full Lagrangian Hessian is stronger than necessary.
If the equality Jacobian is rank deficient, multiplier uniqueness and the standard \((n-m)\)-column null-space representation may fail.

notation.meaning: Hessian of the Lagrangian with respect to primal variables.

children.title: Equality Stationarity Representations
children.top_down_role: Equivalent primal-dual, projected, and reduced-coordinate views of equality-constrained criticality.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) and \(c:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) be continuously differentiable. At a feasible point \(x\), put \(A=Dc(x)\), assume \(\operatorname{rank}A=m\), choose \(Z\in\mathbb R^{n\times(n-m)}\) with \(AZ=0\) and full column rank, and define \(P=Z(Z^TZ)^{-1}Z^T\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional smooth equalities under full row rank. The three representations are pointwise and exact; approximate stationarity measures are outside this definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The equality-stationarity representation class at a feasible point \(x\) is the common condition expressed in any of the following forms: \[(i)\quad \exists\lambda\in\mathbb R^m:\ 
abla f(x)-A^T\lambda=0;\] \[(ii)\quad P
abla f(x)=0;\] \[(iii)\quad Z^T
abla f(x)=0.\] These are equivalent because \(\operatorname{range}(A^T)=(\ker A)^\perp\), \(\operatorname{range}Z=\ker A\), and \(P\) is the orthogonal projector onto \(\ker A\). If \(x=\phi(y)\) is a local feasible parameterization with \(D\phi(y)=ZB\) for a nonsingular matrix \(B\), the same class is represented by \[
abla_y(f\circ\phi)(y)=D\phi(y)^T
abla f(x)=0.\] Full row rank also makes the multiplier representation unique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a regular feasible point, equality stationarity is one condition with four interchangeable coordinate descriptions: the objective gradient lies in the range of the transposed constraint Jacobian; its orthogonal projection onto the tangent space vanishes; its coordinates against any tangent basis vanish; or the gradient of the locally reduced objective vanishes. Full row rank makes the associated multiplier unique.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
\[\exists\lambda:
abla f(x)=A^T\lambda\iff P
abla f(x)=0\iff Z^T
abla f(x)=0.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: For a regular feasible chart \(x=\phi(y)\), \[Z^T\nabla f(x)=0\iff \nabla(f\circ\phi)(y)=0.\]
special_cases_latex: If \(Z\) is orthonormal, then \(P=ZZ^T\).
For affine equalities \(Ax=b\), the matrices \(A\), \(Z\), and \(P\) are constant.
immediate_consequences_latex: Any norm of \(P\nabla f(x)\) or \(Z^T\nabla f(x)\), with a fixed well-conditioned basis, is a stationarity residual.
Changing the tangent basis does not change whether reduced stationarity holds.
boundary_notes: Without full row rank, the primal projected condition can remain meaningful while multipliers may be nonunique.
For inequality constraints, the tangent cone and complementarity conditions replace this linear-subspace equivalence.

notation.meaning: Orthogonal projector onto the tangent space \(\ker A\).
Full-column-rank tangent or null-space basis matrix.

knowledge_statements.title: Equivalent Equality-Stationarity Representations

children.title: Lagrangian Stationarity
children.top_down_role: Stationarity represented jointly by primal variables and equality multipliers.

knowledge_statements.title: Lagrangian Stationarity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order stationarity for smooth equality constraints under full-row-rank regularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the problem \(\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n} f(x)\) subject to \(h(x)=0\), define \(L(x,\lambda)=f(x)+\lambda^{\mathsf T}h(x)\). A feasible point \(x_*\) is Lagrangian-stationary if there exists \(\lambda_*\in\mathbb{R}^m\) such that \(h(x_*)=0\) and \(\nabla_xL(x_*,\lambda_*)=\nabla f(x_*)+Dh(x_*)^{\mathsf T}\lambda_*=0\). If \(Dh(x_*)\) has full row rank, this multiplier is unique, and every local minimizer satisfies this condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a regular feasible local minimizer, the objective gradient is canceled by a unique linear combination of equality-constraint gradients.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(x_*\) is a local minimizer, there is a unique \(\lambda_*\) satisfying \(h(x_*)=0\) and \(\nabla f(x_*)+Dh(x_*)^{\mathsf T}\lambda_*=0\).

source_refs.locator: 3.2.1 Equality constrained problems and the Lagrangian function p. 76

source_witnesses.locator: 3.2.1 Equality constrained problems and the Lagrangian function p. 76

knowledge_statements.statement_title: A Degenerate Equality Minimizer without a Lagrange Multiplier
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shows failure of the regular first-order multiplier conclusion when the equality Jacobian loses rank.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min_{x\in\mathbb R} x\) subject to \(h(x)=x^2=0\). The feasible set is \(\{0\}\), so \(x_*=0\) is a local minimizer. However, \(Dh(0)=0\) and \(\nabla f(0)=1\), so \(1+Dh(0)^{\mathsf T}\lambda=1\ne0\) for every \(\lambda\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rank-deficient equality can have a local minimizer at which no Lagrange multiplier satisfies stationarity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_*=0\) is a local minimizer but admits no \(\lambda\) with \(\nabla f(0)+Dh(0)^{\mathsf T}\lambda=0\).
knowledge_statements.title: A Degenerate Equality Minimizer without a Lagrange Multiplier

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates existence of stationarity multipliers from uniqueness when constraint gradients are dependent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an arbitrary constraint Jacobian \(J\), a multiplier satisfying \(\nabla f(x)+J^{\mathsf T}\lambda=0\) exists if and only if \(-\nabla f(x)\in\operatorname{range}(J^{\mathsf T})\). If \(\lambda_0\) is one solution, all solutions are \(\lambda_0+\ker(J^{\mathsf T})\). Thus the multiplier is unique exactly when \(J\) has full row rank. Without a constraint qualification, a local minimizer need not admit any such multiplier.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Rank loss can make equality multipliers nonunique, and without a constraint qualification a local minimizer may have no stationarity multiplier at all.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: When nonempty, \(\{\lambda:\nabla f(x)+J^{\mathsf T}\lambda=0\}=\lambda_0+\ker(J^{\mathsf T})\); rank deficiency destroys uniqueness.
knowledge_statements.title: Multiplier Nonuniqueness under Rank Loss

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Least-Squares Formula for the Equality Multiplier
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit multiplier representation at a regular feasible point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(J=Dh(x)\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) have full row rank. The unique multiplier minimizing \(\lVert\nabla f(x)+J^{\mathsf T}\lambda\rVert_2\) is \[\lambda_{\mathrm{ls}}=-(JJ^{\mathsf T})^{-1}J\nabla f(x).\] The point is Lagrangian-stationary exactly when the resulting residual is zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under full row rank, least squares projects the negative objective gradient onto the constraint-gradient span and gives the unique equality multiplier at stationarity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lambda_{\mathrm{ls}}=-(JJ^{\mathsf T})^{-1}J\nabla f(x)\), and stationarity holds exactly when \(\nabla f(x)+J^{\mathsf T}\lambda_{\mathrm{ls}}=0\).
knowledge_statements.title: Least-Squares Formula for the Equality Multiplier

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) and \(c:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) be continuously differentiable, and define \(\mathcal L(x,\lambda)=f(x)-\lambda^Tc(x)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise first-order stationarity for smooth equality constraints. The definition does not assert local optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A pair \((x_*,\lambda_*)\in\mathbb R^n	imes\mathbb R^m\) is a Lagrangian-stationary pair if \[c(x_*)=0,\qquad 
abla_x\mathcal L(x_*,\lambda_*)=
abla f(x_*)-Dc(x_*)^T\lambda_*=0.\] A feasible point \(x_*\) is Lagrangian stationary if at least one \(\lambda_*\) exists for which these equations hold. Equivalently, \[
abla f(x_*)\in\operatorname{range}Dc(x_*)^T.\] The set of compatible multipliers is \[\Lambda(x_*):=\{\lambda\in\mathbb R^m:Dc(x_*)^T\lambda=
abla f(x_*)\}.\] If \(Dc(x_*)\) has full row rank, \(\Lambda(x_*)\) is either empty or a singleton; at a stationary feasible point it is a singleton.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A primal-dual pair is Lagrangian stationary when the primal point satisfies every equality and the gradient of the Lagrangian with respect to the primal variables is zero. A feasible point is stationary if such a multiplier exists. Equivalently, its objective gradient belongs to the range of the transposed constraint Jacobian. The compatible multiplier set is explicitly the solution set of that linear stationarity equation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[(x_*,\lambda_*)\text{ is stationary}\iff c(x_*)=0\ \text{and}\ \nabla f(x_*)=Dc(x_*)^T\lambda_*.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[x_*\text{ is Lagrangian stationary}\iff c(x_*)=0\ \text{and}\ \nabla f(x_*)\in\operatorname{range}Dc(x_*)^T.\]
special_cases_latex: For affine constraints \(c(x)=Ax-b\), stationarity is \(Ax_*=b\) and \(\nabla f(x_*)=A^T\lambda_*\).
With no constraints, the condition reduces to \(\nabla f(x_*)=0\).
immediate_consequences_latex: If \(Dc(x_*)\) has full row rank, the stationary multiplier is unique.
Lagrangian stationarity implies that the directional derivative of \(f\) vanishes along every vector in \(\ker Dc(x_*)\).
boundary_notes: At a rank-deficient point, a multiplier may fail to exist or may be nonunique.
Stationarity alone neither implies positive reduced curvature nor distinguishes a constrained minimum from a constrained saddle.

notation.meaning: Set of multipliers satisfying the stationarity equation at the feasible point.

knowledge_statements.title: Projected-Gradient Stationarity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tangent-space projection form of equality-constrained first-order stationarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x\) be feasible and suppose \(J=Dh(x)\in\mathbb{R}^{m	imes n}\) has full row rank. The orthogonal projector onto the tangent space \(T_x=\ker J\) is \(P_T=I-J^{\mathsf T}(JJ^{\mathsf T})^{-1}J\). Projected-gradient stationarity is the equality \(P_T
abla f(x)=0\). It is equivalent to \(
abla f(x)\in\operatorname{range}(J^{\mathsf T})\), and hence to the existence of a unique multiplier \(\lambda\) satisfying \(
abla f(x)+J^{\mathsf T}\lambda=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stationarity means that the objective gradient has zero orthogonal projection onto the feasible tangent space; under full row rank this is equivalent to Lagrangian stationarity.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) and \(h\) are continuously differentiable near the feasible point \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
\(P_T
abla f(x)=0\iff 
abla f(x)\in\operatorname{range}(J^{\mathsf T})\iff \exists!\lambda:
abla f(x)+J^{\mathsf T}\lambda=0\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extends the algebraic projected-stationarity equivalence to an arbitrary-rank constraint Jacobian.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For any \(J\in\mathbb R^{m	imes n}\), let \(J^\dagger\) be its Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse. Then \[P_{\ker J}=I-J^\dagger J\] is the orthogonal projector onto \(\ker J\), and \[P_{\ker J}
abla f(x)=0\iff 
abla f(x)\in\operatorname{range}(J^{\mathsf T})\iff \exists\lambda:
abla f(x)+J^{\mathsf T}\lambda=0.\] Full row rank is unnecessary for these algebraic equivalences, but it is required for multiplier uniqueness and for the inverse formula \(I-J^{\mathsf T}(JJ^{\mathsf T})^{-1}J\). At a singular nonlinear equality, \(\ker J\) may strictly contain the actual feasible tangent cone, so this linearized condition need not be necessary at a local minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The pseudoinverse gives the projector onto the linearized null space at arbitrary rank, but at a singular nonlinear equality that null space need not equal the true feasible tangent geometry.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((I-J^\dagger J)\nabla f(x)=0\iff\exists\lambda:\nabla f(x)+J^{\mathsf T}\lambda=0\), with no multiplier-uniqueness or nonlinear tangent-manifold guarantee under rank loss.

knowledge_statements.title: Rank-Deficient Linearized Projector Form

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(x\) be feasible for \(c(x)=0\), let \(A=Dc(x)\) have rank \(r\), and let \(T_x=\ker A\). Denote by \(P_x\) the Euclidean orthogonal projector onto \(T_x\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional smooth equality constraints with the Euclidean inner product. A weighted projection is a nearby but distinct variant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The projected gradient of \(f\) at the feasible point \(x\) is \[g_{\mathrm{proj}}(x):=P_x
abla f(x).\] The point is projected-gradient stationary if \[g_{\mathrm{proj}}(x)=0.\] If \(A\) has full row rank, then \[P_x=I-A^T(AA^T)^{-1}A.\] More generally, using the Moore–Penrose inverse gives the orthogonal projector \[P_x=I-A^\dagger A.\] The defining condition is equivalent to the vanishing of every feasible first-order directional derivative: \[d^T
abla f(x)=0\quad	ext{for all }d\in T_x.\] It is also equivalent to \(
abla f(x)\in T_x^\perp=\operatorname{range}A^T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The projected gradient is the orthogonal projection of the objective gradient onto the equality tangent space. A feasible point is projected-gradient stationary exactly when this tangent component is zero, or equivalently when the objective has zero first-order directional derivative along every vector satisfying the linearized equalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[x\text{ is projected-gradient stationary}\iff P_x\nabla f(x)=0.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[P_x\nabla f(x)=0\iff d^T\nabla f(x)=0\ \forall d\in\ker Dc(x).\]
\[P_x\nabla f(x)=0\iff \nabla f(x)\in\operatorname{range}Dc(x)^T.\]
special_cases_latex: If \(Z\) has orthonormal columns spanning \(T_x\), then \(P_x=ZZ^T\) and \(g_{\mathrm{proj}}=ZZ^T\nabla f(x)\).
For affine constraints, the projector is constant.
immediate_consequences_latex: The scalar \(\|P_x\nabla f(x)\|_2\) is a basis-independent first-order stationarity residual.
Projected stationarity is unchanged by replacing the equality equations with another system having the same Jacobian row space.
boundary_notes: For a nonorthonormal tangent basis \(Z\), the projector is \(Z(Z^TZ)^{-1}Z^T\), not generally \(ZZ^T\).
At singular feasible points, \(\ker Dc(x)\) may strictly exceed the true tangent cone, so this condition may be stronger than geometric tangent-cone stationarity.

knowledge_statements.title: Reduced-Gradient Stationarity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Null-space-coordinate form of equality-constrained first-order stationarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\) satisfy \(h(x)=0\), let \(J=Dh(x)\) have full row rank, and let the columns of \(Z\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times(n-m)}\) form a basis of \(\ker J\). The reduced gradient is \(g_R=Z^{\mathsf T}\nabla f(x)\). Reduced-gradient stationarity is \(g_R=0\). Because \(\operatorname{range}(Z)=\ker J\), this condition is independent of the chosen null-space basis and is equivalent to \(\nabla f(x)\in\operatorname{range}(J^{\mathsf T})\), hence to Lagrangian stationarity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The reduced gradient consists of objective derivatives along independent tangent coordinates; its vanishing is basis-independent and equivalent to equality-constrained Lagrangian stationarity.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) and \(h\) are continuously differentiable near the feasible point \(x\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
\(Z^{\mathsf T}
abla f(x)=0\iff 
abla f(x)\in\operatorname{range}(J^{\mathsf T})\iff \exists\lambda:
abla f(x)+J^{\mathsf T}\lambda=0\).

notation.meaning: Null-space basis matrix for the constraint Jacobian.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes basis-invariant vanishing from basis-dependent coordinates and norms.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reduced-gradient vanishing is invariant under every nonsingular coordinate change, whereas its Euclidean norm is invariant only across orthonormal tangent bases.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widetilde g_R=M^{\mathsf T}g_R\); vanishing is invariant, while Euclidean norm equality requires orthonormal coordinates.
knowledge_statements.title: Reduced-Gradient Transformation under Basis Change

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(x\) be feasible for \(c(x)=0\), let \(A=Dc(x)\) have full row rank \(m\), and choose a full-column-rank matrix \(Z\in\mathbb R^{n\times(n-m)}\) satisfying \(AZ=0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional smooth equality constraints in independent tangent coordinates. The reduced gradient is coordinate dependent, while its vanishing is coordinate invariant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The reduced gradient associated with the tangent basis \(Z\) is \[g_Z(x):=Z^T\nabla f(x)\in\mathbb R^{n-m}.\] The feasible point \(x\) is reduced-gradient stationary if \[g_Z(x)=0.\] If a local feasible chart \(\phi:V\subseteq\mathbb R^{n-m}\to\mathbb R^n\) satisfies \(c(\phi(y))=0\), \(x=\phi(y)\), and \(D\phi(y)=Z\), then \[g_Z(x)=\nabla(f\circ\phi)(y).\] If another basis is \(\widetilde Z=ZR\) with \(R\) nonsingular, then \(g_{\widetilde Z}=R^Tg_Z\); hence the numerical coordinates change but the zero condition does not.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Given independent coordinates for the Jacobian null space, the reduced gradient is the vector obtained by transposing the null-space basis against the objective gradient. Reduced-gradient stationarity means that this coordinate vector is zero. It is precisely ordinary stationarity of the objective after a local elimination of the equality constraints. Different nonsingular tangent coordinates transform the vector but preserve whether it vanishes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[x\text{ is reduced-gradient stationary}\iff Z^T\nabla f(x)=0.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: For a feasible parameterization \(x=\phi(y)\), \[Z^T\nabla f(x)=0\iff \nabla(f\circ\phi)(y)=0.\]
For \(\widetilde Z=ZR\) with \(R\) nonsingular, \[\widetilde Z^T\nabla f(x)=0\iff Z^T\nabla f(x)=0.\]
special_cases_latex: Under variable elimination \(x=(x_B(x_N),x_N)\), the reduced gradient is the derivative of the eliminated objective with respect to the independent variables \(x_N\).
If \(n=m\) and \(A\) is nonsingular, the reduced space has dimension zero and the reduced-gradient condition is vacuous.
immediate_consequences_latex: A nonzero reduced gradient supplies a first-order descent direction within the linearized feasible space after choosing a compatible metric.
The condition is equivalent to projected-gradient and Lagrangian stationarity under full row rank.
boundary_notes: The norm \(\|Z^T\nabla f\|\) depends on scaling unless \(Z\) is normalized or uniformly well conditioned.
If the Jacobian rank changes, a fixed-dimensional reduced coordinate system may cease to exist.

notation.meaning: Gradient expressed against the selected independent tangent basis.

children.title: Multiplier Estimation Families
children.top_down_role: Multiplier recovery mechanisms associated with projected, reduced, and primal-dual formulations.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: For a smooth equality problem, write \(A(x)=Dc(x)\), \(g(x)=\nabla f(x)\), and define the stationarity residual \(r_s(x,\lambda)=g(x)-A(x)^T\lambda\). Let \(\mathcal D\) denote any auxiliary data used by an estimator, such as a step, Hessian model, weighting matrix, or rank threshold.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise multiplier recovery at stationary and nonstationary iterates. The definition covers exact, least-squares, step-corrected, and generalized-inverse estimators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A multiplier-estimation family is a collection of maps \[E_\theta:(x,\mathcal D)\longmapsto \widehat\lambda_\theta(x;\mathcal D)\in\mathbb R^m,\qquad \theta\in\Theta,\] whose members select a solution or approximate solution of a stationarity-fitting problem \[\widehat\lambda_\theta\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\lambda\in\mathbb R^m}\|W_\theta(A(x)^T\lambda-b_\theta(x;\mathcal D))\|_2,\] possibly with a minimum-norm tie-breaking rule. First-order estimators use \(b_	heta=g(x)\); second-order estimators use a curvature-corrected vector such as \(b_	heta=g(x)+B(x)p\); generalized-inverse estimators set \(\widehat\lambda=(A^T)^\dagger b_	heta\). An estimator is consistent at a regular stationary pair \((x_*,\lambda_*)\) if \[x_k\to x_*,\quad \mathcal D_k\to\mathcal D_*\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \widehat\lambda_	heta(x_k;\mathcal D_k)\to\lambda_*.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multiplier-estimation family is a parameterized collection of maps that recover dual variables by fitting the Lagrangian stationarity equation. Members differ in the fitted right-hand side, weighting, factorization, curvature correction, and tie-breaking rule. Consistency means that the estimated multipliers converge to the exact regular multiplier whenever the primal and auxiliary data converge to their limiting values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathcal E=\{E_\theta:\widehat\lambda_\theta\in\operatorname*{argmin}_\lambda\|W_\theta(A^T\lambda-b_\theta)\|_2\}_{\theta\in\Theta}.\]
special_cases_latex: Least-squares first-order estimate: \(b_\theta=g(x)\) and \(W_\theta=I\).
Step-corrected second-order estimate: \(b_\theta=g(x)+B(x)p\).
Minimum-norm generalized-inverse estimate: \(\widehat\lambda=(A^T)^\dagger b_\theta\).
immediate_consequences_latex: At an exactly stationary regular point, all consistent family members recover the unique multiplier.
Different estimators can agree at the solution yet have different conditioning and off-solution accuracy.
boundary_notes: Consistency is not guaranteed merely because an estimator solves a least-squares problem; rank stability and appropriate auxiliary-data limits are required.
For rank-deficient constraints, a minimum-norm convention selects one multiplier but does not restore uniqueness of the underlying multiplier set.

notation.meaning: Estimator-specific target for the stationarity equation.

knowledge_statements.title: First-Order Multiplier Estimates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multiplier recovery from the current objective gradient and constraint Jacobian.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given a point \(x\) and a full-row-rank constraint Jacobian \(J=Dh(x)\), compute the first-order multiplier estimate by solving \((JJ^{\mathsf T})\widehat\lambda=-J
abla f(x)\), equivalently \(\widehat\lambda=-(JJ^{\mathsf T})^{-1}J
abla f(x)\). This estimate uniquely minimizes \(\|
abla f(x)+J^{\mathsf T}\lambda\|_2\) over \(\lambda\in\mathbb{R}^m\). Output \(\widehat\lambda\) together with the stationarity residual \(r=
abla f(x)+J^{\mathsf T}\widehat\lambda\); exact first-order stationarity is detected when \(x\) is feasible and \(r=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Solve the normal equations that best fit the negative objective gradient by constraint gradients, and report the multiplier estimate and remaining stationarity residual.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat\lambda=-(JJ^{\mathsf T})^{-1}J\nabla f(x)\) is the unique minimizer of \(\min_\lambda\|\nabla f(x)+J^{\mathsf T}\lambda\|_2\).

notation.meaning: Constraint Jacobian at the current point.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: At an iterate \(x\), let \(A=Dc(x)\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) and \(g=\nabla f(x)\in\mathbb R^n\). Assume initially that \(A\) has full row rank.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Smooth finite-dimensional equality constraints. The canonical estimate uses only first derivatives and the current primal point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The least-squares first-order multiplier estimate is the unique vector \[\widehat\lambda_{\mathrm{FO}}(x):=\operatorname*{argmin}_{\lambda\in\mathbb R^m}\|A^T\lambda-g\|_2.\] Under full row rank, \[\widehat\lambda_{\mathrm{FO}}(x)=(AA^T)^{-1}Ag.\] It is called first order because, near a regular stationary pair \((x_*,\lambda_*)\), smoothness and rank stability give an estimation error of the same local order as the primal error: \[\|x-x_*\|=O(\varepsilon)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad \|\widehat\lambda_{\mathrm{FO}}(x)-\lambda_*\|=O(\varepsilon).\] A variable-reduction first-order estimate instead selects an invertible row-space block \(V\) and solves \(V^T\widehat\lambda_V=g_V\), where \(g_V\) contains the corresponding components of \(g\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The canonical first-order multiplier estimate is the least-squares fit of the current objective gradient by a linear combination of the constraint gradients. With full row rank it has the normal-equation expression \((AA^T)^{-1}Ag\), although stable factorizations should be used computationally. Its local error is ordinarily first order in the primal displacement. A variable-reduction estimate fits an independent subset of the same stationarity equations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\widehat\lambda_{\mathrm{FO}}=\operatorname*{argmin}_{\lambda}\|A^T\lambda-g\|_2=(AA^T)^{-1}Ag.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[AA^T\widehat\lambda_{\mathrm{FO}}=Ag.\]
The residual \(A^T\widehat\lambda_{\mathrm{FO}}-g\) is orthogonal to \(\operatorname{range}A^T\).
special_cases_latex: At an exactly stationary regular point, \(g=A^T\lambda_*\) and \(\widehat\lambda_{\mathrm{FO}}=\lambda_*\).
If \(A\) has orthonormal rows, \(\widehat\lambda_{\mathrm{FO}}=Ag\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The residual norm equals the norm of the component of \(g\) orthogonal to the constraint-gradient range.
Near linear dependence of the constraint gradients can amplify multiplier-estimation errors.
boundary_notes: Forming \(AA^T\) explicitly squares the condition number; a QR, LQ, or SVD computation is preferable.
If \(A\) is rank deficient, the minimizer need not be unique unless a minimum-norm rule is imposed.

notation.meaning: Least-squares multiplier estimate based only on current first derivatives.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: First-order least-squares and variable-reduction multiplier estimates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multiplier estimates obtained from stationarity information for constraints believed active at the current iterate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \widehat c_k denote the constraints believed active at x_k, let \widehat A_k contain their gradients, and let g_k=\nabla F(x_k). Define \lambda_L\in\arg\min_\lambda\|\widehat A_k^T\lambda-g_k\|_2^2. This estimate always exists and is unique if \operatorname{rank}(\widehat A_k)=t. If V is a nonsingular t\times t submatrix of \widehat A_k and g_V contains the corresponding components of g_k, define \lambda_V by V^T\lambda_V=g_V. If \widehat A_k^T\lambda=g_k is compatible, then \lambda_V=\lambda_L. If \|x_k-x^*\|=O(\epsilon) and \operatorname{rank}(\widehat A(x^*))=t, then \|\lambda_L-\lambda^*\|=O(\epsilon) and \|\lambda_V-\lambda^*\|=O(\epsilon). Even when the least-squares residual is zero, \lambda_L is only an estimate of the nonlinear-problem multiplier unless \widehat c(x_k)=0. When \widehat A_k has full row rank, an estimate accounting for nonzero \widehat c_k is \lambda_L-(\widehat A_k\widehat A_k^T)^{-1}\widehat c_k.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The gradients of constraints believed active define an always-existing least-squares multiplier estimate, unique under full row rank, and a variable-reduction estimate based on a nonsingular gradient submatrix. The estimates agree when the stationarity equations are compatible and are first-order accurate near a regular solution. A zero stationarity residual does not make the estimate an exact nonlinear-problem multiplier at an infeasible iterate.
assumptions_latex: \widehat c_k\text{ contains the constraints believed active at }x_k
V\in\mathbb R^{t\times t}\text{ is a nonsingular submatrix of }\widehat A_k
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \lambda_L\in\arg\min_\lambda\|\widehat A_k^T\lambda-g_k\|_2^2,\quad V^T\lambda_V=g_V,\quad \|\lambda_L-\lambda^*\|=O(\epsilon),\quad \|\lambda_V-\lambda^*\|=O(\epsilon).

knowledge_statements.title: Second-Order Multiplier Estimates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multiplier update obtained jointly with a Newton or quasi-Newton primal correction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Given \((x_k,\lambda_k)\), set \(J_k=Dh(x_k)\), choose a symmetric curvature model \(B_k\) for \(
abla_{xx}^2L(x_k,\lambda_k)\), and solve \[ egin{pmatrix}B_k&J_k^{\mathsf T}\J_k&0\end{pmatrix} egin{pmatrix}p_k\\delta\lambda_k\end{pmatrix}=- egin{pmatrix}
abla f(x_k)+J_k^{\mathsf T}\lambda_k\h(x_k)\end{pmatrix}.\] Set \(x_{k+1}=x_k+p_k\) and \(\widehat\lambda_{k+1}=\lambda_k+\delta\lambda_k\). Output \((x_{k+1},\widehat\lambda_{k+1})\). If the solve is used iteratively, terminate when \(\|h(x_{k+1})\|\) and \(\|
abla f(x_{k+1})+Dh(x_{k+1})^{\mathsf T}\widehat\lambda_{k+1}\|\) meet prescribed tolerances. The update is uniquely defined whenever the displayed KKT matrix is nonsingular.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Solve the Newton-type KKT system for a primal correction and multiplier correction, apply both corrections, and test feasibility and Lagrangian stationarity at the resulting pair.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Superlinear Accuracy of Quasi-Newton Second-Order Updates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combined primal-dual and multiplier-component rate under a Dennis–Moré condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F(z^*)=0\), with \(F\) continuously differentiable near \(z^*\) and \(F'(z^*)\) nonsingular. Generate full steps from \(M_ks_k=-F(z_k)\), \(z_{k+1}=z_k+s_k\). If \(z_k\to z^*\), the inverses \(M_k^{-1}\) are uniformly bounded, and \[\frac{\|(M_k-F'(z_k))s_k\|}{\|s_k\|}\to0,\] then \(\|z_{k+1}-z^*\|=o(\|z_k-z^*\|)\). Hence \(\|\lambda_{k+1}-\lambda^*\|=o(\|z_k-z^*\|)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stable KKT-structured quasi-Newton model satisfying the Dennis–Moré condition gives superlinear combined primal-dual convergence and the corresponding multiplier-component error bound.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is continuously differentiable near \(z^*\), \(F(z^*)=0\), and \(F'(z^*)\) is nonsingular.
knowledge_statements.title: Superlinear Accuracy of Quasi-Newton Second-Order Updates

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local Quadratic Accuracy of Exact Second-Order Updates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Combined primal-dual and multiplier-component error bound for exact KKT Newton updates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(z=(x,\lambda)\) and \(F(z)=(\nabla_xL(x,\lambda),h(x))\). Suppose \(F(z^*)=0\), \(F'\) is Lipschitz continuous near \(z^*\), and \(F'(z^*)\) is nonsingular. For all sufficiently close \(z_k\), the full Newton update \(F'(z_k)s_k=-F(z_k)\), \(z_{k+1}=z_k+s_k\), is well defined and satisfies \[\|z_{k+1}-z^*\|\le C\|z_k-z^*\|^2.\] Consequently, \(\|\lambda_{k+1}-\lambda^*\|\le C\|z_k-z^*\|^2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Near a regular KKT pair, exact primal-dual Newton updates have quadratic combined error, and the new multiplier error obeys the same bound relative to the preceding combined error.
knowledge_statements.title: Local Quadratic Accuracy of Exact Second-Order Updates

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: At an iterate \(x_k\), let \(A_k=Dc(x_k)\) have full row rank, let \(g_k=\nabla f(x_k)\), let \(G_k\) be a Hessian or curvature model for the objective or relevant Lagrangian model, and let \(p_k\) approximate the displacement \(q_k=x_*-x_k\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local smooth equality-constrained estimation coordinated with a Newton-type step. The second-order label concerns local accuracy, not merely the use of a Hessian matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The least-squares second-order multiplier estimate is \[\widehat\lambda_{\mathrm{SO}}(x_k,p_k):=\operatorname*{argmin}_{\lambda\in\mathbb R^m}\|A_k^T\lambda-(g_k+G_kp_k)\|_2.\] Under full row rank, \[\widehat\lambda_{\mathrm{SO}}=(A_kA_k^T)^{-1}A_k(g_k+G_kp_k).\] It qualifies as a second-order estimate at a regular solution \((x_*,\lambda_*)\) when, for \(\|q_k\|=O(\varepsilon)\), the step satisfies \(\|p_k-q_k\|=O(\varepsilon^2)\) and the curvature model is sufficiently accurate, yielding \[\|\widehat\lambda_{\mathrm{SO}}-\lambda_*\|=O(\varepsilon^2).\] If the corrected stationarity equations are compatible, the estimate may equivalently be recovered from any independent subsystem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A second-order multiplier estimate fits the constraint-gradient combination to a gradient predicted at the end of a Newton-like step, namely \(g_k+G_kp_k\). It has genuinely second-order local accuracy only when the step predicts the solution displacement to second order and the curvature model is correspondingly accurate. Merely inserting an arbitrary step into the formula does not guarantee improved accuracy.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\widehat\lambda_{\mathrm{SO}}=\operatorname*{argmin}_{\lambda}\|A_k^T\lambda-(g_k+G_kp_k)\|_2.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: Under full row rank, \[A_kA_k^T\widehat\lambda_{\mathrm{SO}}=A_k(g_k+G_kp_k).\]
special_cases_latex: With \(p_k=0\), the formula reduces to the first-order least-squares estimate.
When \(p_k\) is the exact Newton-type subproblem step and the corrected equations are compatible, least-squares and independent-equation recovery coincide.
immediate_consequences_latex: A poor step can make the second-order formula less accurate than the first-order estimate.
Near a regular solution, a second-order accurate step can improve multiplier error from \(O(\varepsilon)\) to \(O(\varepsilon^2)\).
boundary_notes: The estimate is local; no second-order accuracy is asserted far from the solution.
If the Jacobian is nearly rank deficient, conditioning can dominate the formal asymptotic order.

notation.meaning: Available approximation to the displacement from the iterate to the solution.
Second-derivative or curvature model used to predict the gradient.

If z_k\to z^*, the matrices M_k and M_k^{-1} remain bounded, and the Dennis–Moré condition \[\frac{\|(M_k-F'(z^*))s_k\|}{\|s_k\|}\to0\] holds, then \(\|z_{k+1}-z^*\|/\|z_k-z^*\|\to0\). Consequently the multiplier estimates converge Q-superlinearly as components of the primal-dual iterates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stable KKT-structured quasi-Newton model satisfying the Dennis–Moré condition yields superlinear primal-dual, hence multiplier, convergence.
assumptions_latex: \(z_k\to z^*\), and \(M_k\) and \(M_k^{-1}\) are uniformly bounded.
The Dennis–Moré condition holds and full steps are taken.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local Quadratic Accuracy of Exact Second-Order Multiplier Updates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local convergence rate of the multiplier component in the exact primal-dual Newton iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define F(x,\lambda)=(\nabla_xL(x,\lambda),h(x)) and suppose F(x^*,\lambda^*)=0. If F' is Lipschitz near (x^*,\lambda^*) and the KKT Jacobian F'(x^*,\lambda^*) is nonsingular, then the exact second-order update F'(x_k,\lambda_k)(p_k,\delta\lambda_k)=-F(x_k,\lambda_k) is well defined for all sufficiently close iterates and satisfies \[\|(x_{k+1},\lambda_{k+1})-(x^*,\lambda^*)\|\le C\|(x_k,\lambda_k)-(x^*,\lambda^*)\|^2.\] In particular, the updated multiplier estimate is quadratically accurate: \(\|\lambda_{k+1}-\lambda^*\|\le C\|(x_k,\lambda_k)-(x^*,\lambda^*)\|^2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Near a regular KKT pair, exact primal-dual Newton updates produce quadratically convergent multiplier estimates.
assumptions_latex: The full Newton step is taken.
knowledge_statements.title: Local Quadratic Accuracy of Exact Second-Order Multiplier Updates

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Second-order least-squares multiplier estimate and validity regime
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Curvature-corrected multiplier estimation near a regular solution, with its equality-constrained QP interpretation and local failure boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let q=x^*-x_k, let W_k(\lambda)=\nabla_{xx}^2L(x_k,\lambda), and let p and \lambda approximate q and \lambda^*, respectively. Define \eta_L\in\arg\min_\eta\|\widehat A_k^T\eta-[g_k+W_k(\lambda)p]\|_2^2. If \operatorname{rank}(\widehat A_k)=t, \|q\|=O(\epsilon), \|\lambda-\lambda^*\|=O(\epsilon), and \|p-q\|=O(\epsilon^2), then \|\eta_L-\lambda^*\|=O(\epsilon^2). Thus the improved accuracy requires proximity to x^*, a first-order multiplier approximation, and a second-order displacement approximation; absent these conditions, a second-order estimate can be inaccurate. If p solves \min_p\ g_k^Tp+\tfrac12p^TW_k(\lambda)p subject to \widehat A_kp=\widehat d_k, then the least-squares residual is zero and \eta_L is the multiplier of that equality-constrained QP.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A second-order multiplier estimate least-squares fits a curvature-corrected stationarity vector. Full row rank, a nearby iterate, a first-order multiplier approximation, and a second-order displacement approximation give second-order multiplier accuracy. If the displacement solves the associated equality-constrained quadratic subproblem, the estimate is its exact multiplier. The accuracy improvement is local and may fail without the stated approximation conditions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \eta_L\in\arg\min_\eta\|\widehat A_k^T\eta-(g_k+W_k(\lambda)p)\|_2^2,\qquad \|\eta_L-\lambda^*\|=O(\epsilon^2).

children.title: Generalized-Inverse Multiplier Recovery Family
children.top_down_role: Dual recovery in overdetermined, ill-conditioned, or rank-deficient stationarity systems.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) be an equality Jacobian, let \(b\in\mathbb R^n\) be a stationarity target, and let \(M=A^T\in\mathbb R^{n\times m}\). No full-rank assumption is imposed.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional exact arithmetic definition covering overdetermined, inconsistent, and rank-deficient stationarity systems. Numerical rank truncation is treated as a variant.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The Moore–Penrose generalized-inverse multiplier recovery is \[\widehat\lambda^\dagger:=M^\dagger b=(A^T)^\dagger b.\] It is characterized uniquely by \[\widehat\lambda^\dagger\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\lambda\in\mathbb R^m}\|A^T\lambda-b\|_2,\qquad \|\widehat\lambda^\dagger\|_2=\min\{\|\lambda\|_2:\lambda\text{ minimizes the residual}\}.\] If \(A^T=U\Sigma V^T\) is a singular-value decomposition, then \[(A^T)^\dagger=V\Sigma^\dagger U^T,\] where each nonzero singular value is inverted and each zero singular value remains zero. A truncated family replaces \(\Sigma^\dagger\) by \(\Sigma_\tau^\dagger\), inverting only singular values exceeding a declared threshold \(\tau\), and defines \(\widehat\lambda_\tau=V\Sigma_\tau^\dagger U^Tb\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Generalized-inverse recovery selects the minimum-Euclidean-norm multiplier among all least-squares fits to the stationarity equation. It is defined even when the equation is inconsistent or the equality Jacobian is rank deficient. An SVD supplies the canonical construction. Thresholded variants regularize directions associated with singular values judged numerically negligible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\widehat\lambda^\dagger=(A^T)^\dagger b=\operatorname*{argmin}_{\lambda\in\operatorname*{argmin}_\mu\|A^T\mu-b\|_2}\|\lambda\|_2.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[A^T\widehat\lambda^\dagger=\Pi_{\operatorname{range}A^T}b,\qquad \widehat\lambda^\dagger\in\operatorname{range}A.\]
special_cases_latex: If \(A\) has full row rank, \((A^T)^\dagger=(AA^T)^{-1}A\).
If \(b\in\operatorname{range}A^T\), the residual is zero and \(\widehat\lambda^\dagger\) is the minimum-norm exact multiplier.
immediate_consequences_latex: Redundant equality equations do not prevent the recovery of a canonical minimum-norm multiplier.
Truncation bounds amplification from very small retained singular values at the cost of a nonzero regularization bias.
boundary_notes: The threshold \(\tau\) is scale dependent unless the system is appropriately scaled.
The minimum-norm multiplier is a convention; other exact multipliers can have distinct modeling interpretations when constraints are redundant.

knowledge_statements.title: Least-Squares Multiplier Estimates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generalized-inverse least-squares fit of the Lagrangian stationarity equation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At a point \(x\), let \(J=Dh(x)\) and \(g=\nabla f(x)\). Define a least-squares multiplier estimate as any solution of \(\min_{\lambda\in\mathbb{R}^m}\|g+J^{\mathsf T}\lambda\|_2\). The complete solution set is \[\widehat\lambda=-(J^{\mathsf T})^\dagger g+\bigl(I-(J^{\mathsf T})^\dagger J^{\mathsf T}\bigr)w,\qquad w\in\mathbb{R}^m.\] Compute one such vector and output it with residual \(r=g+J^{\mathsf T}\widehat\lambda\). Every output has the same fitted vector \(J^{\mathsf T}\widehat\lambda\) and satisfies the normal equation \(Jr=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fit the negative objective gradient by constraint gradients in Euclidean least squares; all solutions share the same fitted gradient and have residual orthogonal to that span.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat\lambda\in\operatorname*{argmin}_\lambda\|g+J^{\mathsf T}\lambda\|_2\) and its residual satisfies \(J(g+J^{\mathsf T}\widehat\lambda)=0\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Derivative of the least-squares multiplier estimate
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Differentiability formula under AW.1 and full row rank of the constraint Jacobian.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose AW.1 holds and \(A(x)A(x)^T\) is nonsingular. Then \(y^{\mathrm{LS}}(x)\) is differentiable and \[
abla_xy^{\mathrm{LS}}(x)= igl(A^+(x) igr)^T
abla_{xx}\ell igl(x,y^{\mathrm{LS}}(x) igr)+ igl(A(x)A(x)^T igr)^{-1}E(x),\] where row \(i\) of \(E(x)\) is \[ igl(g(x)-A(x)^Ty^{\mathrm{LS}}(x) igr)^T
abla_{xx}c_i(x).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under AW.1 and nonsingularity of the constraint-Jacobian Gram matrix, the least-squares multiplier estimate is differentiable. Its derivative is a generalized-inverse projection of the Lagrangian Hessian plus a correction involving the stationarity residual and constraint Hessians.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \nabla_xy^{\mathrm{LS}}(x)=\bigl(A^+(x)\bigr)^T\nabla_{xx}\ell\bigl(x,y^{\mathrm{LS}}(x)\bigr)+\bigl(A(x)A(x)^T\bigr)^{-1}E(x).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The least-squares multiplier estimate \(y^{\mathrm{LS}}(x)\) is the minimum-norm solution of \[\min_y\|g(x)-A(x)^Ty\|_2.\] Whenever \(A(x)A(x)^T\) is nonsingular, \[y^{\mathrm{LS}}(x)=\bigl(A^+(x)\bigr)^Tg(x),\qquad A^+(x)=A(x)^T\bigl(A(x)A(x)^T\bigr)^{-1}.\] Consequently, if \(g(x_*)=A(x_*)^Ty_*\), then \(y^{\mathrm{LS}}(x_*)=y_*\).

knowledge_statements.title: Minimum-Norm Multiplier Estimates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical least-squares multiplier selected by minimum Euclidean norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(J=Dh(x)\) and \(g=\nabla f(x)\), with no rank assumption on \(J\). Among all minimizers of \(\|g+J^{\mathsf T}\lambda\|_2\), there is a unique vector of minimum Euclidean norm. It is \[\widehat\lambda_{\min} =-(J^{\mathsf T})^\dagger g=-(JJ^{\mathsf T})^\dagger Jg.\] This vector lies in \(\operatorname{range}(J)\), is orthogonal to \(\ker(J^{\mathsf T})\), and reduces to \(-(JJ^{\mathsf T})^{-1}Jg\) when \(J\) has full row rank.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The pseudoinverse selects the unique least-squares multiplier with smallest Euclidean norm, including when redundant constraints make ordinary multiplier estimates nonunique.
assumptions_latex: The multiplier norm and residual norm are Euclidean.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\widehat\lambda_{\min}=-(J^{\mathsf T})^\dagger g\) uniquely minimizes \(\|\lambda\|_2\) over \(\operatorname*{argmin}_\lambda\|g+J^{\mathsf T}\lambda\|_2\).

knowledge_statements.title: Rank-Deficient Multiplier Recovery
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Multiplier recovery and nonuniqueness when equality gradients are linearly dependent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(J=Dh(x)\) be rank deficient and let \(g=\nabla f(x)\). Exact multiplier recovery is possible precisely when \(-g\in\operatorname{range}(J^{\mathsf T})\). In that case, the multiplier set is \[\Lambda(x)=\{-(J^{\mathsf T})^\dagger g+v:v\in\ker(J^{\mathsf T})\},\] and \(-(J^{\mathsf T})^\dagger g\) is its unique minimum-norm member. If \(-g\notin\operatorname{range}(J^{\mathsf T})\), no exact multiplier exists; the same pseudoinverse vector instead minimizes the stationarity residual, whose minimum norm is \(\|(I-J^{\mathsf T}(J^{\mathsf T})^\dagger)g\|_2\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With dependent equality gradients, exact multipliers exist only when the objective gradient lies in their span; otherwise the pseudoinverse returns the minimum-residual estimate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exact recovery holds iff \(-g\in\operatorname{range}(J^{\mathsf T})\); when it holds, all multipliers differ by elements of \(\ker(J^{\mathsf T})\).
