knowledge_statements.title: Ill-Conditioned Multiplier Recovery
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sensitivity of least-squares multiplier recovery near constraint-Jacobian rank loss.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(J\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) have full row rank and let \(g\in\mathbb{R}^n\). The least-squares multiplier estimate for \(J^{\mathsf T}\lambda\approx-g\) is \(\widehat\lambda=-(JJ^{\mathsf T})^{-1}Jg\). For a gradient perturbation \(\delta g\), \[\delta\lambda=-(JJ^{\mathsf T})^{-1}J\delta g,\qquad \|\delta\lambda\|_2\leq \sigma_{\min}(J)^{-1}\|\delta g\|_2.\] Equality is attained for a perturbation aligned with a right singular vector associated with \(\sigma_{\min}(J)\). Thus multiplier recovery becomes arbitrarily sensitive as \(\sigma_{\min}(J)\downarrow0\), even while \(J\) remains full row rank.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Least-squares multipliers amplify gradient errors by as much as the reciprocal of the constraint Jacobian’s smallest singular value, becoming unstable near rank loss.
assumptions_latex: The Euclidean vector norm and its induced operator norm are used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\|\delta\lambda\|_2\leq \sigma_{\min}(J)^{-1}\|\delta g\|_2\), with the factor attained in a worst-case direction.

notation.meaning: Smallest singular value of the full-row-rank Jacobian.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bias-stability response for a full-row-rank but poorly conditioned multiplier fit.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(J\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) have full row rank, let \(g\in\mathbb R^n\), and choose \(\mu>0\). The regularized estimate is \[\lambda_\mu=\operatorname*{argmin}_{\lambda}\bigl(\|g+J^{\mathsf T}\lambda\|_2^2+\mu\|\lambda\|_2^2\bigr)=-(JJ^{\mathsf T}+\mu I)^{-1}Jg.\] Its gradient-data perturbation operator has norm \[\max_i\frac{\sigma_i(J)}{\sigma_i(J)^2+\mu}\leq\frac1{2\sqrt\mu}.\] Thus regularization uniformly caps noise amplification but generally biases the result relative to the unregularized least-squares multiplier.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Tikhonov regularization caps noise amplification for an ill-conditioned multiplier fit, at the cost of bias.
assumptions_latex: \(J\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) has full row rank.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lambda_\mu=-(JJ^{\mathsf T}+\mu I)^{-1}Jg\) is unique and \(\|\delta\lambda_\mu\|_2\leq(2\sqrt\mu)^{-1}\|\delta g\|_2\).

notation.meaning: Positive singular values of the full-row-rank Jacobian.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regularized multiplier recovery with an explicit noise-amplification bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(J\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(g\in\mathbb R^n\), and \(\mu>0\), define \[\lambda_\mu=\operatorname*{argmin}_{\lambda}\bigl(\|g+J^{\mathsf T}\lambda\|_2^2+\mu\|\lambda\|_2^2\bigr)=-(JJ^{\mathsf T}+\mu I)^{-1}Jg.\] This estimate is unique for every rank and has perturbation operator norm \[\sup_{\delta g\ne0}\frac{\|\delta\lambda_\mu\|_2}{\|\delta g\|_2}=\max_i\frac{\sigma_i(J)}{\sigma_i(J)^2+\mu}\le\frac{1}{2\sqrt\mu}.\] Thus positive regularization uniformly limits noise amplification, at the cost of bias relative to an unregularized least-squares multiplier.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Tikhonov regularization makes multiplier recovery unique and caps gradient-noise amplification, trading instability for bias.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lambda_\mu=-(JJ^{\mathsf T}+\mu I)^{-1}Jg\) is unique and \(\|\delta\lambda_\mu\|_2\le(2\sqrt\mu)^{-1}\|\delta g\|_2\).

children.title: Reduced-Curvature Principle
children.top_down_role: Second-order equality geometry organized by Lagrangian curvature restricted to tangent directions.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Lagrangian Curvature Restricted to Equality Tangents
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: For \(\min f(x)\) subject to \(c(x)=0\), let \((x_*,\lambda_*)\) be a feasible stationary pair, let \(A_*=Dc(x_*)\), and let \(H_*=\nabla_{xx}^2\mathcal L(x_*,\lambda_*)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Twice-smooth finite-dimensional equality constraints. The principle evaluates second-order behavior only on first-order feasible directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The reduced-curvature principle associates with the stationary pair the restricted quadratic form \[q_T(d):=d^TH_*d,\qquad d\in T_*:=\ker A_*.\] Curvature classifications relevant to the equality-constrained problem are made from \(q_T\), not from the definiteness of \(H_*\) on all of \(\mathbb R^n\). The form is tangent-positive semidefinite if \[d^TH_*d\ge 0\quad\forall d\in T_*,\] tangent-positive definite if \[d^TH_*d>0\quad\forall d\in T_*\setminus\{0\},\] and tangent-indefinite if it takes both positive and negative values on \(T_*\). For any full-column-rank basis \(Z\) of \(T_*\), these conditions are equivalently imposed on \(Z^TH_*Z\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The reduced-curvature principle says that second-order equality-constrained geometry is determined by the Lagrangian Hessian restricted to the Jacobian null space. Positive, flat, or negative curvature in directions normal to the feasible set is irrelevant to this classification. A null-space basis converts the restricted quadratic form to the reduced Hessian without changing its intrinsic definiteness or inertia.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[q_T=H_*|_{\ker A_*},\qquad q_T(Zu)=u^T(Z^TH_*Z)u.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[H_*\text{ is positive definite on }\ker A_*\iff Z^TH_*Z\succ0.\]
\[H_*\text{ is positive semidefinite on }\ker A_*\iff Z^TH_*Z\succeq0.\]
special_cases_latex: For affine equalities, the Lagrangian Hessian equals the objective Hessian.
If \(\ker A_*=\{0\}\), tangent positive definiteness is vacuous because there are no nonzero first-order feasible directions.
immediate_consequences_latex: Tangent positive semidefiniteness is the equality-constrained second-order necessary curvature condition at a regular local minimizer.
Tangent positive definiteness, together with regular stationarity, gives the standard strict local second-order condition.
boundary_notes: The full Hessian may be indefinite while the restricted Hessian is positive definite.
At a singular feasible point, the Jacobian null space may not accurately represent the actual feasible tangent geometry.

notation.meaning: Lagrangian Hessian quadratic form restricted to the equality tangent space.

knowledge_statements.title: Null-Space Reduced Hessians
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit-coordinate representation of Lagrangian curvature on the equality-constraint tangent space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At an equality-constrained KKT point \((x^*,\lambda^*)\), let \(J=\nabla c(x^*)\) have rank \(m\), let \(H=\nabla_{xx}^2L(x^*,\lambda^*)\), and choose \(Z\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times(n-m)}\) with full column rank and \(JZ=0\). The reduced Hessian is \[R=Z^{\mathsf T}HZ.\] Every tangent direction has the unique form \(d=Zp\), and its Lagrangian curvature satisfies \(d^{\mathsf T}Hd=p^{\mathsf T}Rp\). Hence \(R\) is the matrix of the tangent-space quadratic form in the coordinates supplied by \(Z\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A null-space basis converts the Lagrangian Hessian’s tangent quadratic form into the reduced matrix obtained by congruence with that basis.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) and \(c\) are twice continuously differentiable near \(x^*\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R=Z^{\mathsf T}HZ\) and \(d^{\mathsf T}Hd=p^{\mathsf T}Rp\) whenever \(d=Zp\).

notation.meaning: Hessian of the Lagrangian with respect to primal variables.
Full-column-rank basis matrix for the null space of the constraint Jacobian.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) have rank \(r\), let \(H\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) be symmetric, and let \(Z\in\mathbb R^{n\times(n-r)}\) have full column rank with \(\operatorname{range}Z=\ker A\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional symmetric curvature models. In nonlinear programming, \(A\) is the equality Jacobian and \(H\) is normally the Lagrangian Hessian.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The null-space reduced Hessian of \(H\) relative to \(A\) and the chosen tangent basis \(Z\) is \[H_{m red}[Z]:=Z^THZ\in\mathbb R^{(n-r)\times(n-r)}.\] It is the coordinate matrix of the restricted bilinear form \((d,e)\mapsto d^THe\) on \(\ker A\): for \(d=Zu\) and \(e=Zv\), \[d^THe=u^TH_{m red}[Z]v.\] Thus \(H_{m red}[Z]\) represents precisely the curvature visible to linearized feasible displacements. If \(Z\) is orthonormal, it is the compression of \(H\) to the tangent subspace; orthonormality is not required for the definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A null-space reduced Hessian is obtained by placing a basis of the equality-Jacobian null space on both sides of a symmetric Hessian or Hessian model. It is the coordinate matrix of the curvature bilinear form restricted to tangent directions. Its size is the number of first-order degrees of freedom, namely \(n-r\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[H_{m red}[Z]=Z^THZ,\qquad d=Zu\Longrightarrow d^THd=u^TH_{m red}[Z]u.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[H_{m red}[Z]\succ0\iff d^THd>0\quad\forall d\in\ker A\setminus\{0\}.\]
special_cases_latex: If \(A\) has full row rank, \(H_{m red}\) has order \(n-m\).
If \(A=0\), one may take \(Z=I\), giving \(H_{m red}=H\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Only Hessian-vector actions on tangent vectors are needed to apply the reduced Hessian.
The number of positive, negative, and zero eigenvalues of the reduced Hessian classifies tangent curvature.
boundary_notes: The numerical entries and eigenvalues depend on the scaling of a nonorthonormal basis, although inertia and definiteness do not.
If a computed \(Z\) fails to span the entire null space, the matrix omits feasible curvature directions.

notation.meaning: Coordinate matrix of the Hessian bilinear form on the null space.

knowledge_statements.title: Projected Hessian Operators
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Ambient-coordinate representation of tangent curvature using the orthogonal tangent projector.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(J\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) have full row rank, let \(H\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) be symmetric, and define the orthogonal projector onto \(\ker J\) by \[P=I-J^{\mathsf T}(JJ^{\mathsf T})^{-1}J.\] The projected Hessian operator is \(PHP\). It maps every vector into \(\ker J\), and for every tangent direction \(d\in\ker J\), \[d^{\mathsf T}PHPd=d^{\mathsf T}Hd.\] If \(Z\) is an orthonormal basis of \(\ker J\), then \(P=ZZ^{\mathsf T}\) and the restriction of \(PHP\) to \(\ker J\) has coordinate matrix \(Z^{\mathsf T}HZ\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projecting the Hessian on both sides represents tangent curvature in ambient coordinates and agrees with the null-space reduced Hessian on the tangent space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d^{\mathsf T}PHPd=d^{\mathsf T}Hd\) for every \(d\in\ker J\).

notation.meaning: Orthogonal projector onto the constraint tangent space.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Ambient-Space Null Modes of the Projected Hessian
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes definiteness of the ambient projected operator from definiteness of its tangent restriction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(J\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) have full row rank, let \(P\) be the orthogonal projector onto \(\ker J\), and let \(H=H^{\mathsf T}\). Then \(PHPv=0\) for every \(v\in\operatorname{range}(J^{\mathsf T})\). Hence, if \(m>0\), \(PHP\) is singular on \(\mathbb{R}^n\), even when \(H\) is positive definite on \(\ker J\). Equality-constrained positive curvature therefore means positive definiteness of the restriction \(PHP|_{\ker J}\), not ambient-space positive definiteness of \(PHP\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The projected Hessian has normal-space zero modes, so constrained positive curvature concerns only its tangent-space restriction.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is the orthogonal projector onto \(\ker J\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{range}(J^{\mathsf T})\subseteq\ker(PHP),\qquad m>0\Longrightarrow PHP\text{ is singular on }\mathbb{R}^n.

notation.meaning: Normal space of the linearized equality constraints.

knowledge_statements.title: Ambient-Space Null Modes of the Projected Hessian

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), let \(T=\ker A\), let \(P_T\) be the Euclidean orthogonal projector onto \(T\), and let \(H\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) be symmetric.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Euclidean finite-dimensional tangent projection. The operator acts in ambient coordinates and does not require an explicit reduced-coordinate calculation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The two-sided projected Hessian operator associated with \((A,H)\) is \[H_T:=P_THP_T:\mathbb R^n\to T.\] Its intrinsic restriction to the tangent space is \[H_T|_T:T\to T,\qquad d\mapsto P_THd.\] For every \(d,e\in T\), \[d^TH_Te=d^THe,\] so the projected operator represents the same restricted bilinear form as a null-space reduced Hessian. If \(Z\) is an orthonormal basis of \(T\), then \[P_T=ZZ^T,
\qquad Z^TH_TZ=Z^THZ.\] If \(A\) has full row rank, \(P_T=I-A^T(AA^T)^{-1}A\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The projected Hessian is the ambient symmetric operator obtained by projecting both the input and output of a Hessian onto the equality tangent space. On tangent vectors its bilinear form agrees with the original Hessian, so it represents tangent curvature without selecting independent reduced coordinates. With an orthonormal null-space basis, its matrix compression is the usual reduced Hessian.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
\[H_T=P_THP_T,
\qquad d,e\in T\Longrightarrow d^TH_Te=d^THe.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex:
For orthonormal \(Z\), \[H_T=ZZ^THZZ^T,
\qquad Z^TH_TZ=Z^THZ.\]
special_cases_latex: If \(T=\mathbb R^n\), then \(P_T=I\) and \(H_T=H\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The nonzero tangent spectral information of \(H_T\) agrees with that of \(Z^THZ\) when \(Z\) is orthonormal.
Matrix-free products can be evaluated as \(v\mapsto P_T(H(P_Tv))\).
boundary_notes: The ambient operator always has at least \(\dim T^\perp\) zero eigenvalues, so its full-space inertia must not be confused with tangent inertia.
A one-sided product \(P_TH\) need not be symmetric on the ambient space.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Null-Space Projector Representation of Restricted Curvature
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Represents equality-constraint tangent curvature without constructing an explicit orthonormal null-space basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) have full row rank, let \(L=L^T\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\), and define \(P_A=I-A^T(AA^T)^{-1}A\). Then \(P_A\) is the orthogonal projector onto \(\ker A\), so \(x\in\ker A\) if and only if \(x=P_Az\) for some \(z\in\mathbb{R}^n\). Moreover, \(x^TLx\geq0\) for every \(x\in\ker A\) if and only if \(P_ALP_A\succeq0\). If \(P_ALP_A\succeq0\) and \(\operatorname{rank}(P_ALP_A)=n-m\), then \(L\) is positive definite on \(\ker A\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a full-row-rank constraint Jacobian, I minus A transpose times the inverse of A A transpose times A is the orthogonal projector onto the tangent null space. Restricted semidefiniteness is equivalent to semidefiniteness of the projected Hessian; together with rank equal to the tangent-space dimension, it yields restricted positive definiteness.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \ker A=\operatorname{range}(P_A),\qquad \bigl(L\succeq0\text{ on }\ker A\bigr)\iff P_ALP_A\succeq0;\qquad \bigl(P_ALP_A\succeq0\ \land\ \operatorname{rank}(P_ALP_A)=n-m\bigr)\Rightarrow L\succ0\text{ on }\ker A.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Projected Hessian Test for Tangent-Space Positive Definiteness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterizes strict symmetric curvature on an equality-constraint tangent space using the ambient projected Hessian.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A=\nabla h\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) have full row rank, let \(M=\ker A\), let \(L=L^T\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\), and define \(P_A=I-A^T(AA^T)^{-1}A\). Then \(L\) is positive definite on \(M\) if and only if \(P_ALP_A\) is positive semidefinite and has rank \(n-m\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A symmetric curvature matrix is positive definite along every nonzero tangent direction exactly when its null-space-projected matrix is positive semidefinite and has rank equal to the tangent-space dimension.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigl(x^TLx>0\ \forall x\in M\setminus\{0\}\bigr)\iff\bigl(P_ALP_A\succeq0\ \land\ \operatorname{rank}(P_ALP_A)=n-m\bigr).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the symmetric Lagrangian-curvature operator compressed to a constraint-tangent subspace and its orthonormal reduced-coordinate representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be a subspace of dimension \(n-m\), let \(P_M\) be the orthogonal projector onto \(M\), and let \(L=L^T\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\). The compressed operator \(L_M:M\to M\) is defined by \(L_My=P_MLy\). A nonzero \(y\in M\) is an eigenvector of \(L_M\) with eigenvalue \(\lambda\in\mathbb{R}\) if and only if \(P_MLy=\lambda y\), equivalently \(Ly-\lambda y\in M^\perp\). If \(E\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times(n-m)}\) has orthonormal columns spanning \(M\), then \(E^TLE\) is the matrix of \(L_M\) in that basis, and its eigenvalues are independent of the chosen orthonormal basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Apply the symmetric curvature matrix to a tangent vector and project the result back onto the tangent space. In any orthonormal tangent-space basis, the compressed operator is represented by E transpose L E, with basis-independent eigenvalues.
assumptions_latex: M\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\text{ is a subspace with }\dim M=n-m
P_M\text{ is the orthogonal projector onto }M
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: L_M=P_ML\vert_M,\qquad [L_M]_E=E^TLE,\qquad \operatorname{spec}(L_M)=\operatorname{spec}(E^TLE)\text{ independently of }E.

children.top_down_role: Coordinate-independent curvature classification across admissible tangent bases.

knowledge_statements.title: Reduced-Hessian Basis Invariance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Invariance of constrained-curvature classification under changes of tangent coordinates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Z_1,Z_2\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times(n-m)}\) be full-column-rank matrices with \(\operatorname{range}(Z_1)=\operatorname{range}(Z_2)=\ker J\), and let \(H\) be symmetric. There is a nonsingular matrix \(T\) such that \(Z_2=Z_1T\). Consequently, their reduced Hessians satisfy \[R_2=Z_2^{\mathsf T}HZ_2=T^{\mathsf T}R_1T.\] By congruence invariance, \(R_1\) and \(R_2\) have the same numbers of positive, negative, and zero eigenvalues. Thus definiteness, singularity, and inertia of constrained curvature do not depend on the chosen tangent basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Any two tangent bases produce congruent reduced Hessians, so their positive, negative, and zero inertia counts—and therefore curvature classifications—are identical.
assumptions_latex: \(Z_1\) and \(Z_2\) are bases of the same tangent subspace.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_2=T^{\mathsf T}R_1T\) for nonsingular \(T\), so \(\operatorname{In}(R_2)=\operatorname{In}(R_1)\).

notation.meaning: Reduced Hessian in tangent basis i.
Ordered positive, negative, and zero inertia counts of a symmetric matrix.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Ordinary Reduced Eigenvalues Are Not Invariant Under Nonorthogonal Basis Changes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp boundary on what reduced-Hessian congruence preserves.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a nonorthogonal basis change \(Z_2=Z_1T\), the reduced Hessians satisfy \(R_2=T^{\mathsf T}R_1T\), which preserves inertia but generally not ordinary eigenvalues or Euclidean-coordinate condition numbers. For example, on a one-dimensional tangent space with \(H=[1]\), \(Z_1=[1]\) gives \(R_1=[1]\), whereas \(Z_2=[2]\) gives \(R_2=[4]\). The basis-independent tangent eigenvalues are the generalized eigenvalues of \[(Z^{\mathsf T}HZ)p=\lambda(Z^{\mathsf T}Z)p,\] equivalently the ordinary eigenvalues obtained using an orthonormal tangent basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonorthogonal basis changes preserve reduced inertia, not ordinary reduced eigenvalues; generalized eigenvalues with the basis Gram matrix restore coordinate invariance.
assumptions_latex: \(Z\) has full column rank and spans the fixed tangent space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{In}(T^{\mathsf T}RT)=\operatorname{In}(R),\qquad \sigma(T^{\mathsf T}RT)\ne\sigma(R)\ \text{in general}.

knowledge_statements.title: Ordinary Reduced Eigenvalues Are Not Invariant Under Nonorthogonal Basis Changes

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(T\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) have dimension \(q\), let \(H\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) be symmetric, and let \(Z,\widetilde Z\in\mathbb R^{n\times q}\) be full-column-rank matrices with \(\operatorname{range}Z=\operatorname{range}\widetilde Z=T\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional coordinate invariance for symmetric tangent curvature. It concerns congruence invariants, not equality of numerical eigenvalues under arbitrary basis scaling.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Reduced-Hessian basis invariance is the fact that any two basis representations of the same restricted quadratic form are congruent. There is a unique nonsingular \(R\in\mathbb R^{q\times q}\) such that \(\widetilde Z=ZR\), and hence \[\widetilde Z^TH\widetilde Z=R^T(Z^THZ)R.\] Consequently, Sylvester inertia, rank, nonsingularity, and positive definiteness or semidefiniteness are independent of the selected tangent basis: \[\operatorname{inertia}(\widetilde Z^TH\widetilde Z)=\operatorname{inertia}(Z^THZ).\] If both bases are orthonormal, \(R\) is orthogonal, so the two reduced Hessians are orthogonally similar and have the same eigenvalues as well.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two matrices whose columns are bases of the same tangent space differ by a nonsingular coordinate transformation. Their reduced Hessians are therefore related by congruence. The intrinsic curvature classification—its positive, negative, and zero directions, rank, and definiteness—is basis independent. Exact eigenvalues are also preserved when both bases are orthonormal, but not under arbitrary rescaling.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
\[\widetilde Z=ZR\Longrightarrow \widetilde Z^TH\widetilde Z=R^T(Z^THZ)R,
\quad R\text{ nonsingular}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[Z^THZ\succ0\iff \widetilde Z^TH\widetilde Z\succ0.\]
\[\operatorname{inertia}(Z^THZ)=\operatorname{inertia}(\widetilde Z^TH\widetilde Z).\]
special_cases_latex: If \(R\) is orthogonal, the transformation is an orthogonal similarity because \(R^T=R^{-1}\).
For \(q=1\), rescaling \(Z\\) by a nonzero scalar rescales the reduced Hessian by its square while preserving its sign.
immediate_consequences_latex: Second-order optimality classifications do not depend on the particular admissible null-space basis.
Condition numbers and eigenvalue magnitudes can still depend strongly on a nonorthonormal basis.
boundary_notes: Congruence does not preserve individual eigenvalues for a general nonsingular \(R\).
The conclusion fails if either matrix omits tangent directions or spans a different subspace.

notation.meaning: Nonsingular change-of-basis matrix between tangent coordinates.

children.title: Reduced-Curvature Inertia Regimes
children.top_down_role: Minimizing, flat, and constrained-saddle curvature regimes.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \((x_*,\lambda_*)\) be an equality-constrained stationary pair, let \(H_*=\nabla_{xx}^2\mathcal L(x_*,\lambda_*)\), and let \(Z\) be any full-column-rank basis of \(\ker Dc(x_*)\). Put \(R_*=Z^TH_*Z\) and \(\operatorname{inertia}(R_*)=(n_+,n_-,n_0)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional twice-smooth equality constraints. The regimes classify the second-order tangent model, not the complete nonlinear critical point in degenerate higher-order cases.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The reduced-curvature inertia regime of \((x_*,\lambda_*)\) is the basis-independent triple \[\mathcal I_{m red}(x_*,\lambda_*):=\operatorname{inertia}(R_*)=(n_+,n_-,n_0).\] It is called strictly minimizing when \(n_-=n_0=0\); weakly minimizing or flat when \(n_-=0\) and \(n_0>0\); constrained-saddle when \(n_->0\) and \(n_+>0\); and strictly tangent-maximizing when \(n_+=n_0=0\). A negative-curvature regime means merely \(n_->0\), including negative semidefinite and indefinite cases. Since different tangent bases produce congruent reduced Hessians, these labels are intrinsic to the restricted Lagrangian quadratic form.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The inertia regime records the numbers of positive, negative, and zero curvature directions in the equality tangent space. All positive directions give the strict minimizing regime; positive directions together with zero directions but no negative direction give a flat or weakly minimizing second-order model; both signs give a constrained saddle. The classification is independent of the chosen null-space basis.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathcal I_{m red}=\operatorname{inertia}(Z^TH_*Z)=(n_+,n_-,n_0).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[\mathcal I_{m red}=(q,0,0)\iff d^TH_*d>0\quad\forall d\in\ker A_*\setminus\{0\}.\]
\[n_->0\iff \exists d\in\ker A_*:\ d^TH_*d<0.\]

children.title: Positive Reduced Curvature
children.top_down_role: Tangent-space curvature associated with locally minimizing constrained behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Positive Reduced Curvature
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive definiteness of Lagrangian curvature restricted to feasible first-order directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At an equality-constrained KKT point, let \(J\) be the constraint Jacobian, let \(H\) be the Lagrangian Hessian, and let the columns of \(Z\) form a basis of \(\ker J\). Positive reduced curvature holds precisely when \[p^{\mathsf T}Z^{\mathsf T}HZp>0\quad\text{for every }p\neq0,\] equivalently when \(d^{\mathsf T}Hd>0\) for every nonzero \(d\in\ker J\). Under full row rank of \(J\), this is the equality-constrained second-order sufficient condition and implies that the KKT point is a strict local minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reduced curvature is positive when the Lagrangian Hessian is positive in every nonzero feasible tangent direction; at a regular KKT point this ensures strict local minimality.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) and \(c\) are twice continuously differentiable near the KKT point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Z^{\mathsf T}HZ\succ0\), equivalently \(d^{\mathsf T}Hd>0\) for all nonzero \(d\in\ker J\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative coercivity equivalent to positive reduced curvature in finite dimensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H=H^{\mathsf T}\) and \(T=\ker J\). Positive reduced curvature holds if and only if there exists \(\mu>0\) such that \[d^{\mathsf T}Hd\ge \mu\lVert d\rVert_2^2\qquad\text{for every }d\in T.\] If \(Z\) is an orthonormal basis of \(T\), the largest admissible constant is \(\lambda_{\min}(Z^{\mathsf T}HZ)>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In finite dimensions, positive reduced curvature is equivalent to a uniform positive lower bound on tangent Rayleigh quotients.
assumptions_latex: \(Z\) is orthonormal for the eigenvalue formula.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Z^{\mathsf T}HZ\succ0\iff \exists\mu>0\ \forall d\in\ker J:\ d^{\mathsf T}Hd\ge\mu\lVert d\rVert_2^2.

children.title: Singular Reduced Curvature
children.top_down_role: Flat or degenerate tangent-space curvature requiring higher-order or regularized interpretation.

knowledge_statements.title: Singular Reduced Curvature
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Degeneracy of Lagrangian curvature along at least one tangent direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be symmetric and let the columns of \(Z\) form a basis of the equality-constraint tangent space \(\ker J\). Singular reduced curvature holds when \[\det(Z^{\mathsf T}HZ)=0,\] equivalently when there exists \(p\neq0\) such that \(Z^{\mathsf T}HZp=0\). The associated nonzero tangent direction \(d=Zp\) satisfies \(Z^{\mathsf T}Hd=0\), so the first-order tangent component of the Hessian action vanishes. Singularity alone does not determine whether the point is a minimizer, maximizer, or saddle; higher-order information may be required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reduced curvature is singular when a nonzero tangent direction lies in the reduced Hessian’s null space; second-order curvature then cannot classify that direction by itself.
assumptions_latex: \(Z\) has full column rank and \(\operatorname{range}(Z)=\ker J\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Z^{\mathsf T}HZ\) is singular, equivalently \(Z^{\mathsf T}HZp=0\) for some \(p\neq0\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Zero Reduced Hessian Does Not Classify a Stationary Point
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical one-dimensional examples showing the sharp limitation of singular second-order curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In the unconstrained one-dimensional case, the stationary point \(x=0\) has the same singular reduced Hessian \(f''(0)=0\) for \(f_1(x)=x^4\), \(f_2(x)=-x^4\), and \(f_3(x)=x^3\). Nevertheless, \(0\) is a strict local minimum of \(f_1\), a strict local maximum of \(f_2\), and neither a local minimum nor a local maximum of \(f_3\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A zero reduced Hessian can occur at a strict minimum, a strict maximum, or a nonextremal stationary point, so higher-order terms are indispensable.
assumptions_latex: The unconstrained case is the equality-constrained case with zero constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f_i'(0)=f_i''(0)=0\ \text{for }i=1,2,3,\quad\text{but the three local classifications differ}.
knowledge_statements.title: Zero Reduced Hessian Does Not Classify a Stationary Point

children.title: Indefinite Reduced Curvature
children.top_down_role: Mixed-sign tangent-space curvature associated with constrained saddle behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Indefinite Reduced Curvature
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coexistence of positive and negative Lagrangian curvature within the tangent space at a regular equality-constrained KKT point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the equality-constrained problem \(\min_{x\in\mathbb{R}^n} f(x)\) subject to \(c(x)=0\), where \(c:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\). At a KKT point \((x^*,\lambda^*)\), let \(J=\nabla c(x^*)\) have rank \(m\), let \(H=\nabla_{xx}^2L(x^*,\lambda^*)\), and let the columns of \(Z\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times(n-m)}\) form a basis of \(\ker J\). Indefinite reduced curvature holds precisely when there exist nonzero vectors \(p_+,p_-\in\mathbb{R}^{n-m}\) such that \[p_+^{\mathsf T}Z^{\mathsf T}HZp_+>0,\qquad p_-^{\mathsf T}Z^{\mathsf T}HZp_-<0.\] Equivalently, \(Z^{\mathsf T}HZ\) has at least one positive and at least one negative eigenvalue. The corresponding negative tangent direction violates the second-order necessary condition for a constrained local minimum, while the positive tangent direction violates the second-order necessary condition for a constrained local maximum. Hence \(x^*\) is neither a constrained local minimum nor a constrained local maximum.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a regular equality-constrained KKT point, reduced curvature is indefinite when feasible tangent directions exhibit both positive and negative Lagrangian curvature; such a point is neither a constrained local minimum nor a constrained local maximum.
assumptions_latex: \(f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) and \(c:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m\) are twice continuously differentiable near \(x^*\).
\((x^*,\lambda^*)\) is a KKT point for the equality-constrained problem.
\(Z\) has full column rank and \(\operatorname{range}(Z)=\ker J\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Z^{\mathsf T}HZ\) has both a positive and a negative eigenvalue, and \(x^*\) is neither a constrained local minimum nor a constrained local maximum.

children.title: Reduced-Curvature Regime Transitions
children.top_down_role: Changes in tangent-space curvature classification under perturbation or iteration.

knowledge_statements.title: Reduced-Curvature Regime Transitions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Eigenvalue-crossing boundary between reduced-curvature inertia regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R(t)\) be a continuous family of real symmetric reduced Hessians of fixed dimension on an interval. If \(R(t_0)\) is nonsingular, then there exists a neighborhood of \(t_0\) on which the positive and negative inertia counts of \(R(t)\) are constant. Consequently, a transition between positive-definite, negative-definite, or indefinite inertia regimes can occur only at a parameter \(t_*\) satisfying \[\det R(t_*)=0,\] equivalently when at least one eigenvalue reaches zero. Passage through singular reduced curvature is therefore necessary for any change of reduced-curvature inertia.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a continuous reduced Hessian family, inertia is locally constant while the matrix is nonsingular; curvature regimes can change only when an eigenvalue reaches zero.
assumptions_latex: \(R(t)\) is real symmetric for every parameter value.
The entries of \(R(t)\) depend continuously on \(t\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An inertia change at \(t_*\) requires \(\det R(t_*)=0\).

source_refs.locator: 4.3 Direct Methods for Solving Linear Systems p. 60

source_witnesses.locator: 4.3 Direct Methods for Solving Linear Systems p. 60

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative perturbation radius within which a nonsingular reduced-curvature regime cannot change.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R=R^{\mathsf T}\) be nonsingular and define \(\delta=\min_i|\lambda_i(R)|\). For every symmetric perturbation \(E\) satisfying \(\lVert E\rVert_2<\delta\), \(R+E\) has the same inertia as \(R\). Moreover, \[\min\{\lVert E\rVert_2:E=E^{\mathsf T},\ R+E\text{ is singular}\}=\delta.\] Thus the smallest absolute reduced eigenvalue is exactly the spectral-norm distance to a curvature-regime transition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonsingular reduced Hessian keeps its inertia under symmetric perturbations smaller than its smallest absolute eigenvalue, which is exactly its distance to singularity.
assumptions_latex: Perturbation size is measured in the spectral norm.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \lVert E\rVert_2<\min_i|\lambda_i(R)|\Longrightarrow \operatorname{In}(R+E)=\operatorname{In}(R).

notation.meaning: Smallest absolute eigenvalue and spectral-norm transition margin.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) have full row rank \(m\), let \(H\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) be symmetric, let \(Z\in\mathbb R^{n\times(n-m)}\) span \(\ker A\), and define \[K=\begin{bmatrix}H&-A^T\\A&0\end{bmatrix},\qquad R=Z^THZ.\]
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional symmetric saddle-point systems with a full-row-rank constraint block. The correspondence is exact and independent of the null-space basis.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The KKT regularity–inertia profile of \((H,A)\) is the linked pair \[\mathfrak I(H,A):=\bigl(\operatorname{inertia}(R),\operatorname{inertia}(K)\bigr)\] satisfying \[\operatorname{inertia}(K)=\operatorname{inertia}(R)+(m,m,0).\] Hence \[K\text{ is nonsingular}\iff R\text{ is nonsingular},\] and \[R\succ0\iff \operatorname{inertia}(K)=(n,m,0).\] More generally, if \(\operatorname{inertia}(R)=(r_+,r_-,r_0)\), then \[\operatorname{inertia}(K)=(r_++m,r_-+m,r_0).\] The full-row-rank hypothesis supplies the \(m\) positive and \(m\) negative saddle directions; all zero eigenvalues of the KKT matrix correspond to degeneracy of the reduced curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a symmetric KKT matrix with a full-row-rank constraint Jacobian, its inertia is obtained by adding one positive and one negative direction for each equality to the inertia of the reduced Hessian. Thus the KKT matrix is nonsingular exactly when the reduced Hessian is nonsingular, and it has inertia \((n,m,0)\) exactly when the reduced Hessian is positive definite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{inertia}(K)=\operatorname{inertia}(Z^THZ)+(m,m,0).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \[K\text{ nonsingular}\iff Z^THZ\text{ nonsingular}.\]
\[Z^THZ\succ0\iff \operatorname{inertia}(K)=(n,m,0).\]
special_cases_latex: If \(m=0\), then \(K=H\) and the correspondence is the identity.
If the reduced Hessian has one zero eigenvalue, the KKT matrix also has one zero eigenvalue.
immediate_consequences_latex: A symmetric-indefinite factorization of \(K\) can certify the desired reduced positive-definite regime without explicitly constructing \(Z\).
Even when \(R\succ0\), the KKT matrix is indefinite whenever \(m>0\).
boundary_notes: The formula requires full row rank of \(A\); redundant equality rows introduce additional singularity not represented by the standard reduced Hessian.
Changing the sign convention in the off-diagonal KKT blocks does not change the stated inertia.

notation.meaning: Paired reduced-Hessian and KKT-matrix inertia profile.

children.title: Regular KKT Nonsingularity
children.top_down_role: The regularity family supporting unique primal-dual Newton corrections.

knowledge_statements.title: Regular KKT Nonsingularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonsingularity criterion for the equality-constrained primal-dual Newton matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(J\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) have full row rank, let \(H\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) be symmetric, and let \(Z\) be any basis matrix for \(\ker J\). Define \[K=\begin{pmatrix}H&J^{\mathsf T}\\J&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad R=Z^{\mathsf T}HZ.\] Then \(K\) is nonsingular if and only if \(R\) is nonsingular. Therefore, under constraint regularity and nonsingular reduced curvature, every primal-dual Newton right-hand side has a unique correction \((d,\delta\lambda)\). Positive definiteness of \(R\) is sufficient but not necessary for this algebraic nonsingularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With independent equality constraints, the KKT matrix is nonsingular exactly when the reduced Hessian is nonsingular, yielding a unique primal-dual Newton correction.
assumptions_latex: \(\operatorname{range}(Z)=\ker J\) and \(Z\) has full column rank.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K\) is nonsingular if and only if \(Z^{\mathsf T}HZ\) is nonsingular.

notation.meaning: Reduced Hessian on the constraint null space.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Regular nonsingularity of an equality-constrained KKT matrix
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(c:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^m\) and \(f:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R\) be twice continuously differentiable near a primal-dual pair \((x,\lambda)\). Set \(A=\nabla c(x)\), \(H=\nabla_{xx}^2L(x,\lambda)\), where \(L(x,\lambda)=f(x)+\lambda^Tc(x)\), and let \(Z\in\mathbb R^{n\times(n-m)}\) have full column rank with \(AZ=0\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional smooth equality constraints, with the constraint Jacobian required to have full row rank; definiteness of the reduced Hessian is not required.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The KKT linearization at \((x,\lambda)\) is called regularly nonsingular when \(\operatorname{rank}(A)=m\) and the reduced Hessian \(R=Z^THZ\) is nonsingular. Equivalently, under full row rank, the symmetric saddle-point matrix \[K=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}H&A^T\\A&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)\] is nonsingular. This property is independent of the selected null-space basis: if \(\widetilde Z=ZT\) for an invertible \(T\), then \(\widetilde Z^TH\widetilde Z=T^TRT\), so nonsingularity is unchanged. Regular nonsingularity means that every right-hand side \((r_d,r_p)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^m\) has a unique primal-dual correction \((p,\delta\lambda)\) satisfying \(Hp+A^T\delta\lambda=r_d\) and \(Ap=r_p\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a smooth equality-constrained primal-dual pair, regular KKT nonsingularity means that the constraint Jacobian has independent rows and the Lagrangian Hessian restricted to tangent directions is nonsingular. Under these conditions the full saddle-point KKT matrix is nonsingular, independently of which basis represents the tangent space, and every primal-dual linear correction is unique.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{rank}(A)=m\ \text{ and }\ \det(Z^THZ)\ne0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\det\left(\begin{smallmatrix}H&A^T\\A&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)\ne0.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: For every \((r_d,r_p)\), the system \(K(p,\delta\lambda)^T=(r_d,r_p)^T\) has exactly one solution.
special_cases_latex: If \(Z^THZ\succ0\), regular nonsingularity holds and \(\operatorname{inertia}(K)=(n,m,0)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The primal and multiplier components of a Newton or quadratic-programming correction are uniquely determined.
boundary_notes: Positive definiteness of \(Z^THZ\) is stronger than regular nonsingularity; an invertible indefinite reduced Hessian also gives a nonsingular KKT matrix.
If \(A\) is rank deficient, the KKT matrix is singular regardless of the curvature matrix.

notation.meaning: Equality-constraint Jacobian at the reference point.
Hessian of the Lagrangian with respect to primal variables.
Any full-column-rank basis matrix for the null space of the constraint Jacobian.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Positive Reduced Curvature Implies KKT Nonsingularity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equality-quadratic specialization of regular KKT nonsingularity and uniqueness of the primal-dual pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{n\times m}\) have full column rank, let \(G=G^T\), and let the columns of \(Z\) form a basis of \(\mathcal N(A^T)\). If \(Z^TGZ\succ0\), then \(K=\begin{bmatrix}G&-A\\-A^T&0\end{bmatrix}\) is nonsingular. Consequently, for the given \(g\in\mathbb R^n\) and \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), there is a unique pair \((x^*,\lambda^*)\) satisfying \(K(x^*,\lambda^*)^T=-(g,b)^T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Full constraint rank and positive-definite curvature on the constraint null space make the quadratic KKT matrix nonsingular, yielding a unique primal-dual KKT pair.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \det\begin{bmatrix}G&-A\\-A^T&0\end{bmatrix}\ne0\quad\text{and}\quad \exists!\,(x^*,\lambda^*):\begin{bmatrix}G&-A\\-A^T&0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x^*\\\lambda^*\end{bmatrix}=-\begin{bmatrix}g\\b\end{bmatrix}.

knowledge_statements.title: Saddle-Point Inertia Classification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Inertia identity linking a regular KKT matrix to its reduced Hessian.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(J\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) have full row rank, let \(H\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\) be symmetric, and let \(Z\) be a basis matrix for \(\ker J\). For \[K=\begin{pmatrix}H&J^{\mathsf T}\\J&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad R=Z^{\mathsf T}HZ,\] if \(\operatorname{In}(R)=(r_+,r_-,r_0)\), then \[\operatorname{In}(K)=(r_++m,\ r_-+m,\ r_0).\] In particular, \(K\) is nonsingular exactly when \(r_0=0\); if \(R\) is positive definite, then \(\operatorname{In}(K)=(n,m,0)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A full-rank equality Jacobian adds exactly one positive and one negative KKT eigenvalue per constraint, while preserving the reduced Hessian’s nullity.
assumptions_latex: The inertia ordering is positive, negative, then zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{In}(K)=\operatorname{In}(R)+(m,m,0)\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Inertia classification of an equality-constrained saddle-point matrix
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(H\in\mathbb S^n\), let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) have rank \(m\), let \(Z\in\mathbb R^{n\times(n-m)}\) satisfy \(AZ=0\) and \(\operatorname{rank}(Z)=n-m\), and set \(K=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}H&A^T\\A&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Real symmetric finite-dimensional KKT matrices with an independent equality-constraint Jacobian.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a real symmetric matrix \(M\), define \(\operatorname{inertia}(M)=(n_+(M),n_-(M),n_0(M))\), the numbers of positive, negative, and zero eigenvalues counted with multiplicity. The saddle-point inertia classification of \(K\) is determined by the reduced curvature \(R=Z^THZ\) through \[\operatorname{inertia}(K)=\operatorname{inertia}(R)+(m,m,0).\] Thus every equality contributes one positive and one negative eigenvalue, while all remaining signs and all zero eigenvalues are inherited from the Hessian restricted to \(\ker A\). The minimum-curvature class is \(\operatorname{inertia}(K)=(n,m,0)\), equivalently \(R\succ0\). If \(R\) has \(q>0\) negative eigenvalues, then \(K\) has \(m+q\) negative eigenvalues and represents negative curvature along \(q\) independent tangent directions. If \(R\) has a zero eigenvalue, the KKT matrix belongs to the singular class.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The inertia classification counts the positive, negative, and zero eigenvalues of the KKT saddle-point matrix. With independent equality constraints, its inertia equals the inertia of the tangent-space reduced Hessian plus one positive and one negative eigenvalue per equality. Positive reduced curvature gives the minimum-type signature; negative reduced curvature gives tangent saddle directions; zero reduced curvature gives singularity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\operatorname{inertia}\left(\begin{smallmatrix}H&A^T\\A&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)=\operatorname{inertia}(Z^THZ)+(m,m,0).\]
special_cases_latex: \(Z^THZ\succ0\) if and only if \(\operatorname{inertia}(K)=(n,m,0)\).
If \(m=0\), the classification reduces to the ordinary inertia of \(H\).
immediate_consequences_latex: A symmetric-indefinite factorization that reveals \(\operatorname{inertia}(K)\) can certify reduced positive definiteness without explicitly forming \(Z\).
boundary_notes: The displayed identity assumes \(A\) has full row rank.
The inertia determines curvature signs and singularity, not numerical conditioning or the magnitudes of eigenvalues.

notation.meaning: Ordered triple of positive, negative, and zero eigenvalue counts.
Reduced Hessian on the null space of the constraint Jacobian.

knowledge_statements.title: Singular KKT Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complete singularity mechanisms for symmetric equality-constrained KKT matrices.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For symmetric \(H\) and \(J\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), consider \(K=\begin{pmatrix}H&J^{\mathsf T}\\J&0\end{pmatrix}\). If \(J\) lacks full row rank, some \(y\neq0\) satisfies \(J^{\mathsf T}y=0\), so \((0,y)\) is a null vector of \(K\). If \(J\) has full row rank and \(Z\) spans \(\ker J\), then \(K\) is singular exactly when \(Z^{\mathsf T}HZ\) is singular. Thus KKT singularity arises either from dependent constraints or, after constraint regularity is imposed, from a flat reduced-curvature direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A symmetric equality KKT matrix is singular because constraints are dependent or, when they are independent, because the reduced Hessian has a null direction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{rank}(J)<m\) implies singular \(K\); if \(\operatorname{rank}(J)=m\), then singular \(K\) is equivalent to singular \(Z^{\mathsf T}HZ\).

notation.meaning: Basis matrix for the null space of a full-row-rank Jacobian.
Multiplier-space null direction caused by dependent constraints.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constructive kernel characterization under a full-row-rank equality Jacobian.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K=\begin{pmatrix}H&J^{\mathsf T}\\J&0\end{pmatrix}\), where \(H=H^{\mathsf T}\), let \(J\) have full row rank, and let the columns of \(Z\) span \(\ker J\). If \(0\ne p\in\ker(Z^{\mathsf T}HZ)\) and \(d=Zp\), then \(Hd\in\operatorname{range}(J^{\mathsf T})\); hence a unique \(y\) satisfies \(J^{\mathsf T}y=-Hd\), and \(K\binom d y=0\). Conversely, every \(\binom d y\in\ker K\) has \(d=Zp\) with \(Z^{\mathsf T}HZp=0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With independent constraints, reduced-Hessian null directions lift uniquely to primal-dual KKT null vectors, and every KKT null vector arises this way.
assumptions_latex: \(J\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) has full row rank.
The columns of \(Z\) form a basis of \(\ker J\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\ker K=\left\{\binom{Zp}{y}:Z^{\mathsf T}HZp=0,\ J^{\mathsf T}y=-HZp\right\}\), with \(y\) unique for each \(p\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Singularity of an equality-constrained KKT system
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(H\in\mathbb S^n\), \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), and \(K=\left(\begin{smallmatrix}H&A^T\\A&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)\). When \(A\) has full row rank, let \(Z\) be any basis matrix for \(\ker A\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional symmetric equality-constrained systems; both constraint degeneracy and tangent-curvature degeneracy are included.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The KKT system is singular when \(K\) is not invertible, equivalently when there exists a nonzero pair \((p,\mu)\) satisfying \(Hp+A^T\mu=0\) and \(Ap=0\). There are two canonical mechanisms. Constraint singularity occurs when \(\operatorname{rank}(A)<m\); then a nonzero \(\mu\in\ker A^T\) gives the null vector \((0,\mu)\). If \(A\) has full row rank, curvature singularity occurs precisely when the reduced Hessian \(Z^THZ\) has a zero eigenvalue. In that regular-constraint case, \[n_0(K)=n_0(Z^THZ),\] so the nullity of the KKT matrix equals the number of independent flat tangent-curvature directions. A system may exhibit both mechanisms when the constraints are dependent and the primal curvature is also degenerate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A KKT system is singular when its homogeneous primal-dual equations have a nonzero solution. Dependence among equality constraints always causes singularity through a multiplier null vector. With independent constraints, singularity is exactly the presence of a zero eigenvalue in the Hessian restricted to feasible tangent directions. The two defects can coexist.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[K\ \text{is singular}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\exists(p,\mu)\ne(0,0):\ Hp+A^T\mu=0,\ Ap=0.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: If \(\operatorname{rank}(A)=m\), then \(K\) is singular if and only if \(Z^THZ\) is singular.
If \(\operatorname{rank}(A)<m\), then \(\{0\}\times\ker A^T\subseteq\ker K\).
special_cases_latex: For \(Z^THZ\succeq0\), singularity corresponds to a nonzero tangent vector with zero reduced quadratic curvature.
immediate_consequences_latex: A singular KKT system may have no solution or multiple solutions for a given right-hand side.
Unique primal-dual Newton corrections cannot be asserted without regularization or a compatible generalized-inverse formulation.
boundary_notes: A small but nonzero eigenvalue represents ill-conditioning, not exact singularity.
The reduced-Hessian characterization alone is valid only after full row rank of \(A\) has been established.

notation.meaning: Null space of the complete KKT matrix.
Multiplicity of the zero eigenvalue of a symmetric matrix.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equivalent representations of a linearized equality correction
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(H\in\mathbb S_{++}^n\), let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) have full row rank, and consider the unique correction \((p,\lambda)\) satisfying \(Hp+A^T\lambda=-g\) and \(Ap=r\). Let \(Z\) span \(\ker A\), and let \(p_F\) satisfy \(Ap_F=r\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact finite-dimensional linear algebra for positive-definite weighted equality corrections; the representations describe the same correction, not different optimization problems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The equality correction representation family is the collection of algebraically equivalent coordinate descriptions of the unique solution of \[\left(\begin{smallmatrix}H&A^T\\A&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)\binom{p}{\lambda}=\binom{-g}{r}.\] It includes: the full-space primal-dual representation above; the range-space representation \((AH^{-1}A^T)\lambda=-r-AH^{-1}g\), followed by \(p=-H^{-1}(g+A^T\lambda)\); the null-space representation \(p=p_F+Zz\), where \((Z^THZ)z=-Z^T(g+Hp_F)\); and, after selecting an invertible variable block of \(A\), an explicit dependent-variable elimination. These belong to one family because each produces the same vector \(p\) and multiplier \(\lambda\) whenever its stated factors are nonsingular and all solves are exact.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An equality correction can be represented as one coupled primal-dual system, as a multiplier equation in constraint space, as a reduced equation in tangent coordinates, or by eliminating dependent variables. Under the stated rank and positive-definiteness conditions these are exact coordinate descriptions of the same unique correction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\mathcal R(H,A,g,r)=\{\text{full-space, range-space, null-space, and explicit-elimination descriptions yielding the same }(p,\lambda)\}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(p=p_F+Zz\) with \(AZ=0\) is equivalent to imposing \(Ap=r\) before minimizing the quadratic model.
Eliminating \(p\) from the full KKT system gives the range-space equation; eliminating feasibility coordinates gives the null-space equation.
special_cases_latex: For \(r=0\), every representation produces a tangent correction satisfying \(Ap=0\).
For \(H=I\), the range-space matrix becomes \(AA^T\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Representation choice changes system dimension and sparsity but not the exact correction.
boundary_notes: With inexact solves, regularization, or different generalized inverses, nominally related representations need not produce identical numerical corrections.
If \(H\) is indefinite but positive definite on \(\ker A\), the null-space and full-space formulations remain meaningful while the displayed range-space elimination through \(H^{-1}\) may fail.

notation.meaning: Any particular vector satisfying the linearized equality equation.
Coordinates of the tangent component in a null-space basis.

children.title: Explicit Constraint Elimination
children.top_down_role: Representations that remove equality variables before the optimization calculation.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Consider \(\min_{x\in X} f(x)\) subject to \(c(x)=0\), where \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), \(c:X\to\mathbb R^m\), and the variables are partitioned as \(x=(v,u)\in\mathbb R^m\times\mathbb R^{n-m}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact elimination on a specified parameter domain; the parameterization may be global for affine constraints or only local for nonlinear constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Explicit constraint elimination is a representation by a map \(\phi:U\to\\mathbb R^m\) such that \(c(\phi(u),u)=0\) for every \(u\in U\), together with the parameterization \(\Phi(u)=(\phi(u),u)\). It is exact on \(U\) when \[\Phi(U)=\{(v,u)\in X:c(v,u)=0,\ u\in U\}\] and \(\Phi\) is one-to-one. The equality-constrained problem over this set is then defined equivalently as the unconstrained reduced problem \(\min_{u\in U}F(u)\), where \(F(u)=f(\Phi(u))\). The variables \(v\) are dependent variables and are removed before the optimization calculation; \(u\) are independent or reduced variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Explicit constraint elimination replaces selected dependent variables by a function of the remaining independent variables. The map must satisfy the equalities identically and parameterize exactly the feasible portion under consideration. Substitution into the objective then yields an equivalent reduced problem involving only the independent variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[c(\Phi(u))=0\ \forall u\in U,\qquad \min_{x\in\Phi(U)}f(x)=\min_{u\in U}f(\Phi(u)).\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The feasible set under consideration is the graph \(\{(\phi(u),u):u\in U\}\).
Optimization over feasible \(x\) is optimization over the reduced coordinates \(u\).
special_cases_latex: For affine constraints, \(\phi\) is affine and may parameterize the entire feasible set.
For regular nonlinear constraints, the implicit-function theorem supplies \(\phi\) only in a neighborhood of a reference feasible point.
immediate_consequences_latex: Every reduced iterate \(u\in U\) maps to an exactly feasible full-space point \(\Phi(u)\).
boundary_notes: A parameterization covering only one local branch is not a global elimination of all feasible points.
Elimination can produce a dense or poorly conditioned reduced objective even when the original constraint representation is sparse.

notation.meaning: Dependent variables removed by the equality equations.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Benefit and risk of constraint-based variable elimination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Applies when constraints permit some variables to be expressed in terms of the remaining variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Using constraints to eliminate variables can reduce the number of degrees of freedom in a constrained optimization problem. The reduction must be used carefully because elimination may alter the represented problem or introduce ill conditioning.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Constraint-based variable elimination can simplify a problem by reducing its degrees of freedom, but it can also change the represented problem or introduce ill conditioning.
assumptions_latex: \text{A constrained optimization problem is being reduced by eliminating variables through its constraints.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Elimination can reduce the degrees of freedom, but may alter the problem or introduce ill conditioning.}

knowledge_statements.title: Affine Variable Elimination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact global reduction of affine equalities through an invertible variable block.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min_{x_B,x_N} f(x_B,x_N)\) subject to \(A_Bx_B+A_Nx_N=b\), where the square block \(A_B\) is nonsingular. Every feasible point is uniquely represented by \[x_B=A_B^{-1}(b-A_Nx_N).\] Hence the constrained problem is equivalent to the unconstrained reduced problem \[\min_{x_N}\ \phi(x_N),\qquad \phi(x_N)=f\bigl(A_B^{-1}(b-A_Nx_N),x_N\bigr).\] A minimizer of either problem maps to a minimizer of the other through this substitution, and feasibility is satisfied exactly rather than iteratively.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An invertible block of an affine equality system can be solved globally for dependent variables, producing an equivalent unconstrained problem in the remaining variables.
assumptions_latex: The objective is defined on every point generated by the substitution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The feasible set is parameterized bijectively by \(x_N\mapsto\bigl(A_B^{-1}(b-A_Nx_N),x_N\bigr)\).

notation.meaning: Variables eliminated through the invertible affine block.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Global elimination under affine equality constraints
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) have full row rank, let \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), and partition, after a possible column permutation, \(A=[B\ R]\) and \(x=(x_B,x_R)\), where \(B\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}\) is nonsingular.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global, exact elimination for a consistent affine equality system with a nonsingular selected dependent-variable block.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Affine variable elimination is the global parameterization of \(Ax=b\) obtained by solving the dependent block: \[x_B=B^{-1}(b-Rx_R).\] With \(u=x_R\), every feasible point is represented uniquely by \[x(u)=\binom{B^{-1}b-B^{-1}Ru}{u},\qquad u\in\mathbb R^{n-m}.\] Hence minimizing \(f(x)\) subject to \(Ax=b\) is equivalent to minimizing \(F(u)=f(x(u))\) over \(\mathbb R^{n-m}\), or over those \(u\) for which additional domain restrictions on \(x(u)\) hold. The direction matrix \(Z=(-B^{-1}R,I)^T\) satisfies \(AZ=0\), while \((B^{-1}b,0)^T\) is a particular feasible point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For independent affine equalities, select a square nonsingular block of constraint columns. The corresponding dependent variables are an affine function of the remaining variables. This formula uniquely parameterizes the entire affine feasible set and converts the equality-constrained problem into a reduced problem in the free variables.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\{x:Ax=b\}=\left\{\binom{B^{-1}(b-Ru)}{u}:u\in\mathbb R^{n-m}\right\}.\]
special_cases_latex: If \(m=n\), there are no reduced variables and the consistent equality system has the single feasible point \(x=A^{-1}b\).
If \(b=0\), the feasible set is the linear null space represented by \(Zu\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The reduced objective is \(F(u)=f(B^{-1}(b-Ru),u)\).
The parameterization maintains affine feasibility exactly in exact arithmetic.
boundary_notes: The selected block \(B\) can be nonsingular but ill-conditioned, making the elimination numerically unreliable.
Dependent-variable bounds or other side constraints become transformed restrictions on \(u\).

notation.meaning: Nonsingular constraint block associated with dependent variables.
Remaining constraint columns associated with free variables.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Applies when affine equalities are eliminated from a problem that retains inequality constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: When variables are eliminated using affine equalities in a problem that also contains inequalities, the inequalities must be rewritten in the reduced variables. Simple bounds such as \(x\ge 0\) may thereby become coupled linear inequalities, so elimination need not benefit algorithms that exploit bound structure. When substitution does not substantially complicate the retained inequalities, performing the equality elimination may still be beneficial.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Eliminating equalities can turn simple bounds into coupled inequalities and destroy useful structure. The reduction may remain worthwhile when the retained inequalities do not become substantially more complicated.
assumptions_latex: \text{Affine equality constraints are used to eliminate variables.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Equality elimination may complicate the retained inequality system, and its usefulness depends on whether exploitable inequality structure is preserved.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Coordinate null-space representation from a basis partition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interprets simple affine elimination as a particular feasible point plus a null-space displacement and records the limitation of pivot-based basis selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A=[B\mid N]\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), where \(B\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}\) is nonsingular, and define \(Y=\begin{bmatrix}B^{-1}\\0\end{bmatrix}\) and \(Z=\begin{bmatrix}-B^{-1}N\\I\end{bmatrix}\). Then \(AZ=0\), \(Z\) has \(n-m\) linearly independent columns, and every solution of \(Ax=b\) has the form \(x=Yb+Zx_N\). Thus \(Yb\) is a particular solution and the columns of \(Z\) form a basis for \(\ker A\). Gaussian elimination can select a valid \(B\) through pivot columns, but it does not guarantee the best basis choice with respect to conditioning, factorization ease, or sparsity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A basis-column partition expresses every feasible point as a coordinate-relaxation particular solution plus an arbitrary null-space displacement. Gaussian elimination can select a valid basis, but it need not select the most favorable basis for conditioning, factorization, or sparsity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax=b\}=\{Yb+Zx_N:x_N\in\mathbb R^{n-m}\},\quad AZ=0,\quad \operatorname{rank}(Z)=n-m,\quad \operatorname{range}(Z)=\ker A.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Generalized Null-Space Elimination for Equality-Constrained Quadratics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine feasible-space parametrization, reduced solution, basis choices, and the numerical boundary of coordinate elimination.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{n\times m}\) have full column rank. Let the columns of \(Z\) form a basis of \(\mathcal N(A^T)\), and choose \(Y\in\mathbb R^{n\times m}\) so that \(A^TY\) is nonsingular. Then \([Y\ Z]\) is nonsingular and every feasible point has the unique representation \(x=Y(A^TY)^{-1}b+Z\hat x\). Substitution reduces the equality-constrained quadratic to an unconstrained quadratic with \(H_r=Z^TGZ\) and \(r=Z^T(g+GY(A^TY)^{-1}b)\). If \(H_r\succ0\), then \(\hat x^*=-H_r^{-1}r\) and \(x^*=Y(A^TY)^{-1}b-ZH_r^{-1}r\). For a coordinate partition with nonsingular \(A_B\), one may take \(Y=(A_B^{-T},0)^T\) and \(Z=(-A_B^{-T}A_N^T,I)^T\). From \(A=Q_1R\), the QR choice is \(Y=Q_1R^{-T}\), \(Z=Q_2\). Coordinate elimination can be numerically unstable when \(A_B\) is nearly singular.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A complementary matrix and a null-space basis uniquely parametrize the feasible affine space and reduce the quadratic program to an unconstrained reduced quadratic. Positive-definite reduced curvature gives the displayed unique solution. Coordinate and QR constructions are special basis choices, while a nearly singular eliminated block is a numerical failure boundary for coordinate elimination.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \{x:A^Tx=b\}=Y(A^TY)^{-1}b+\mathcal R(Z),\qquad x^*=Y(A^TY)^{-1}b-Z(Z^TGZ)^{-1}Z^T\bigl(g+GY(A^TY)^{-1}b\bigr).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Simple elimination for full-row-rank linear equalities
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Global reduction of a nonlinear objective subject to full-row-rank linear equality constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min_{x\in\mathbb R^n} f(x)\) subject to \(Ax=b\), where \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(b\in\mathbb R^m\), \(m\le n\), and \(\operatorname{rank}(A)=m\). Choose a permutation matrix \(P\) such that \(AP=[B\mid N]\), where \(B\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}\) is nonsingular, and write \(P^Tx=\begin{bmatrix}x_B\\x_N\end{bmatrix}\). Then \(Ax=b\) if and only if \(x_B=B^{-1}b-B^{-1}Nx_N\). Hence the constrained problem is equivalent to \(\min_{x_N\in\mathbb R^{n-m}} f\!\left(P\begin{bmatrix}B^{-1}b-B^{-1}Nx_N\\x_N\end{bmatrix}\right)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For full-row-rank linear equalities, an invertible set of m columns can be selected as a basis. The basic variables are determined uniquely by the remaining variables, and substitution produces an equivalent unconstrained problem in n−m variables.
assumptions_latex: AP=[B\mid N]\ \text{for a permutation matrix }P\text{ and nonsingular }B\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Ax=b\iff x_B=B^{-1}b-B^{-1}Nx_N,\qquad \min_{Ax=b}f(x)\equiv\min_{x_N\in\mathbb R^{n-m}}f\!\left(P\begin{bmatrix}B^{-1}b-B^{-1}Nx_N\\x_N\end{bmatrix}\right).

knowledge_statements.title: Nonlinear Local Elimination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Implicit-function reduction using a locally nonsingular dependent-variable Jacobian.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(c:\mathbb{R}^{p}\times\mathbb{R}^{q}\to\mathbb{R}^{p}\) be continuously differentiable near \((y_0,z_0)\), with \(c(y_0,z_0)=0\) and nonsingular \(D_yc(y_0,z_0)\). Then there are neighborhoods \(U\) of \(z_0\) and \(V\) of \(y_0\), and a unique continuously differentiable map \(\phi:U\to V\), such that, for every \((y,z)\in V\times U\), \(c(y,z)=0\) if and only if \(y=\phi(z)\). After shrinking the neighborhoods if necessary, \(D_yc(\phi(z),z)\) is nonsingular for every \(z\in U\), and \(D\phi(z)=-D_yc(\phi(z),z)^{-1}D_zc(\phi(z),z)\). Consequently, for any objective \(f:V\times U\to\mathbb{R}\), feasible points of the problem restricted to \(V\times U\) correspond bijectively to points \(z\in U\), with objective value \(f(\phi(z),z)\); hence minimizers and local minimizers correspond under this parametrization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A regular block of nonlinear equalities uniquely determines the dependent variables as continuously differentiable functions of the free variables, giving an equivalent optimization problem within a sufficiently small neighborhood.
assumptions_latex: \(f:V\times U\to\mathbb{R}\) is an objective defined on the local neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Locally, \(c(y,z)=0\iff y=\phi(z)\), \(D\phi=-D_yc^{-1}D_zc\), and optimization on the local feasible set is equivalent to optimization of \(z\mapsto f(\phi(z),z)\).

notation.meaning: objective on the local product neighborhood

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Local elimination of regular nonlinear equalities
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(c:\mathbb R^m\times\mathbb R^{n-m}\to\mathbb R^m\) be continuously differentiable near \((\bar v,\bar u)\), with \(c(\bar v,\bar u)=0\), and suppose the partial Jacobian \(D_vc(\bar v,\bar u)\) is nonsingular.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local smooth parameterization supplied by the implicit-function theorem; it covers one regular branch near a reference feasible point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Nonlinear local elimination at \((\bar v,\bar u)\) is the representation furnished by neighborhoods \(V\) of \(\bar v\), \(U\) of \(\bar u\), and a unique continuously differentiable map \(\phi:U\to V\) such that \[c(\phi(u),u)=0\quad\text{for all }u\in U,\qquad \phi(\bar u)=\bar v,\] and every zero of \(c\) in \(V\times U\) is of the form \((\phi(u),u)\). Its derivative is \[D\phi(u)=-D_vc(\phi(u),u)^{-1}D_uc(\phi(u),u).\] The locally equivalent reduced objective is \(F(u)=f(\phi(u),u)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Near a feasible point where the Jacobian with respect to selected dependent variables is invertible, the nonlinear equality equations uniquely express those variables as a differentiable function of the remaining variables. The graph of this function is exactly the nearby feasible branch, and substituting it into the objective defines the local reduced problem.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\{(v,u)\in V\times U:c(v,u)=0\}=\{(\phi(u),u):u\in U\}.\]
equivalent_formulations_latex: The local feasible set is the graph of \(\phi\).
Its tangent directions have the form \((D\phi(\bar u)d,d)\) for \(d\in\mathbb R^{n-m}\).
special_cases_latex: For affine \(c(v,u)=Bv+Ru-b\), the map is global and equals \(\phi(u)=B^{-1}(b-Ru)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Reduced iterates in \(U\) map to exactly feasible points on the selected local branch.
If \(f\) is twice continuously differentiable and \(c\) is sufficiently smooth, the reduced derivatives incorporate the curvature of the feasible manifold.
boundary_notes: The definition does not assert that one map covers disconnected or folded portions of the feasible set.
Loss of nonsingularity of \(D_vc\) prevents this selected variable partition from defining a regular local graph.

notation.meaning: Jacobian of the equality map with respect to dependent variables.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dependent-variable correction and step decomposition in generalized elimination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Trial-point reconstruction for nonlinear local elimination, including its approximate-Newton correction, exact full-step decomposition, and identity-coordinate specialization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x_k=S_kw_k\), with \(S_k=[(S_k)_B,(S_k)_N]\). For a trial \(\alpha>0\), the dependent coordinates target
\[
w_B=\bar\phi\bigl((w_k)_N+\alpha\bar d_k\bigr),
\]
where \(w_B\) solves
\[
c\!\left((S_k)_Bw_B+(S_k)_N\bigl[(w_k)_N+\alpha\bar d_k\bigr]\right)=0.
\]
They may be computed by the frozen-Jacobian approximate-Newton iteration
\[
w_B^{(i+1)}=w_B^{(i)}-\left[((\nabla c(x_k)^T)^T(S_k)_B)\right]^{-1}c\!\left((S_k)_Bw_B^{(i)}+(S_k)_N\bigl[(w_k)_N+\alpha\bar d_k\bigr]\right).
\]
For the accepted step,
\[
x_{k+1}=x_k+d_k^{(1)}+d_k^{(2)},\qquad d_k^{(1)}=\alpha_k(S_k)_N\bar d_k,
\]
\[
d_k^{(2)}=(S_k)_B\left[\bar\phi\bigl((w_k)_N+\alpha_k\bar d_k\bigr)-(w_k)_B\right].
\]
If \(S_k=I\) at every iteration, the generalized elimination method is the original elimination method.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For each trial reduced-space step, the dependent coordinates are obtained by solving the nonlinear constraint equations, using the displayed frozen-Jacobian approximate-Newton iteration. The accepted full-space increment decomposes exactly into a free-coordinate step and a dependent-coordinate correction. With the identity coordinate transformation at every iteration, generalized elimination reduces to the original elimination method.
assumptions_latex: ((\nabla c(x_k)^T)^T(S_k)_B)\text{ is nonsingular whenever the approximate-Newton update is applied}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: x_{k+1}-x_k=d_k^{(1)}+d_k^{(2)};\qquad (S_k=I\ \forall k)\Longrightarrow\text{generalized elimination is the original elimination method}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Reliability boundary for nonlinear variable elimination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Contrasts direct elimination through nonlinear constraint equations with elimination applied after constraint linearization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Direct elimination using nonlinear constraint equations may produce errors that are difficult to trace. Consequently, many optimization algorithms instead linearize the constraints and apply elimination to the resulting linearized system.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Direct nonlinear elimination can produce difficult-to-trace errors, so many algorithms instead linearize the constraints and eliminate variables from the linearized system.
assumptions_latex: \text{Variable elimination through nonlinear constraint equations is under consideration.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The risk of difficult-to-trace errors motivates elimination on a linearized constraint system rather than direct nonlinear elimination.}

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Null-space condition for a linearized-feasible generalized-elimination component
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sufficient null-space condition placing the free-coordinate step component in the linearized equality-constraint tangent space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
d_k^{(1)}=\alpha_k(S_k)_N\bar d_k.
\]
If
\[
(S_k)_N^T\nabla c(x_k)^T=0,
\]
then, equivalently by transposition, \(\nabla c(x_k)(S_k)_N=0\), and hence
\[
\nabla c(x_k)d_k^{(1)}=0.
\]
Thus \(d_k^{(1)}\) is a linearized feasible direction. With this null-space choice, feasible-direction methods can be viewed as special generalized-elimination methods.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If the free-coordinate block lies in the null space of the constraint Jacobian, the corresponding first step component satisfies the linearized equality constraints. Under this choice, feasible-direction methods form a special case of generalized elimination.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \nabla c(x_k)d_k^{(1)}=0;\qquad d_k^{(1)}\text{ is linearized feasible, and feasible-direction methods are special generalized-elimination methods under this choice}.

children.title: Structured State Elimination
children.top_down_role: Block elimination and condensing for state-equation and staged equality systems.

knowledge_statements.title: Structured State Elimination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Forward condensing of linearized staged state equalities into free control increments.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given matrices \(F_k\) and \(G_k\), residuals \(b_k\), a prescribed increment \(\bar d_0\), and an objective \(q(\delta x,\delta u)\), for \(k=0,\ldots,N-1\), consider the staged equalities \(\delta x_{k+1}=F_k\delta x_k+G_k\delta u_k+b_k\) with \(\delta x_0=\bar d_0\). Define the stacked control vector \(\delta u=(\delta u_0,\ldots,\delta u_{N-1})\), initialize \(T_0=0\) and \(t_0=\bar d_0\), and recursively substitute the affine representation \(\delta x_k=T_k\delta u+t_k\) into the next staged equality to obtain \(\delta x_{k+1}=T_{k+1}\delta u+t_{k+1}\), where only controls through stage \(k\) occur. Substitute these expressions into \(q\) and any remaining constraints, solve the condensed problem in \(\delta u\), and recover every \(\delta x_k\) by forward recursion. The recovered pair satisfies every staged equality by construction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Forward substitution expresses all state increments in terms of the stacked controls, produces a condensed control problem, and recovers equality-feasible states afterward.
assumptions_latex: The staged equalities explicitly determine each \(\delta x_{k+1}\).
The initial increment satisfies \(\delta x_0=\bar d_0\) for a prescribed vector \(\bar d_0\).
All matrices, residuals, and objective arguments have compatible dimensions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The condensed variables are \(\delta u=(\delta u_0,\ldots,\delta u_{N-1})\), and forward recovery produces \(\delta x_{k+1}=F_k\delta x_k+G_k\delta u_k+b_k\) for every \(k=0,\ldots,N-1\).

notation.meaning: free control increment at stage k
stacked vector of all control increments
