knowledge_statements.statement_title: Projected Stationarity and Coupled KKT Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence between projected stationarity and existence of a full-space multiplier correction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) have full row rank and let \(Z\) satisfy \(\operatorname{range}(Z)=\ker A\). For any \(p\) with \(Ap=-c\), set \(r:=Bp+g\). Then \[Z^Tr=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad r\in\operatorname{range}(A^T)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\exists\,\delta\lambda\in\mathbb R^m:\ Bp+A^T\delta\lambda=-g.\] Full row rank makes \(\delta\lambda\) unique.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Projected stationarity is equivalent to full KKT stationarity with a uniquely recoverable multiplier correction.
assumptions_latex: \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) has full row rank.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Z^T(Bp+g)=0\iff\exists!\,\delta\lambda:\ Bp+A^T\delta\lambda=-g.\)
knowledge_statements.title: Projected Stationarity and Coupled KKT Correspondence

children.title: Equivalence Failure Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Rank, basis, or consistency regimes that obstruct the standard correspondence.

knowledge_statements.title: Equivalence Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditions under which full–reduced correction correspondence, existence, or uniqueness fails.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(B=B^\top\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\), \(g\in\mathbb R^n\), and \(c\in\mathbb R^m\). If \(c\notin\operatorname{range}(A)\), then no \(v\in\mathbb R^n\) satisfies \(Av=-c\), so the affine feasible correction set is empty. If \(v\) is feasible but the columns of \(Z\in\mathbb R^{n\times k}\) do not form a basis of \(\ker A\), then \(u\mapsto v+Zu\) is not a bijection onto the feasible set: column dependence destroys injectivity, while \(\operatorname{range}(Z)\subsetneq\ker A\) destroys surjectivity. If \(Z\) is a valid null-space basis, the coordinate correspondence remains bijective even when \(Z^\top BZ\) is singular; in that case the reduced equation
\[
Z^\top BZ\,u=-Z^\top(g+Bv)
\]
has no solution when \(-Z^\top(g+Bv)\notin\operatorname{range}(Z^\top BZ)\), and has nonunique solutions when it is consistent and \(\ker(Z^\top BZ)\neq\{0\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Feasibility is lost when the linearized constraints are incompatible, and coordinate equivalence is lost when the proposed null-space matrix is not a basis. A singular reduced Hessian does not destroy the coordinate bijection, but it can make the reduced correction equation inconsistent or nonunique.
assumptions_latex: \(Z\in\mathbb R^{n\times k}\) is a candidate null-space coordinate matrix
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A bijective full–reduced coordinate correspondence requires a feasible \(v\) and a basis matrix \(Z\) for \(\ker A\); unique solvability of the reduced correction additionally requires \(Z^\top BZ\) to be nonsingular.

notation.meaning: reduced Hessian when Z is a null-space basis
particular feasible correction when one exists

knowledge_statements.title: Full–Reduced Correction Equivalence Failure Conditions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditions under which full–reduced correction correspondence, existence, or uniqueness fails.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), \(B=B^\top\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\), \(g\in\mathbb R^n\), and \(c\in\mathbb R^m\). If \(c\notin\operatorname{range}(A)\), then no \(v\in\mathbb R^n\) satisfies \(Av=-c\), so the affine feasible correction set is empty. If \(v\) is feasible but the columns of \(Z\in\mathbb R^{n\times k}\) do not form a basis of \(\ker A\), then \(u\mapsto v+Zu\) is not a bijection onto the feasible set: column dependence destroys injectivity, while \(\operatorname{range}(Z)\subsetneq\ker A\) destroys surjectivity. If \(Z\) is a valid null-space basis, the coordinate correspondence remains bijective even when \(Z^\top BZ\) is singular; in that case the reduced equation
\[
Z^\top BZ\,u=-Z^\top(g+Bv)
\]
has no solution when \(-Z^\top(g+Bv)\notin\operatorname{range}(Z^\top BZ)\), and has nonunique solutions when it is consistent and \(\ker(Z^\top BZ)\neq\{0\}\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Leading-order dense arithmetic terms relevant to the full-versus-null-space selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(r=n-m\). A dense direct factorization of the \((n+m)\)-order KKT matrix costs \(O((n+m)^3)\). An explicit null-space route using a dense orthogonal factorization to construct \(Z\in\mathbb R^{n\times r}\), followed by forming \(Z^{\mathsf T}HZ\) and factoring it, has representative costs \[O(nm^2)+O(n^2r+nr^2)+O(r^3).\] Constants and lower-order terms depend on symmetry and the chosen factorizations. Consequently, \(O(r^3)\) alone is not a valid total-cost comparison.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dense reduction includes basis construction and reduced-matrix formation as well as the smaller factorization; comparing only cubic solve dimensions can be misleading.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(m\) independent equalities in \(n\) variables, the full KKT representation has order \(n+m\), whereas a null-space reduction has order \(n-m\) after constructing a null-space basis and a feasible particular correction. In a dense direct-factorization model, the nominal factorization costs scale respectively as \(O((n+m)^3)\) and \(O((n-m)^3)\), excluding basis construction and reduced-matrix formation. Hence dimension alone favors reduction when \(n-m\ll n+m\); it does not justify reduction when forming or storing \(Z\) dominates, especially when \(m\ll n\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A representation-selection definition based on reduced system dimensions; it does not assert a universal runtime optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Dimension-driven representation selection classifies an exact correction formulation by the principal system dimension it exposes: full-space uses dimension \(n+m\); range-space uses dimension \(m\), provided the Hessian block can be solved with economically; and null-space uses reduced dimension \(d=n-m\), provided a suitable null-space representation is available. A dimension-preferred representation is one minimizing the relevant reduced dimension among admissible formulations: \[R_{\rm dim}\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{R\in\mathcal A}\{n+m,m,n-m\}_R,\] where \(\mathcal A\) contains only representations satisfying their algebraic assumptions. Thus small \(m\) favors range space, while small \(n-m\) favors null space; the full system remains available when reduction prerequisites or formation costs dominate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Dimension-driven selection compares the full system size with the number of constraints and the number of remaining degrees of freedom. Range-space reduction is dimensionally attractive for few constraints, null-space reduction for few free degrees of freedom, and full-space treatment when reductions are inadmissible or costly to form.

Only algebraically admissible representations enter the comparison.
Dimension is the selection attribute; sparsity, conditioning, and setup cost are separate attributes.

equivalent_formulations_latex: The rule may be stated as comparing constraint count \(m\) with tangent dimension \(n-m\).
A hybrid decision may retain full space when neither reduced system can be formed reliably.
special_cases_latex: If \(m\ll n\), range-space dimension is small.
If \(n-m\ll n\), null-space dimension is small.
immediate_consequences_latex: Dimension alone cannot rank methods having substantially different fill-in or operator costs.
The selected exact representation must still return the same correction as the full KKT system.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(K=\begin{bmatrix}G&A^T\\A&0\end{bmatrix}\), with candidate full-, range-, and null-space representations of the same correction.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sparse or matrix-free finite-dimensional linear algebra; selection concerns representation requirements rather than a fixed solver implementation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Sparsity-operator representation selection assigns to each admissible representation \(R\) a structural signature \[\sigma(R)=\bigl(\operatorname{fill}(R),\operatorname{storage}(R),\mathcal O(R),\operatorname{setup}(R)\bigr),\] where \(\mathcal O(R)\) lists required operations such as products with \(G\), \(A\), and \(A^T\), solves with \(G\), explicit construction of \(AG^{-1}A^T\), or construction and application of a null-space basis \(Z\). A representation is structurally admissible only if its required operators are available and its anticipated factor fill and storage meet the prescribed resource bounds. Selection is then a preference relation over admissible signatures, not an algebraic change to the correction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Sparsity-operator selection chooses among equivalent formulations by comparing predicted factor fill, storage, block structure, setup work, and available matrix or product interfaces. A method requiring an unavailable inverse, basis, or explicit matrix is excluded before numerical cost is compared.
assumptions_latex: All compared representations are algebraically equivalent for the correction under consideration.
Sparsity patterns or operator interfaces for \(G\), \(A\), and \(A^T\) are known.
Fill and setup estimates are representation- and ordering-dependent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The selected representation is any admissible \(R\) whose structural signature is preferred under the declared fill, storage, setup, and operator-availability criteria.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Full-space selection requires access to the saddle-point matrix or its block operators.
Range-space selection requires economical solves with \(G\); null-space selection requires construction or implicit action of \(Z\).
special_cases_latex: Sparse full-KKT factorization is attractive when symmetric ordering preserves sparse factors.
A matrix-free iterative formulation is attractive when products are available but explicit reduced matrices are not.
immediate_consequences_latex: A smaller reduced dimension can still be rejected because forming the reduced matrix destroys sparsity.
Dense columns in \(A\) can make normal-equation or Schur-complement formation substantially denser.
boundary_notes: No ordering-independent scalar fill measure determines the best representation universally.
The definition does not guarantee numerical stability; pivoting and conditioning remain separate requirements.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For algebraically admissible full-space, null-space, or Schur correction formulations, compare sparsity only after fixing the ordering, partition, basis construction, and whether derived operators are formed or applied implicitly. Selection should minimize predicted or measured storage, operator-formation work, factor fill, factorization work, and solve work for the actual implementation. Sparse \(A\) and \(B\) do not by themselves imply a sparse null-space basis or sparse \(Z^\top BZ\), while a larger KKT matrix can retain exploitable block sparsity; conversely, a structured sparse \(Z\) or small sparse Schur operator can favor reduction. Therefore dimensions or input nonzero counts alone do not determine the preferred representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose among full-space, null-space, and Schur forms using the fill and costs of the actual ordered factors and derived operators; sparse input matrices alone do not determine the winner.

Ordering, partition, basis construction, and explicit-versus-implicit realization are specified
Sparse storage and factorization costs are evaluated for the actual implementation

knowledge_statements.title: Operator-Driven Representation Selection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Selection among equivalent equality-correction formulations according to available operator actions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), \(H=H^T\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\), and \(c\in\mathbb{R}^m\). Consider correction equations containing \(Ap=-c\) for \(p\in\mathbb{R}^n\) and the model operator \(H\). Select a representation only if every product, projection, factorization, and inner solve required by its solver is available. When only the actions \(Av\), \(A^Tw\), and \(Hv\) are available, use an implicit full-space, null-space, or Schur-complement method only if any additional projection or inner-solve actions it requires are also available. When stable reusable factors of \(A\), \(H\), or the KKT matrix are available, a corresponding explicit reduced or direct representation may be selected. Two representations have the same exact solution only when their rank and invertibility hypotheses hold and all required algebraic operations are evaluated exactly; inexact implementations must instead be qualified by residuals for the original correction equations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choose a correction representation whose required products, projections, solves, and factorizations are available. Exact equivalence requires the relevant rank and invertibility conditions and exact algebra; inexact implementations must be checked using residuals of the original equations.
assumptions_latex: Each selected representation is algebraically well-defined under its stated rank and invertibility conditions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A selected representation uses only declared operator primitives; it yields the same exact correction as the original equations only under the stated equivalence hypotheses and exact evaluation.

knowledge_statements.title: Block-Structure Selection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representation selection for partitioned equality-correction systems with exploitable block structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(u,r_1\in\mathbb{R}^p\), \(v,r_2\in\mathbb{R}^q\), \(K_{11}\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times p}\), \(K_{12}\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times q}\), \(K_{21}\in\mathbb{R}^{q\times p}\), and \(K_{22}\in\mathbb{R}^{q\times q}\). For the partitioned equations \(K_{11}u+K_{12}v=r_1\) and \(K_{21}u+K_{22}v=r_2\), if \(K_{11}\) admits stable economical solves, eliminate \(u\), solve \((K_{22}-K_{21}K_{11}^{-1}K_{12})v=r_2-K_{21}K_{11}^{-1}r_1\), and recover \(u=K_{11}^{-1}(r_1-K_{12}v)\). Use the reverse ordering when \(K_{22}\) is nonsingular and is the preferable block to eliminate. In exact arithmetic either valid ordering solves the original system; computational selection should account for sparsity, reusable factors, and whether a Schur block should be formed or applied implicitly.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Eliminate a nonsingular block for which stable economical solves are available, choosing the ordering and explicit or implicit Schur representation according to sparsity and factor reuse.
assumptions_latex: \(p,q\in\mathbb{N}\), with the blocks and vectors having the displayed conforming dimensions.
\(K_{11}\) is nonsingular for the displayed ordering.
The partition conforms to the equality-correction equations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed Schur equation and recovery equation solve the original partitioned system exactly in exact arithmetic.

notation.meaning: blocks of the partitioned correction operator

knowledge_statements.statement_title: A Singular Elimination Block Need Not Make the Full System Singular
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of a diagonal-block Schur ordering without failure of the original system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \[K=\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{bmatrix},\] the full matrix is nonsingular, but \(K_{11}=K_{22}=0\). Thus neither diagonal-block Schur formula is defined although \(K[u\;v]^\top=r\) has a unique solution for every \(r\). Singularity of a proposed elimination block invalidates that ordering, not necessarily the original correction equations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonsingular block system may have singular diagonal blocks, so failure of a Schur ordering does not imply failure of the original system.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\det K=-1\ne0\) although both diagonal blocks are singular.

children.title: Matrix-Free Selection Regimes
children.top_down_role: Representation choices when explicit matrices or bases are unavailable.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Whole-solve access condition for a matrix-free equality-correction representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For linear operators \(A\) and \(H\), a correction method is matrix-free only if initialization, every iteration, residual testing, preconditioning or inner solves, and recovery use vector arithmetic, declared actions such as \(Av\), \(A^\top w\), and \(Hv\), and explicitly declared auxiliary operator actions, without requiring assembly or storage of \(A\), \(H\), a null-space basis, the KKT matrix, or a Schur complement. Select this regime when those actions and an original-equation residual test are available and explicit storage or factorization is impractical. Its work and storage comparison must include all operator products, inner actions, retained Krylov vectors, and recovery operations rather than only the nominal outer iteration.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A solve is matrix-free only when its entire workflow, including residual checks, preconditioning, and recovery, uses declared operator actions without hidden matrix assembly.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) and \(H\) define finite-dimensional linear operator actions
All auxiliary preconditioner and inner-solve actions are declared
A computable residual for the original correction equations is available
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The representation is matrix-free admissible exactly when every required stage respects the declared operator-only access model.

Matrix-Free Selection Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Admissibility condition for matrix-free equality-correction representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For operators \(A\) and \(H\), a correction representation is matrix-free admissible if its initialization, every iteration, residual test, and recovery step require only vector arithmetic, products \(Av\), \(A^Tw\), \(Hv\), and explicitly declared preconditioner or inner-solve actions. It must not require assembling or storing \(A\), \(H\), a null-space basis, the KKT matrix, or a Schur complement. A matrix-free regime is selected when these actions are available and explicit storage or factorization is infeasible; termination at tolerance \(\varepsilon\) requires a computable residual norm no larger than \(\varepsilon\) for the represented correction equations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A regime is matrix-free only when initialization, iterations, residual checks, and recovery use operator products and declared preconditioners without assembling reduced or KKT matrices.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) and \(H\) define linear operator actions on finite-dimensional Euclidean spaces.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The representation is matrix-free admissible precisely when all solver operations satisfy the stated access restriction.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Solution family for equality-constrained quadratic KKT systems
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(q(x)=\tfrac12x^TGx+c^Tx\), where \(G=G^T\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\), subject to \(Ax=b\), with \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional equality-constrained quadratic programming, including direct, reduced, and iterative representations of its KKT equations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The equality quadratic KKT solution family consists of the primal–dual solution set \[\mathcal S(G,c,A,b):=\left\{(x,\lambda):\begin{bmatrix}G&-A^T\\A&0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x\\\lambda\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-c\\b\end{bmatrix}\right\}\] together with algebraically equivalent procedures that compute its members: direct factorization of the full KKT matrix, range-space Schur-complement reduction when \(G\) is suitably invertible, null-space reduction using a basis of \(\ker A\), and convergent iterative solution of the full or projected system. If \(A\) has full row rank and \(Z^TGZ\succ0\), the family contains exactly one pair \((x^*,\lambda^*)\), and \(x^*\) is the unique global minimizer of the quadratic program.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The solution family is the set of primal points and equality multipliers satisfying the quadratic KKT equations, together with exact full-space, range-space, null-space, and iterative representations of that same set. Under independent constraints and positive reduced curvature, the set is a singleton and its primal member is the unique global minimizer.
assumptions_latex: For the stated uniqueness conclusion, \(\operatorname{rank}(A)=m\) and \(Z^TGZ\succ0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal S(G,c,A,b)\) is the canonical primal–dual KKT solution set; under full row rank and positive reduced curvature it equals \(\{(x^*,\lambda^*)\}\), with \(x^*\) the unique global minimizer.
equivalent_formulations_latex: The correction form uses \(x^*=x+p\) and the KKT system for \((p,\lambda)\).
Full-, Schur-complement, and null-space systems represent the same unique pair when their assumptions hold.
special_cases_latex: For \(m=0\), the family reduces to unconstrained quadratic stationarity \(Gx=-c\).
For \(G\succ0\) and full-row-rank \(A\), both full and range-space solution forms are nonsingular.
immediate_consequences_latex: Positive definiteness is required only on feasible directions, not necessarily on all of \(\mathbb{R}^n\).
The computational representation may be selected without changing the exact minimizer.
boundary_notes: With singular or indefinite reduced curvature, KKT points need not be unique minimizers.
Inexact iterative outputs are approximations and are not members of the exact set until residuals vanish.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Feasibility and reduced-curvature regimes of equality quadratics
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Consider \(\min_x q(x)=\tfrac12x^TGx+c^Tx\) subject to \(Ax=b\), with \(G=G^T\). Let \(Z\) span \(\ker A\), and let \(R=Z^TGZ\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional exact quadratic models classified by feasibility and the inertia of the reduced Hessian.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The regime of an equality-constrained quadratic is determined first by whether \(b\in\operatorname{range}(A)\), and, when feasible, by the reduced Hessian \(R=Z^TGZ\). The positive reduced-curvature regime has \(R\succ0\). The singular reduced regime has \(R\succeq0\) and \(\ker R
e\{0\}\); it has a finite minimizer precisely when the reduced linear term is orthogonal to \(\ker R\), in which case minimizers are nonunique along flat directions. The indefinite regime has a vector \(d
e0\) with \(d^TRd<0\), so the quadratic is unbounded below along a feasible line. The infeasible regime has \(b
otin\operatorname{range}(A)\) and no feasible point.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Equality quadratics are partitioned first by consistency of the equalities and then by reduced curvature on feasible directions. Positive reduced curvature gives a unique minimizer, singular semidefinite curvature gives either a flat family of minimizers or no finite minimum depending on the reduced linear term, and negative reduced curvature gives unbounded descent.
assumptions_latex: For the reduced linear-term test, choose any feasible \(x_0\) and set \(r=Z^T(Gx_0+c)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The feasible problem belongs to exactly one inertia regime of \(R\): positive definite, positive-semidefinite singular, or indefinite; the singular regime is bounded below exactly when \(r\in\operatorname{range}(R)\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: Writing \(x=x_0+Zz\) gives the reduced quadratic \(\tfrac12z^TRz+r^Tz+q(x_0)\).
The signs of feasible-direction curvature are the signs of the eigenvalues of \(R\).
special_cases_latex: If \(n=m\) and \(A\) is nonsingular, the feasible set is a singleton and there are no nonzero feasible directions.
If \(R=0\), boundedness requires the entire reduced linear term to vanish.
immediate_consequences_latex: The full Hessian may be indefinite while the constrained quadratic lies in the positive reduced-curvature regime.
Negative reduced curvature prevents a finite global minimum on an affine feasible space without additional bounds.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence, uniqueness, and unboundedness after eliminating full-rank equality constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(\min_x g^Tx+\tfrac12x^TGx\) subject to \(A^Tx=b\), where \(G=G^T\), \(A\in\mathbb R^{n\times m}\), and \(\operatorname{rank}(A)=m\). Choose a partition with nonsingular \(A_B\), and set \(x_p=(A_B^{-T}b,0)^T\) and \(N=(-A_B^{-T}A_N^T,I)^T\). Every feasible point is uniquely \(x=x_p+Nt\), and the problem reduces to \(\min_t \tfrac12t^T\widehat Gt+\widehat g^Tt+\widehat c\), where \(\widehat G=N^TGN\) and \(\widehat g=N^T(g+Gx_p)\). If \(\widehat G\succ0\), its unique minimizer is \(t^*=-\widehat G^{-1}\widehat g\). If \(\widehat G\succeq0\), a finite minimum exists exactly when \(\widehat g\in\mathcal R(\widehat G)\), equivalently \((I-\widehat G\widehat G^+)\widehat g=0\); then all minimizers are \(t^*=-\widehat G^+\widehat g+(I-\widehat G^+\widehat G)v\). If the range condition fails, or \(\widehat G\) has a negative eigenvalue, both the reduced and original problems are unbounded below.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Eliminating the equality constraints gives an equivalent quadratic on the constraint null space. Positive-definite reduced curvature gives a unique minimizer. Positive-semidefinite reduced curvature gives a finite minimum exactly when the reduced gradient belongs to the reduced Hessian's range. A failed range condition or negative reduced curvature implies unboundedness below.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \widehat G\succ0\Rightarrow\exists!x^*;\quad \widehat G\succeq0\Rightarrow\bigl(\min Q\text{ exists}\iff\widehat g\in\mathcal R(\widehat G)\bigr);\quad \lambda_{\min}(\widehat G)<0\text{ or }\widehat g\notin\mathcal R(\widehat G)\Rightarrow\inf Q=-\infty.

knowledge_statements.title: Positive Reduced-Curvature Quadratics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional equality quadratic with positive curvature on the feasible tangent space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H=H^T\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\), \(g\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), and \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\), where \(A\) has rank \(m\) and \(\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax=b\}\neq\varnothing\). Define \(q(x)=\tfrac12x^THx+g^Tx\), and let \(Z\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times(n-m)}\) have columns forming a basis of \(\ker A\). If \(Z^THZ\succ0\), then \(q\) has a unique global minimizer \(x_*\) over \(Ax=b\). There is a unique \(\lambda_*\in\mathbb{R}^m\) satisfying \(Hx_*+g+A^T\lambda_*=0\), and the KKT matrix \(\begin{pmatrix}H&A^T\\A&0\end{pmatrix}\) is nonsingular.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a feasible equality-constrained quadratic with a full-row-rank constraint matrix, positive definiteness of the Hessian on the constraint null space gives a unique constrained minimizer, a unique multiplier, and a nonsingular KKT matrix.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: There exists a unique KKT pair \((x_*,\lambda_*)\in\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}^m\), and \(x_*\) uniquely minimizes \(q\) over \(Ax=b\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Exact Reduced Error and Coercivity Identity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantitative geometry of the unique minimizer in the positive reduced-curvature regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the seed assumptions, write each feasible point uniquely as \(x=x_p+Zy\), set \(R=Z^THZ\succ0\), and let \(y_*\) solve \(Ry_*=-Z^T(Hx_p+g)\). Then \[q(x_p+Zy)-q(x_p+Zy_*)=\tfrac12(y-y_*)^TR(y-y_*).\] Consequently the restricted quadratic is coercive and strongly convex in reduced coordinates. If \(Z^TZ=I\), then \[q(x)-q(x_*)\geq\tfrac12\lambda_{\min}(R)\|x-x_*\|^2\] for every feasible \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The objective gap equals one half of the reduced-Hessian energy of the coordinate error, yielding coercivity and a quantitative strong-convexity bound.
assumptions_latex: The feasible affine set is nonempty and \(A\) has full row rank.
\(Z\) is a basis of \(\ker A\) and \(R=Z^THZ\succ0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(q(x)-q(x_*)=\tfrac12(y-y_*)^TR(y-y_*)\geq0\), with equality only at \(x=x_*\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equality quadratic with positive reduced curvature
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(q(x)=\tfrac12x^TGx+c^Tx\) with \(G=G^T\), subject to a consistent system \(Ax=b\). Let \(Z\) span \(\ker A\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional equality-constrained quadratic programming with strict curvature on every nonzero feasible direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The equality-constrained quadratic has positive reduced curvature when \[Z^TGZ\succ0,\] equivalently, \[d^TGd>0\qquad\text{for every }d\ne0\text{ satisfying }Ad=0.\] This condition is independent of the chosen null-space basis. If \(A\) has full row rank, positive reduced curvature makes the KKT matrix nonsingular, gives a unique primal–dual stationary pair, and makes its primal component the unique global minimizer over \(\{x:Ax=b\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quadratic has positive reduced curvature when its Hessian is strictly positive on all nonzero directions tangent to the equality constraints. Under independent constraints this yields a nonsingular KKT system and a unique global constrained minimizer, even if the full Hessian is not positive definite.
assumptions_latex: \(Z\) has full column rank and \(\operatorname{range}(Z)=\ker A\).
For multiplier uniqueness, \(A\) has full row rank.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Positive reduced curvature is the condition \(Z^TGZ\succ0\); with full-row-rank \(A\), it implies a unique KKT pair and a unique global constrained minimizer.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(d^TGd>0\) for all nonzero \(d\in\ker A\).
The reduced quadratic in coordinates \(x=x_0+Zz\) is strictly convex.
special_cases_latex: If \(G\succ0\), positive reduced curvature holds for every constraint matrix.
The condition may hold although \(G\) has negative curvature outside \(\ker A\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The KKT inertia is \((n,m,0)\) when \(A\) has rank \(m\).
The reduced Hessian admits a Cholesky factorization.
boundary_notes: Positive semidefiniteness without strictness belongs to the singular reduced regime.
The condition guarantees exact well-posedness but not favorable numerical conditioning.

knowledge_statements.title: Singular Reduced Quadratics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classification of equality quadratics with positive-semidefinite but singular reduced Hessian.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H=H^T\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\), \(g\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), and \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\), and define \(q(x)=\tfrac12x^THx+g^Tx\) on the nonempty set \(\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax=b\}\). Fix \(x_p\in\mathbb{R}^n\) with \(Ax_p=b\), let the columns of \(Z\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times k}\) form a basis of \(\ker A\), and define \(R=Z^THZ\) and \(c=Z^T(Hx_p+g)\). If \(R\succeq0\) is singular, the reduced quadratic is bounded below if and only if \(c\in\operatorname{range}(R)\). In that case every solution \(y\in\mathbb{R}^k\) of \(Ry=-c\) gives a global minimizer \(x_p+Zy\), and the minimizer set is affine with direction \(Z\ker R\), so no minimizer is isolated. If \(c\notin\operatorname{range}(R)\), then \(q\) is unbounded below on \(Ax=b\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a feasible equality-constrained quadratic with a singular positive-semidefinite reduced Hessian, the objective has an affine nonisolated family of minimizers exactly when the reduced linear coefficient lies in the reduced Hessian's range; otherwise it is unbounded below.
assumptions_latex: \(Ax_p=b\), and \(Z\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times k}\) has columns forming a basis of \(\ker A\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The objective is bounded below if and only if \(c\in\operatorname{range}(R)\); in that case its minimizers form the affine set \(x_p+Z\{y:Ry=-c\}\), and otherwise its infimum is \(-\infty\).

notation.meaning: reduced linear coefficient at a feasible reference point
basis matrix for the null space of A

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical pseudoinverse certificate for a singular positive-semidefinite reduced quadratic.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: With \(R=Z^THZ\succeq0\) singular and \(c=Z^T(Hx_p+g)\), boundedness is equivalent to \((I-RR^\dagger)c=0\). When this holds, all reduced minimizers are \[y_*=-R^\dagger c+v,\qquad v\in\ker R,\] the canonical minimum-norm reduced minimizer is \(-R^\dagger c\), and \[\min_{Ax=b}q(x)=q(x_p)-\tfrac12c^TR^\dagger c.\] If \((I-RR^\dagger)c\neq0\), its nonzero projection identifies a flat component with a nonzero linear term, and the problem is unbounded below.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A pseudoinverse projector tests boundedness, supplies the minimum-norm reduced minimizer and minimum value, and exposes the flat linear component causing unboundedness.
assumptions_latex: \(Ax_p=b\), the columns of \(Z\) form a basis of \(\ker A\), and \(R=Z^THZ\succeq0\) is singular.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((I-RR^\dagger)c=0\) is equivalent to boundedness; when it holds, the minimizers are \(-R^\dagger c+\ker R\) and the minimum value is \(q(x_p)-\tfrac12c^TR^\dagger c\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Equality quadratic with singular reduced Hessian
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(x_0\) satisfy \(Ax_0=b\), let \(Z\) span \(\ker A\), and define \(R=Z^TGZ\) and \(r=Z^T(Gx_0+c)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasible finite-dimensional equality quadratics whose reduced Hessian is positive semidefinite but not positive definite.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A singular reduced quadratic is an equality-constrained quadratic for which \[R=Z^TGZ\succeq0,\qquad\ker R\ne\{0\}.\] In reduced coordinates \(x=x_0+Zz\), its objective is \[q(x_0+Zz)=q(x_0)+r^Tz+	frac12z^TRz.\] If \(r\in\operatorname{range}(R)\), the minimizer set is \[\left\{x_0+Z\bigl(-R^\dagger r+w\bigr):w\in\ker R\right\},\] so no minimizer is isolated. If \(r\notin\operatorname{range}(R)\), the objective is unbounded below along a flat reduced direction and no minimizer exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A singular reduced quadratic has nonnegative but zero curvature in at least one feasible direction. Compatibility of the reduced linear term with the reduced Hessian determines whether the problem has a nonisolated affine family of minimizers or is unbounded below along a flat direction.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The problem has minimizers exactly when \(r\in\operatorname{range}(R)\); then all minimizers are \(x_0+Z(-R^\dagger r+w)\) with \(w\in\ker R\), and otherwise the infimum is \(-\infty\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: Compatibility is equivalent to \(v^Tr=0\) for every \(v\in\ker R\).
At a compatible stationary point, every nonzero \(Zv\) with \(v\in\ker R\) is a flat feasible direction.
special_cases_latex: If \(R=0\) and \(r=0\), every feasible point is a minimizer.
If \(R=0\) and \(r\ne0\), the objective is unbounded below on the feasible affine space.
immediate_consequences_latex: A compatible stationary point is a minimizer but not a strict minimizer.
The unregularized KKT matrix is singular when \(A\) has full row rank and \(R\) is singular.
boundary_notes: A singular indefinite reduced Hessian belongs to the indefinite regime, not this positive-semidefinite singular regime.
Additional bounds or trust regions can isolate solutions and are excluded.

notation.meaning: Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse of the reduced Hessian.

knowledge_statements.title: Indefinite Reduced Quadratics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure of bounded minimization under negative curvature along a feasible direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H=H^T\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\), \(g\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), and \(b\in\mathbb{R}^m\), and define \(q(x)=\tfrac12x^THx+g^Tx\) on the nonempty affine set \(\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:Ax=b\}\). If there exists \(d\in\ker A\) such that \(d^THd<0\), then for every feasible \(x_p\in\mathbb{R}^n\), the line \(x_p+td\), \(t\in\mathbb{R}\), is feasible and \(q(x_p+td)\to-\infty\) as \(|t|\to\infty\). Equivalently, if the columns of \(Z\) span \(\ker A\) and \(Z^THZ\) has a negative eigenvalue, the equality-constrained quadratic is unbounded below and has no global minimizer.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A negative-curvature direction in the equality-constraint null space produces a feasible line along which the quadratic tends to minus infinity, so the problem has no global minimizer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf\{q(x):x\in\mathbb{R}^n,\ Ax=b\}=-\infty\), so the problem has no global minimizer.

notation.meaning: feasible tangent direction of negative curvature
basis matrix for the null space of A

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Stationary-Point Classification under Negative Reduced Curvature
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stationary structure of a feasible equality quadratic whose reduced Hessian has a negative eigenvalue.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\) have full row rank, let \(Ax_p=b\), let the columns of \(Z\) span \(\ker A\), and define \(R=Z^THZ\) and \(c=Z^T(Hx_p+g)\). A feasible KKT point \(x_s=x_p+Zy_s\) exists exactly when \(Ry_s=-c\) is solvable. If \(R\) has a negative eigenvalue, no stationary point is a local minimizer. If \(R\prec0\), the stationary point is unique and is the global maximizer on \(Ax=b\). If \(R\preceq0\) is singular and the stationarity equation is solvable, the stationary points form an affine family of global maximizers. If \(R\) has both positive and negative eigenvalues, every stationary point is a saddle point on the feasible affine space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reduced stationarity is the system Ry=-c. Negative reduced curvature rules out local minima; negative-definite curvature gives a unique global maximum, singular negative-semidefinite curvature gives an affine family of global maxima when stationarity is solvable, and mixed-sign curvature gives saddle points.
assumptions_latex: \(R=Z^THZ\) has at least one negative eigenvalue.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Ry_s=-c\) characterizes feasible stationary points; none is a local minimizer, with the negative-definite, singular negative-semidefinite, and mixed-sign cases classified as stated.

notation.meaning: reduced coordinates of a stationary point

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(q(x)=\tfrac12x^TGx+c^Tx\), \(G=G^T\), subject to a nonempty affine set \(Ax=b\). Let \(Z\) span \(\ker A\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unbounded affine equality-constrained quadratic models without trust-region or bound restrictions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An indefinite reduced quadratic is an equality-constrained quadratic for which the reduced Hessian \(R=Z^TGZ\) has a negative eigenvalue. Equivalently, there exists a nonzero feasible direction \(d\in\ker A\) such that \[d^TGd<0.\] For every feasible \(x_0\), the entire line \(x_0+td\) is feasible and \[q(x_0+td)=q(x_0)+t(Gx_0+c)^Td+	frac12t^2d^TGd\longrightarrow-\infty\quad\text{as }|t|\to\infty.\] Consequently, the unconstrained-affine quadratic has no local or global minimizer, although its KKT equations may possess stationary saddle points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A reduced quadratic is indefinite when the Hessian has negative curvature along at least one equality-feasible direction. Along that feasible line the negative quadratic term dominates, so the objective is unbounded below; any KKT stationary point is not a constrained local minimizer.
assumptions_latex: The affine feasible set \(\{x:Ax=b\}\) is nonempty.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The equality-constrained quadratic is unbounded below on its feasible affine set and has no constrained local or global minimizer.
equivalent_formulations_latex: \(Z^TGZ\) has at least one negative eigenvalue.
There exists a reduced coordinate \(v\ne0\) such that \(v^TZ^TGZv<0\).
special_cases_latex: A nonsingular but indefinite reduced Hessian can yield a unique KKT stationary point, which is a saddle point.
The full Hessian may be indefinite without this regime if all its negative directions violate the equalities.
immediate_consequences_latex: A minimization method must detect negative curvature or impose an additional bounded region.
Positive-definite reduced-system solvers are not applicable without modification.
boundary_notes: Trust-region, box-constrained, or otherwise bounded quadratic subproblems need not be unbounded despite reduced negative curvature.
A merely singular positive-semidefinite reduced Hessian belongs to the singular regime.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Direct solve of the coupled KKT matrix
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(K=\begin{bmatrix}G&A^T\\A&0\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{(n+m)\times(n+m)}\) be a nonsingular symmetric KKT matrix and let \(r\in\mathbb{R}^{n+m}\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional direct linear algebra for nonsingular symmetric saddle-point systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A direct full-KKT solve is a procedure that factors the complete coupled coefficient matrix \(K\), without first eliminating primal or multiplier variables, and obtains \(u=K^{-1}r\) by a finite sequence of factor and triangular solves. In symmetry-preserving form, \[P^TKP=LBL^T,\] where \(P\) is a permutation, \(L\) is unit lower triangular, and \(B\) is block diagonal with nonsingular \(1\times1\) and \(2\times2\) pivot blocks. The solution is defined by \[Lz=P^Tr,\qquad B\widehat z=z,\qquad L^T\bar z=\widehat z,\qquad u=P\bar z.\] The primal correction and multiplier are the corresponding blocks of \(u\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A direct full-KKT solve factors the entire coupled saddle-point matrix and obtains both the primal correction and multiplier by permutation, block-diagonal, and triangular solves. It performs no prior null-space or Schur-complement reduction.
assumptions_latex: All selected pivot blocks in \(B\) are nonsingular.
The permutation and pivoting strategy is chosen to control numerical instability and, for sparse systems, fill.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The factorization \(P^TKP=LBL^T\) and its associated substitutions return the unique full-space solution \(u=K^{-1}r\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: A general \(LU\) factorization can solve the same system but does not exploit symmetry.
Dense and sparse symmetric-indefinite factorizations are members of the direct full-KKT family.
special_cases_latex: For repeated right-hand sides with fixed \(K\), the factorization is reused and only substitutions are repeated.
When ordering preserves sparsity, direct full-KKT treatment avoids explicitly forming dense reduced matrices.
immediate_consequences_latex: The factorization returns primal and multiplier components simultaneously.
Its storage and work are governed by fill in \(L\), not solely by the nonzeros of \(K\).
boundary_notes: Ordinary Cholesky is inapplicable because a nontrivial KKT matrix is indefinite.
Singular or nearly singular systems require regularization, rank-revealing treatment, or refinement beyond this definition.

notation.meaning: Permutation, unit lower-triangular factor, and block-diagonal pivot factor.

knowledge_statements.title: Symmetric Indefinite Factorizations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pivoted symmetric factorization and solution of a nonsingular KKT system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a nonsingular symmetric KKT matrix \(K=K^T\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N}\) and \(r\in\mathbb{R}^N\), compute a symmetric-pivoted factorization \(P^TKP=LDL^T\), where \(P\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N}\) is a permutation matrix, \(L\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N}\) is unit lower triangular, and \(D\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N}\) is block diagonal with nonsingular \(1\times1\) and \(2\times2\) pivot blocks. Solve \(Ly=P^Tr\), \(Dz=y\), and \(L^Tw=z\) for \(y,z,w\in\mathbb{R}^N\), and output \(s=Pw\). In sparse problems, combine admissible numerical pivots with a fill-reducing ordering, allowing pivot tests to override the symbolic ordering when required for stability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Factor a nonsingular symmetric KKT matrix using stable one-by-one or two-by-two pivots, perform the triangular and block-diagonal solves, and undo the permutation to obtain the solution.
assumptions_latex: The pivoting procedure produces nonsingular accepted pivot blocks.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output \(s\in\mathbb{R}^N\) satisfies \(Ks=r\) in exact arithmetic.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A nonsingular symmetric KKT matrix can lack a nonzero scalar diagonal pivot.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The KKT matrix \[K=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}\] is nonsingular but both diagonal entries are zero. Symmetric elimination restricted to nonzero \(1\times1\) diagonal pivots therefore cannot begin, whereas the full matrix is a nonsingular \(2\times2\) pivot block. Nonsingularity alone consequently does not justify scalar-only symmetric pivoting.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nonsingular symmetric KKT matrix may have only zero scalar diagonal pivots, making a two-by-two pivot block necessary.
assumptions_latex: Elimination preserves symmetry and selects diagonal principal pivot blocks.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A nonsingular symmetric matrix need not admit a nonzero \(1\times1\) diagonal pivot, although it may admit a nonsingular \(2\times2\) pivot.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(K=K^T\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N}\) be a real symmetric matrix, including a symmetric KKT matrix.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dense or sparse direct factorization with symmetric permutations and one-by-one or two-by-two pivot blocks.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A symmetric indefinite factorization of \(K\) is a decomposition \[P^TKP=LBL^T,\] where \(P\) is a permutation matrix, \(L\) is unit lower triangular, and \(B\) is block diagonal with symmetric \(1\times1\) or \(2\times2\) blocks. For a nonsingular solve, every diagonal block of \(B\) is nonsingular. Symmetric pivoting selects the blocks and permutation to limit element growth and, in sparse problems, excessive fill. Because congruence preserves inertia, \(K\) and \(B\) have the same numbers of positive, negative, and zero eigenvalues; thus the factorization can both solve the KKT system and reveal its inertia.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A symmetric indefinite factorization permutes a symmetric matrix and expresses it as a unit lower-triangular factor, a block-diagonal pivot matrix with one-by-one or two-by-two blocks, and the transpose factor. Pivoting supports stability and sparsity, while the pivot blocks reveal inertia.
assumptions_latex: For a unique linear solve, \(K\) and all accepted pivot blocks are nonsingular.
The factorization uses symmetric row-and-column permutations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P^TKP=LBL^T\) is a symmetry-preserving factorization suitable for indefinite KKT matrices, and \(\operatorname{inertia}(K)=\operatorname{inertia}(B)\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: Writing \(D\) instead of \(B\) gives the common notation \(P^TKP=LDL^T\).
A \(2\times2\) pivot block represents two coupled symmetric pivots that cannot safely be treated as independent scalar pivots.
special_cases_latex: If all pivots are positive \(1\times1\) blocks, the structure reduces to an \(LDL^T\) form for a positive-definite matrix.
For KKT matrices with positive reduced curvature and \(m\) constraints, the revealed inertia is \((n,m,0)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: Linear solutions require two triangular solves and independent solves with the small blocks of \(B\).
The signs of scalar pivots and eigenvalue signs of two-by-two blocks determine inertia.
boundary_notes: A factorization without stability-oriented pivoting may suffer excessive growth.
Sparse fill depends on the permutation and pivot choices; symmetry preservation alone does not guarantee low storage.

knowledge_statements.title: Symmetric-Indefinite Factorizations for KKT Solves
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pivoted symmetric factorization and solution of a nonsingular KKT system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a nonsingular symmetric KKT matrix \(K=K^T\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N}\) and \(r\in\mathbb{R}^N\), compute a symmetric-pivoted factorization \(P^TKP=LDL^T\), where \(P\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N}\) is a permutation matrix, \(L\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N}\) is unit lower triangular, and \(D\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times N}\) is block diagonal with nonsingular \(1\times1\) and \(2\times2\) pivot blocks. Solve \(Ly=P^Tr\), \(Dz=y\), and \(L^Tw=z\) for \(y,z,w\in\mathbb{R}^N\), and output \(s=Pw\). In sparse problems, combine admissible numerical pivots with a fill-reducing ordering, allowing pivot tests to override the symbolic ordering when required for stability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Factor a nonsingular symmetric KKT matrix using stable one-by-one or two-by-two pivots, perform the triangular and block-diagonal solves, and undo the permutation to obtain the solution.
assumptions_latex: The pivoting procedure produces nonsingular accepted pivot blocks.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output \(s\in\mathbb{R}^N\) satisfies \(Ks=r\) in exact arithmetic.

children.title: Inertia-Revealing Factorizations
children.top_down_role: Factorizations serving as both linear solvers and constrained-curvature diagnostics.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction of KKT inertia from the diagonal blocks of a symmetric congruence factorization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K=K^T\) and suppose \(P^TKP=LDL^T\), where \(P\) is a permutation, \(L\) is nonsingular, and \(D=\operatorname{diag}(D_1,\ldots,D_q)\) has symmetric \(1\times1\) or \(2\times2\) blocks. Then \(\operatorname{inertia}(K)=\sum_{j=1}^q\operatorname{inertia}(D_j)\). For an equality KKT matrix with \(n\) primal variables and \(m\) independent constraints, the observed target count \((n,m,0)\) is therefore a factorization-based constrained-curvature certificate when combined with the bordered-KKT inertia identity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The signed eigenvalue counts of the pivot blocks give the KKT inertia and allow the target constrained-curvature count to be checked directly from the factorization.
assumptions_latex: For the constrained-curvature interpretation, K is an equality KKT matrix with a full-row-rank constraint block.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{inertia}(K)=\sum_j\operatorname{inertia}(D_j)\), so the target count \((n,m,0)\) is directly testable from the pivot blocks.

notation.meaning: positive, negative, and zero eigenvalue counts of a symmetric matrix

Inertia-Revealing Factorizations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: KKT-factor inertia as a certificate of curvature on the equality tangent space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\) have full row rank, let \(Z\) span \(\ker A\), and set \(K=\begin{pmatrix}H&A^T\\A&0\end{pmatrix}\) with \(H=H^T\). If a symmetric factorization \(P^TKP=LDL^T\) is computed with nonsingular \(L\), then \(\operatorname{inertia}(K)=\operatorname{inertia}(D)\). Moreover, \(\operatorname{inertia}(K)=\operatorname{inertia}(Z^THZ)+(m,m,0)\). Thus the signed eigenvalue counts obtained from the \(1\times1\) and \(2\times2\) blocks of \(D\) certify positive reduced curvature exactly when \(\operatorname{inertia}(K)=(n,m,0)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The pivot-block signs reveal KKT inertia, which in turn certifies positive definiteness of the Hessian on the equality-constraint null space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Z^THZ\succ0\) if and only if \(\operatorname{inertia}(D)=(n,m,0)\).

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(K\in\mathbb R^{N\times N}\) be symmetric, including the KKT case \(K=\begin{pmatrix}G&A^T\\A&0\end{pmatrix}\). The inertia is \(\operatorname{inertia}(K)=(n_+(K),n_-(K),n_0(K))\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional real symmetric matrices; exact factorization identities are stated, while pivot selection and computed stability belong to numerical implementations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An inertia-revealing factorization of \(K\) is a symmetric-indefinite factorization \[P^TKP=LBL^T,\] where \(P\) is a permutation matrix, \(L\) is nonsingular unit lower triangular, and \(B=\operatorname{diag}(B_1,\ldots,B_s)\) has nonsingular symmetric blocks \(B_i\) of order one or two, such that the inertia is obtained from the pivot blocks: \[\operatorname{inertia}(K)=\sum_{i=1}^s\operatorname{inertia}(B_i).\] If zero or singular pivots are retained to represent a singular matrix, the same formula includes their zero eigenvalues. For a full-row-rank constraint matrix \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\) and any null-space basis \(Z\) satisfying \(AZ=0\), the KKT factorization is inertia-revealing for constrained curvature because \[\operatorname{inertia}(K)=\operatorname{inertia}(Z^TGZ)+(m,m,0).\] Thus the factors simultaneously define triangular/block-diagonal solves and expose the sign pattern of the quadratic form on feasible directions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An inertia-revealing factorization represents a real symmetric matrix as \(P^TKP=LBL^T\), with a permutation \(P\), a nonsingular unit lower-triangular factor \(L\), and one-by-one or two-by-two symmetric pivot blocks in \(B\). Congruence preserves inertia, so the positive, negative, and zero eigenvalue counts of \(K\) are the sums of those counts over the blocks of \(B\). For a full-rank equality KKT matrix, this also diagnoses constrained curvature through \(\operatorname{inertia}(K)=\operatorname{inertia}(Z^TGZ)+(m,m,0)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P^TKP=LBL^T\) is inertia-revealing precisely through \(\operatorname{inertia}(K)=\sum_i\operatorname{inertia}(B_i)\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: By Sylvester's law of inertia, \(K\), \(P^TKP\), and \(B\) have identical inertia because the transformations are nonsingular congruences.
special_cases_latex: If \(Z^TGZ\succ0\), then the full-row-rank KKT matrix has \(\operatorname{inertia}(K)=(n,m,0)\).
immediate_consequences_latex: The signs of the scalar pivots and the two eigenvalues of every \(2\times2\) pivot determine whether the constrained quadratic model has positive, negative, or zero reduced curvature.
boundary_notes: A factorization that merely solves \(Kz=r\) but does not preserve symmetric congruence need not reveal inertia.
Near-zero computed pivots require a numerical tolerance; the exact definition itself does not prescribe that tolerance.

notation.meaning: Any full-column-rank basis matrix for \(\ker A\).

children.title: Regularized KKT Factorizations
children.top_down_role: Modified coupled systems for weak curvature, near rank deficiency, or unstable pivots.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact perturbation identity distinguishing a shifted solve from a solution of the original KKT equations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K_0=\begin{pmatrix}H&A^T\\A&0\end{pmatrix}\), \(K_{\delta,\gamma}=\begin{pmatrix}H+\delta I&A^T\\A&-\gamma I\end{pmatrix}\), and suppose \(K_{\delta,\gamma}(p,\lambda)^T=(r,s)^T\). Then the residual of the same pair in the original system is \[K_0\begin{pmatrix}p\\\lambda\end{pmatrix}-\begin{pmatrix}r\\s\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}-\delta p\\\gamma\lambda\end{pmatrix}.\] Thus regularized and original residuals must be distinguished whenever either shift is nonzero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The original KKT residual of an exact shifted-system solution is determined explicitly by the primal and dual regularization terms.
assumptions_latex: The stated sign convention is used for the primal and dual shifts.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The original-system residual equals \((-\delta p,\gamma\lambda)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Original-System Residual after KKT Regularization

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A sufficient nonsingularity and inertia condition for primal-dual diagonal regularization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B=B^T\succ0\), let \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), and let \(\gamma>0\). Then \[K_\gamma=\begin{pmatrix}B&A^T\\A&-\gamma I\end{pmatrix}\] is nonsingular and has inertia \((n,m,0)\), without requiring \(A\) to have full row rank. In particular, this applies with \(B=H+\delta I\) whenever the primal shift makes \(H+\delta I\) positive definite.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive-definite primal block together with a strictly negative dual shift produces a nonsingular quasi-definite KKT matrix with the target inertia, even for rank-deficient constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K_\gamma\) is nonsingular and \(\operatorname{inertia}(K_\gamma)=(n,m,0)\).
knowledge_statements.title: Quasi-Definite Regularized KKT Matrix
Regularized KKT Factorizations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal-dual regularization of weak or numerically unstable KKT systems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a symmetric KKT equation with blocks \(H\) and \(A\), choose regularization parameters \(\delta\ge0\) and \(\gamma\ge0\) and solve \[\begin{pmatrix}H+\delta I&A^T\\A&-\gamma I\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}p\\\lambda\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}r\\s\end{pmatrix}.\] Factor the modified matrix by a symmetric pivoted factorization and accept the result only when its pivots and residual meet prescribed numerical tests. Primal regularization shifts curvature, while dual regularization removes exact enforcement of the second block equation when \(\gamma>0\); consequently, the computed pair solves the regularized system, not generally the original KKT equations. Setting \(\delta=\gamma=0\) recovers the unregularized representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Diagonal primal-dual shifts can stabilize KKT factorization, but nonzero shifts change the system and therefore require residual and perturbation interpretation.
assumptions_latex: The regularized block matrix is nonsingular.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed system defines a symmetric regularized KKT representation, reducing to the original representation when \(\delta=\gamma=0\).

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(G=G^T\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\), \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), and let \(R_p\succeq0\), \(R_d\succeq0\) be prescribed regularization matrices.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional symmetric equality KKT systems with primal and dual diagonal or structured shifts; the definition concerns the modified system rather than its approximation error relative to the unregularized solution.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A regularized KKT matrix is \[K_{\delta,\gamma}=\begin{pmatrix}G+\delta R_p&A^T\\A&-\gamma R_d\end{pmatrix},\qquad \delta,\gamma\ge0,\] and a regularized KKT factorization is a symmetric-indefinite factorization \[P^TK_{\delta,\gamma}P=LBL^T\] used to solve the correspondingly modified coupled equations. The primal shift \(\delta R_p\) modifies weak or indefinite curvature, while the negative dual shift \(-\gamma R_d\) removes singularity associated with deficient or nearly deficient constraints. The parameters are admissible when \(K_{\delta,\gamma}\) is nonsingular and has the inertia required by the intended constrained model. In the common scalar-shift case \(R_p=I_n\), \(R_d=I_m\), one seeks \(\delta,\gamma\) for which the factorization has no zero pivots and, when positive reduced curvature is required, inertia \((n,m,0)\). The factorization is therefore defined by both the perturbed block matrix and a stable symmetric factorization of that matrix; factoring the unmodified \(K_{0,0}\) is not a regularized factorization unless both parameters are zero by an explicit successful test.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A regularized KKT factorization factors the shifted saddle-point matrix \(K_{\delta,\gamma}=\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix}G+\delta R_p&A^T\\A&-\gamma R_d\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)\). The primal shift controls deficient or unwanted curvature, and the dual shift protects against singular or nearly dependent constraints. The parameters are chosen so that the modified matrix is nonsingular and, when required, has the target inertia. A permutation-based symmetric-indefinite factorization then supplies the linear solve.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A regularized KKT factorization is the pair consisting of an admissibly shifted matrix \(K_{\delta,\gamma}\) and a symmetric factorization \(P^TK_{\delta,\gamma}P=LBL^T\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: With \(R_p=I_n\) and \(R_d=I_m\), regularization is the two-sided diagonal modification \(G\mapsto G+\delta I_n\) and \(0\mapsto-\gamma I_m\).
special_cases_latex: If \(A\) has full row rank and \(G\) already has positive-definite reduced Hessian, \(\delta=\gamma=0\) may pass the nonsingularity and inertia tests.
immediate_consequences_latex: A positive \(\gamma\) makes the dual diagonal block nonsingular and can regularize rank-deficient constraint Jacobians.
Increasing \(\delta\) shifts primal curvature toward the desired positive reduced-curvature regime.
boundary_notes: The solution of the regularized equations generally differs from the solution of the original KKT equations.
The definition does not prescribe universal parameter magnitudes; scaling and acceptable perturbation are problem dependent.

notation.meaning: Nonnegative dual or constraint regularization parameter.

children.title: Range-Space Schur-Complement Solves
children.top_down_role: Constraint-space elimination methods centered on multiplier systems.

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Consider \(Gx+A^T\lambda=r\), \(Ax=s\), with \(G=G^T\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\), \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), and \(G\) nonsingular.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional equality systems in which the primal block can be solved and the constraint-space Schur complement is nonsingular.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A range-space Schur-complement solve eliminates the primal variable and solves first in multiplier space. Define \[S:=AG^{-1}A^T.\] From \(x=G^{-1}(r-A^T\lambda)\), the multiplier is determined by \[S\lambda=AG^{-1}r-s,\] after which the primal variable is recovered from \[Gx=r-A^T\lambda.\] The method is well defined when \(G\) and \(S\) are nonsingular. If \(G\succ0\) and \(A\) has full row rank, then \(S\succ0\). It is called a range-space method because \(A^T\lambda\in\operatorname{range}(A^T)\), and its principal reduced equation has dimension \(m\), the dimension of the constraint or multiplier space. Formation of \(S\) is not part of the general definition: its action may be formed explicitly, applied through solves with \(G\), or evaluated through a structured elimination that is algebraically identical.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A range-space Schur-complement solve eliminates \(x\) from the coupled KKT equations. It solves \((AG^{-1}A^T)\lambda=AG^{-1}r-s\) in multiplier space and then recovers \(x\) from \(Gx=r-A^T\lambda\). It requires nonsingular primal and Schur blocks; positive-definite \(G\) and full-row-rank \(A\) guarantee that the Schur complement is positive definite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The coupled system is reduced to the constraint-space equation \(S\lambda=AG^{-1}r-s\), followed by one primal recovery solve.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Block elimination transforms the KKT coefficient matrix to \(\begin{pmatrix}G&A^T\\0&-S\end{pmatrix}\).
special_cases_latex: When \(G\) is diagonal or block diagonal, applications of \(G^{-1}\) and construction of \(S\) may be inexpensive.
immediate_consequences_latex: The reduced system has order \(m\), so the approach is especially attractive when \(m\ll n\).
boundary_notes: If \(G\) is singular, this definition does not apply without generalized inverses, regularization, or a different pivot block.
Explicit formation may square conditioning effects and is distinct from implicit Schur action.

knowledge_statements.title: Formed Schur-Complement Solves
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit range-space elimination for a KKT system with invertible primal block.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H=H^T\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times n}\), \(A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\), \(r\in\mathbb{R}^n\), and \(s\in\mathbb{R}^m\). For the equations \(Hu+A^T\lambda=r\) and \(Au=s\), with \(u\in\mathbb{R}^n\), \(\lambda\in\mathbb{R}^m\), and nonsingular \(H\), explicitly form \(S=AH^{-1}A^T\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times m}\) by solving with \(H\) for the columns of \(A^T\). Form \(h=AH^{-1}r-s\), solve \(S\lambda=h\), and recover \(u=H^{-1}(r-A^T\lambda)\). If \(H\succ0\) and \(A\) has rank \(m\), then \(S\succ0\). Accept a computed solution only after checking residuals of both original block equations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Explicitly form the constraint-space Schur complement using primal solves, solve for the multiplier, recover the primal variable, and check both original block residuals.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output \((u,\lambda)\in\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}^m\) solves the original two-block system in exact arithmetic.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Original-Residual Certificate from a Formed Schur Residual
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact transfer of the multiplier residual to the two original KKT block residuals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(S=AH^{-1}A^T\), \(h=AH^{-1}r-s\), an approximation \(\widehat\lambda\), and \(\widehat u=H^{-1}(r-A^T\widehat\lambda)\), \[H\widehat u+A^T\widehat\lambda-r=0,\qquad A\widehat u-s=h-S\widehat\lambda.\] Thus exact recovery makes the primal-block residual zero and the constraint residual equal to the negative Schur-equation residual.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With exact primal recovery, the first KKT residual vanishes and the second is exactly the negative formed-Schur residual.
assumptions_latex: Formation and recovery use exact applications of \(H^{-1}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: r_H=0,\qquad r_A=-(S\widehat\lambda-h).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dense Cost of Explicit Schur Formation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Arithmetic and storage costs for materializing and factoring a dense constraint-space Schur complement.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose factors of \(H\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) are available and one solve costs \(T_H\). Computing \(W=H^{-1}A^T\) requires \(m\) solves, forming \(S=AW\) costs \(O(nm^2)\), and storing \(S\) costs \(O(m^2)\). Dense Cholesky factorization of \(S\succ0\) costs \(O(m^3)\). The post-factorization setup work is therefore \[O(mT_H+nm^2+m^3),\] and retaining \(W\) additionally costs \(O(nm)\) storage.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Explicit formation uses one primal solve per constraint column, quadratic Schur storage, and cubic dense Schur factorization.
assumptions_latex: The Schur complement is treated as dense.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname{work}=O(mT_H+nm^2+m^3),\qquad \operatorname{storage}(S)=O(m^2).

notation.meaning: Cost of one solve with the available H factors.

knowledge_statements.title: Dense Cost of Explicit Schur Formation

knowledge_statements.slot_contract: State the canonical mathematical definition of the source node, with its domain, quantifiers, notation, and a precise source locator.
knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(G\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) be nonsingular, \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), and \(S=AG^{-1}A^T\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Direct constraint-space solution in which the entries or complete columns of the Schur complement are materialized before its factorization.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A formed Schur-complement solve is a range-space solve for which the matrix \(S=AG^{-1}A^T\in\mathbb R^{m\times m}\) is explicitly assembled. Equivalently, for columns \(a_j=A^Te_j\), one computes \(w_j\) from \(Gw_j=a_j\) and stores \(S_{ij}=a_i^Tw_j\) for all required indices. One then computes a direct factorization of \(S\), solves \[S\lambda=AG^{-1}r-s,\] and recovers \(x\) from \(Gx=r-A^T\lambda\). If \(G\succ0\) and \(A\) has full row rank, \(S\succ0\) and a Cholesky factorization is admissible. The defining distinction is that \(S\) exists as a stored matrix before the reduced solve; merely evaluating products \(Sv\) through primal solves is an implicit Schur-complement method instead.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A formed Schur-complement solve explicitly assembles \(S=AG^{-1}A^T\), factors that stored matrix, solves the multiplier equation, and back-solves for the primal variable. Its distinguishing property is materialization of the constraint-space operator, not merely algebraic use of the Schur identity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The stored operator \(S\) is directly factored and used for the multiplier solve before primal recovery.
equivalent_formulations_latex: Explicit formation by columns is \(Gw_j=A^Te_j\) and \(Se_j=Aw_j\) for \(j=1,\ldots,m\).
special_cases_latex: For diagonal \(G\), formation reduces to weighted constraint products.
For \(G\succ0\) and full-row-rank \(A\), \(S\) admits a Cholesky factorization.
immediate_consequences_latex: The factors of \(S\) can be reused for multiple right-hand sides while \(G\) and \(A\) remain fixed.
boundary_notes: The matrix \(S\) may be denser than \(A\) and \(G\).
If only \(Sv\) is available, the method is not a formed Schur-complement solve.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(H\succ0\), \(A\) has full row rank, and the action with \(H^{-1}\) is exact and fixed, CG applied to \(S\lambda=h\) satisfies \[\|e_k\|_S\le2\left(\frac{\sqrt{\kappa(S)}-1}{\sqrt{\kappa(S)}+1}\right)^k\|e_0\|_S.\] Each iteration uses one multiplication by \(A^T\), one solve with \(H\), one multiplication by \(A\), and constraint-space vector operations, without storing an \(m\times m\) Schur matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: CG has its standard SPD bound, with one primal solve and two Jacobian products per iteration and no explicit Schur storage.
assumptions_latex: The inverse action is exact and fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \|e_k\|_S\le2\left(\frac{\sqrt{\kappa(S)}-1}{\sqrt{\kappa(S)}+1}\right)^k\|e_0\|_S.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Variable Inner Solves Break Fixed-Operator Krylov Assumptions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between a fixed symmetric Schur action and iteration-dependent approximate primal solves.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If the primal inverse is replaced at iteration \(k\) by \(B_k\), the action is \(v\mapsto AB_kA^Tv\). A single fixed symmetric positive-definite linear map \(B_k=B\) yields a fixed SPD action when \(A\) has full row rank. If \(B_k\) varies, is nonlinear in its right-hand side, or is nonsymmetric, the actions need not represent one fixed self-adjoint operator; ordinary CG or MINRES guarantees then require replacement by an appropriate inexact or flexible framework with controlled inner errors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Variable, nonlinear, or nonsymmetric inner solves can invalidate ordinary fixed-operator CG or MINRES theory.
assumptions_latex: Exact primal solves are replaced by approximate maps \(B_k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{Fixed SPD }B\text{ preserves ordinary SPD Krylov compatibility; incompatible }B_k\text{ need flexible or inexact treatment}.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Symmetry and Definiteness of the Exact Implicit Action
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operator properties preserved by exact primal solves.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The action \(\mathcal S(v)=AH^{-1}A^Tv\) is self-adjoint when \(H=H^T\) is nonsingular. If \(H\succ0\) and \(A\) has full row rank, then \[v^T\mathcal S(v)=(A^Tv)^TH^{-1}(A^Tv)>0\qquad(v\ne0),\] so \(\mathcal S\succ0\) without explicit matrix formation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact implicit Schur actions preserve symmetry and are positive definite under positive primal curvature and independent constraint rows.
assumptions_latex: For positive definiteness, \(H\succ0\) and \(A\) has full row rank.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \mathcal S=\mathcal S^T,\qquad H\succ0\text{ and }\operatorname{rank}(A)=m\Rightarrow\mathcal S\succ0.

Implicit Schur-Complement Actions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Matrix-free application and iterative solution of the constraint-space Schur equation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the block equations \(Hu+A^T\lambda=r\) and \(Au=s\), define the Schur action without forming its matrix: given \(v\), solve \(Hz=A^Tv\) and return \(Sv=Az\). Compute \(h=AH^{-1}r-s\), apply a compatible iterative linear solver to \(S\lambda=h\) using this action and a declared preconditioner, and stop when the Schur residual satisfies the prescribed tolerance. Recover \(u=H^{-1}(r-A^T\lambda)\), then output \((u,\lambda)\) together with residuals for both original block equations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Apply the Schur complement through repeated primal solves, iteratively determine the multiplier, recover the primal variable, and verify the original block residuals.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is nonsingular and available through sufficiently accurate linear solves.
The iterative solver is appropriate for the symmetry and definiteness of \(S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exact inner and outer solves produce the KKT solution; inexact solves return a residual-qualified approximation.

knowledge_statements.ambient_context_latex: Let \(G\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\) be nonsingular, \(A\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), and \(S=AG^{-1}A^T\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Matrix-free or operator-based application of the constraint-space Schur complement; each exact action uses a primal solve.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An implicit Schur-complement action is the linear map \[v\longmapsto Sv:=A\bigl(G^{-1}(A^Tv)\bigr),\qquad v\in\mathbb R^m,\] evaluated without assembling the entries of \(S\). Operationally, it is defined by the three exact relations \[q=A^Tv,\qquad Gw=q,\qquad Sv=Aw.\] An implicit Schur-complement solve applies a constraint-space iterative method to \[S\lambda=AG^{-1}r-s\] using only such actions, and then recovers \(x\) from \(Gx=r-A^T\lambda\). If the inner solve for \(w\) is approximate, the implemented action is \(\widetilde S_kv=A\widetilde w_k\) with residual \(A^Tv-G\widetilde w_k\); this is an inexact or variable Schur action rather than the exact map \(S\). The defining feature is that no stored \(m\times m\) Schur matrix is required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An implicit Schur-complement action computes \(Sv\) as \(A(G^{-1}(A^Tv))\): multiply by \(A^T\), solve once with \(G\), and multiply by \(A\). A multiplier-space iterative solver can therefore use the Schur complement without explicitly forming it.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every \(v\in\mathbb R^m\), the implicit action returns \(Sv=Aw\), where \(Gw=A^Tv\).
equivalent_formulations_latex: The map is the composition \(S=A\circ G^{-1}\circ A^T\).
special_cases_latex: If a factorization of \(G\) is available, each action requires two sparse matrix-vector products and two triangular solves.
immediate_consequences_latex: The storage of a potentially dense explicit \(S\) is avoided.
Any Krylov method for the multiplier equation can access \(S\) through this operator interface.
boundary_notes: An inner iterative solve whose accuracy changes with the outer iteration produces a variable operator and may require a flexible outer method.
Nonsingularity of \(G\) alone does not guarantee nonsingularity or definiteness of \(S\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Variable Inner Solves Can Destroy Krylov Compatibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary between a fixed symmetric implicit operator and iteration-dependent approximate primal solves.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Replace the exact primal solve by maps \(B_k\) and apply \(v\mapsto AB_kA^Tv\) at outer iteration \(k\). If every \(B_k\) equals one fixed symmetric positive-definite linear operator \(B\), then \(ABA^T\) is a fixed SPD operator when \(A\) has full row rank. If \(B_k\) varies with \(k\), depends nonlinearly on its right-hand side, or is nonsymmetric, the resulting actions need not define one fixed self-adjoint operator. Standard CG and MINRES recurrences and their usual convergence guarantees then do not apply without an inexact or flexible Krylov framework and explicit inner-error control.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Iteration-dependent, nonlinear, or nonsymmetric inner solves can make the apparent Schur action variable or nonsymmetric, invalidating ordinary CG or MINRES guarantees.
assumptions_latex: The exact solve with \(H\) is replaced by approximate maps \(B_k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A fixed SPD surrogate action is sufficient for ordinary SPD Krylov theory; variable or incompatible actions require flexible or inexact methods.
